Round 406 (the evasion divisors censused: a measurement that covered two of six
sites was cited for all six): ROUND 405 SETTLED WHICH PARTY EVADES; THIS ROUND
ASKED WHAT THAT COSTS SRREVAMP, AND THE ANSWER WAS A JUSTIFICATION DOING MORE
WORK THAN IT COULD CARRY. Three shipped comments and two tracker paragraphs all
said the critical and block rolls are "unopposed, and that is measured rather
than assumed", citing `GObjMob_PublishStats`: it publishes params 0, 3-12, 23,
24, 27-33 and 140, so a monster has neither 56 (`'evbl'`) nor 57 (`'evcr'`).
True, and it covers exactly TWO of the six divisors srrevamp needs. Because the
divisor is the OPPONENT's evasion -- round 405's rule, `my stat / (1 + my
opponent's evasion of it)` -- the evader alternates with the roll, and the
census is: player->monster crit faces the MONSTER's `'evcr'` (grounded), but
player->monster block faces the PLAYER's `'evbl'`; monster->player block faces
the MONSTER's `'evbl'` (grounded), but monster->player crit faces the PLAYER's
`'evcr'`; and BOTH duel divisors face a player, so `duel.go` was never covered
at all. Four of six cited a measurement about the wrong party. This matters
because monsters really do roll these: characterdata col 78 reads 2 on 7,493 of
7,495 monster rows and col 76 reads 20 on 938 of them.

ALL SIX ARE STILL ZERO, so nothing shipped changes -- but the four uncovered
ones are zero for a weaker reason: srrevamp aggregates no magic options, so no
player can carry `'evcr'` or `'evbl'`. FOUR PROBES WITH DIFFERENT FAILURE MODES,
because an absence is a claim about the probe first: the `TagEvadeCri`/
`TagEvadeBlk` constants have no consumer outside the vocabulary table; the raw
strings `"evcr"`/`"evbl"` appear only in a `PackTag` unit test; no function
anywhere turns an item's magic options into combat stats; and the client never
mentions either. That is a DISCLOSURE, not a grounding, and the difference is
the whole finding.

WHAT MOVED: `combat.EvadedChance(chance, evadePercent)` now implements the
recovered divisor, and all six call sites pass through it with the evader named

`TestNoPlayerEvasionSourceExists` is the tripwire on the precondition: it walks

Round 405 (two recorded claims disagreed about block evasion; the disassembly
settles it and the shipped code was right): GROUNDING_AUDIT's last live combat

Line 950 records block as the DEFENDER's 'bri' opposed by the ATTACKER's 'evbl'.
Line 1523 records it as "attacker block / (1 + defender 'evbl')" -- opposite on
BOTH halves. The shipped comment in internal/session/combat.go follows line 950,
and its reasoning depends on it: block is left unopposed because a monster never
publishes param 56, which only matters if the divisor is the ATTACKER's.

NEITHER AUTHOR COULD HAVE READ IT FROM THE C. Ghidra renders the evbl call as
`(**(code **)(*unaff_retaddr + 0x104))(0x38)` -- unaff_retaddr being its
placeholder for an operand it cannot resolve at all. The two records are two
different guesses at the same unresolved object, which is exactly how a file
comes to contradict itself.

THE DISASSEMBLY SETTLES IT. The call issues on [esp+0x124], and the prologue --
`sub esp,0x110` plus four pushes, 0x120 of displacement -- makes that ARGUMENT 1.
param_1 is the ATTACKER, established independently in round 387 as the object
required to be a PC in the ignore-defence guard. evcr's call issues on piVar12,
the defender. So line 950 is right about evbl and line 1523 is right about evcr:
EACH RECORD IS HALF CORRECT.

AND THE ASYMMETRY IS THE WHOLE POINT. One rule covers both: my stat divided by
(1 + my opponent's evasion of it). Crit is the ATTACKER's stat so the defender
evades it; block is the DEFENDER's stat so the ATTACKER evades it. Writing both
as "attacker ... / defender ..." flattens that into a symmetry -- which is how
the wrong line was written, and it is a failure mode worth naming: prose tidies
an asymmetry that the code does not have.

**What moved:** a self-contradiction in this file resolved from the instruction
stream rather than by preferring the newer entry, the wrong half corrected where
it was written, and the shipped behaviour confirmed correct for a reason that
was measured rather than lucky. No behaviour changed, so no tag.

Round 404 (the vararg-reuse trick is not a one-off: 41 % of call sites use it):
ROUNDS 402-403 EXPLAINED ONE CALL SITE. Understanding the shape made the whole
population cheap: every procedure call goes through FUN_00425f70, the format is
the last push, and THE CALL'S OWN `add esp,N` GIVES THE TRUE VARARG COUNT as
N/4 - 1. Censused, that is 78 sites, written to docs/protocol/procedure_calls.txt
with conversions, true varargs and fresh pushes for each.

THE HEADLINE IS THE THIRD COLUMN. Where fresh pushes < varargs, the call reuses
the preceding call's UNCLEANED arguments -- and that happens at 32 OF 78 SITES,
41 %. So reading a procedure's arguments off the decompiled C is wrong at TWO
SITES IN FIVE, because Ghidra renders only the fresh pushes. Round 401 hit this
and filed it as a decompiler defect; it is a compiler idiom and it is everywhere.

THE FIRST VERSION OF THE CENSUS WAS WRONG AND THE MISMATCH RATE GAVE IT AWAY. I
counted only "%d" in each format, which made most rows look mismatched -- and one
row, `{?=CALL %s`, reported one conversion for a format whose conversions are
mostly %s and %I64d. A suspiciously high anomaly rate is a fact about the probe
first. Counting all conversion specifiers fixed it.

THE CONTROLS ARE THE THREE SITES READ BY HAND, and they reproduce exactly:
_STRG_MOVE_ITEM at 0x45b701 (8 conversions, 8 varargs, 4 fresh), _STRG_SPLIT_ITEM
at 0x45b806 (7, 7, 7 and no reuse), _STRG_SWAP_ITEM at 0x45b8ac (8, 8, 4). A
census that reproduces every case already known by hand is worth trusting about
the rest.

NOT PROMOTED: 34 rows still show conversions != varargs, and the fresh-push
column is approximate because the walk stops at the previous call and can
overcount. Those rows mark where the heuristics are imprecise, not findings, and
the caveat sits in the file's own header rather than in a later correction.

**What moved:** a one-site observation generalised into a measured property of
the binary with its controls, an 78-row artifact filed where the next reader will
need it, and a standing warning that the decompiled C mis-renders procedure
arguments at 41 % of sites. No behaviour changed, so no tag.

Round 403 (all four procedures numbered, and rounds 401-402 misread which call
was which): THE NEXT STEP WAS THE SWAP BRANCH'S DIRECT CALL. Reading the literal

which is "{CALL _STRG_SPLIT_ITEM (?, ?, %d, ...)}", NOT SWAP. Rounds 401 and 402
both called it the swap call. The real swap call is 0x45b8ac, pushing 0x00ae4ee4.

READING THE STRING FROM THE BINARY IS WHAT CAUGHT IT. Both earlier rounds took
the procedure name from the decompiled C, where the branch structure made the
attribution look obvious; the .rdata literal at the pushed address settles which
format belongs to which call and disagreed.

AND THE SLOTS ARE SINGLE BYTES. At the split call they are
`movzx ecx, BYTE PTR [edi+0x3]` and `movzx eax, BYTE PTR [edi+0x4]`, which Ghidra
rendered as param_1[3]/param_1[4] -- an int-indexed array in the C, two adjacent
BYTES in the instruction stream. Round 401's conclusion survives; its picture of
the operand did not.

ALL FOUR OF THIS FUNCTION'S PROCEDURES ARE NOW NUMBERED: MOVE and MERGE args 5/6
at the shared site, SPLIT args 6/7 at 0x45b806, SWAP args 5/6 at 0x45b8ac -- and
SWAP PASSES THE TWO SLOTS IN THE OPPOSITE ORDER, BYTE[edi+4] then BYTE[edi+3],
which is what an operation that exchanges two slots should do.

THE SWAP CALL ALSO PROVES THE VARARG-REUSE MECHANISM A SECOND TIME, and this
time the proof is the stack cleanup rather than an inference: `add esp,0x24` pops
NINE slots -- format plus eight varargs -- while only four values and the format
are pushed fresh. The other four are FUN_004ea580's uncleaned arguments. Round
402 deduced that mechanism; here the compiler's own cleanup arithmetic confirms
it.

**What moved:** four procedures' slot arguments numbered from the instruction
stream, a two-round misattribution corrected by reading the binary's own string
table, the slot operand's real width established, and round 402's mechanism
independently confirmed. No behaviour changed, so no tag.

Round 402 (four varargs for eight %d: the compiler reuses a dead call's
arguments, and round 285 is re-derived): ROUND 401 CALLED THE SHARED CALL SITE A
DECOMPILER ARTIFACT and said disassembly was needed. The disassembly shows GHIDRA
WAS EXACTLY RIGHT -- four varargs really are pushed for a format with eight %d --
and the explanation is a compiler trick, not a defect.

FUN_00425f70 IS A REAL vsnprintf_s WRAPPER: it calls __vsnprintf_s(buf, size,
count, format, &stack0x00000008), so the varargs are read straight off the stack
after the format. AND THE PRECEDING CALL'S FOUR ARGUMENTS ARE NEVER CLEANED OFF.
FUN_004ea580(param_1[3], param_1[4], local_c3c, iVar6) pushes them at
45b6d3-45b6d6, the call returns, four more values and the format are pushed, and
the formatter walks straight past the fresh four into the dead ones. Varargs 5-8
are that dead call's arguments.

SO VARARGS 5 AND 6 ARE param_1[3] AND param_1[4] -- EXACTLY THE TWO VALUES
RESOLVED THROUGH CGStorage::GetItem at the top of the function. _STRG_MOVE_ITEM
args 5/6 are storage slots, WHICH IS PRECISELY WHAT ROUND 285 RECORDED, now
re-derived from the disassembly by an entirely different route. A recorded fact
confirmed rather than a new one claimed -- and worth more than a new one, given
how many recorded facts this session has had to withdraw. _STRG_MERGE_ITEM
reaches the same site through the same goto after the same call with the same
eight-%d format, so its args 5/6 are the same slots.

WHAT IS KNOWN IS ITS SHAPE, WHICH IS NOT ITS NAME. The handler is a
change-tracking writer: for a record reached through member+0x3c it compares live
against stored field by field -- +0x38 as a short, then +0x3c, +0x40, +0x44 --
and on a difference writes it back and touches a dirty mask at +0xc. That is
"update only the columns that changed", and it is worth recording because it says
what the scope DOES without pretending to say what it IS.

ONE NEW FACT FITS THE PATTERN: the member's constructor is 0x484290, called from
CGObjPC::Create, 0x70 before the handler -- round 394's ctor/saver co-location
holding a fifth time, which is what puts both in GObj.cpp's neighbourhood without
proving they are in its translation unit.

is a full one -- the mask exists so other callers can request PARTIAL saves,
which is what makes this a scope vocabulary rather than a parameter list.

**What moved:** a wrong row retracted with its mechanism, the join's unverified

Round 387 (the mitigation-skipping flag: no attack sets it, and the question was
mis-shaped): THE OPEN ITEM ASKED "which attacks set descriptor flag 0x20". The
answer is that NONE DOES -- it is not a property of an attack at all.

THE DESCRIPTOR IS ASSEMBLED PER SWING, not read off a skill. Combat_ResolveDamage
builds a byte at +6 of the attack record: = 1 or = 2 for the damage class, |= 4
or |= 8 for physical/magical -- the same vocabulary combat.AttackType already
models -- plus |= 0x10 and |= 0x20. It reaches both mitigation formulas in CL,
their __fastcall first argument, which the decompiled C cannot show. objdump
does: `mov cl, BYTE PTR [ebp+0x6]` immediately before each call, at two of the
eight sites.

AN EARLIER GUESS OF MINE WAS WRONG AND IS NOT REPEATED: I had taken +0x230 for a
flags word. It is the skill's `att` field. The descriptor is a different byte,
derived from the same vocabulary.

0x20 IS A PER-SWING PROC OFF AN ATTACKER STAT, disassembled at 0x0058edf9 rather
than inferred from adjacency -- which mattered, because Ghidra drops RollChance's
arguments and the chain GetParam(188) -> RollChance -> set-the-flag was
adjacency-only until the disassembly showed the float conversion and the
accumulator pointer between them. The guard is: defender NOT a PC, attacker IS a
PC. So it is an ignore-defence chance a player rolls against a monster, never
against another player.

AND A TENSION LEFT STANDING RATHER THAN EXPLAINED AWAY. Param 188 is a 0-100
percentage defaulting to 0, with exactly one writer (the skill-effect applier).
skill_params.md records the code `dtt` writing it, and `dtt` occurs on 13 real
rows, ALL NAMED SKILL_ETC_DETECT_*. Whether a "detect" skill really grants an
ignore-defence chance is NOT READ. The association is recorded; the mismatch
between the code's name and the param's use is left open rather than smoothed
over with a plausible story.

**What moved:** an open item closed by showing the question was mis-shaped, the
flag's full setter disassembled rather than inferred, one of my own earlier
guesses withdrawn, and a name/use mismatch recorded as open. For srrevamp the
feature is unreachable rather than unimplemented: the param defaults to 0 and no

Round 386 (the 172 counterexamples were the confirmation, and it still does not
license a rename): ROUND 385 NAMED THE PROBE -- read the 172 class-B rows whose
names carry SWORD or SPEAR, the counterexamples blocking a melee/ranged reading.
They are all SKILL_CH_SWORD_GEOMGI_*, real player skills, mask 6.

THE NAME WAS NOT USED TO JUDGE THEM. Reasoning from what "GEOMGI" means would
have been the outside-knowledge trap this project has recorded before. Instead an
INDEPENDENT COLUMN settles it: skilldata col 21 is Range, and it separates the
two classes of sword/spear player skills with ZERO OVERLAP --

	sword/spear class A   n = 1194   range min 0,   max 0
	sword/spear class B   n =  172   range min 120, max 160

The groups were formed by the `att` mask, not by range, so this is a measurement
on a column that had no part in defining them. The 172 counterexamples turn out
to be the strongest evidence FOR the reading: they are sword skills that strike
at 120-160.

AND THE CONCLUSION IS NOT THE ONE I EXPECTED TO DRAW. Settling the correlation
does NOT license renaming AttackClassA/B to Melee/Ranged, because what the ENGINE
does with the bits is pick the defender's flat-absorption param, 130 or 131 --
nothing range-related. Melee-versus-ranged is a CONTENT-AUTHORING CONVENTION that
aligns with the damage class, not the meaning of the bits. A name like
AttackMelee would record the correlation and hide the mechanism, which is the
opposite of what a recovered name is for.

So the constants stay positional, the measurement sits beside them in
attacktype.go, and the distinction between "what the bit selects" and "what

data position, which is why its counts disagree with the verified ones (efr
10,627 against 9,534; getv 4,050 against 2,553).

a four-character pack is a specific value near 1.6-1.9 billion), absence from the
server dump, and absence from a parser-table built with no reference to either.

unpacks gives 138 distinct codes, and 129 OF THEM ARE ALREADY DOCUMENTED IN THIS
PROJECT -- 93.5 %. That overlap is the control: a method that reproduces 129 known
codes is worth trusting about the other 9.

alcu occur in real skill rows (36, 23, 18, 8 and 8 of them) AND are compared by

`if (uVar1 != <packed>) goto ...`. WHAT THEY DO IS NOT READ, which is a smaller
claim than knowing their effect and is recorded as such.

FOUR REJECTED, AND THE RULE IS PRINCIPLED RATHER THAN CONVENIENT. cj, xc, ka and
nc decode cleanly but are numeric coincidences: a TWO-character pack is a small
integer (25450, 30819, 27489, 28259) that collides with ordinary numeric fields,
while a FOUR-character pack is a specific value near 1.6-1.9 billion that nothing
else in a skill row plausibly holds. THE BINARY AGREES WITH THE RULE EXACTLY --
all five four-character candidates appear in the dump, none of the four
two-character ones does. The probe's controls were att and dru, both known-real,
so the search was known to fire before the candidates were judged by it.

THE FIRST PROBE WAS ONE PROBE WEARING TWO HATS. Selecting monsters by CharGender
and by a MOB_ code-name prefix returned 2,106 and ZERO rows -- the second

'bri' -- so "0 for every monster" is false. And cols 75/77 equal 2*level+25 on

table, and the docs stated them as facts about the table.

THE FIX IS THE DISTINCTION, NOT THE FORMULA. MonsterRate keeps its arithmetic and

sums BODY ARMOUR ONLY, and that is the data's own division rather than a choice

block ratio and every one a shield, and no row with both. A broken piece parries

THE LO END IS TAKEN AND THE REASON IS RECORDED. defenderDefence interpolates its
pairs through a recovered per-instance variance group; NO SUCH GROUP IS
RECOVERED FOR PARRY. Reusing that walk would have claimed a group this project
does not have, so the parry walk is its own and takes lo -- the documented rule
for the field. That is a smaller, checkable claim rather than a borrowed one.

THE FULL SUITE PASSED IMMEDIATELY, WHICH WAS THE WARNING SIGN. No existing
fixture carries armour parry, so every test took the fallback and the new path
was never exercised -- a guard that is always false is indistinguishable from a
feature that was never wired. The counterattack's roll is therefore extracted
into monsterBlow and tested directly: no parry -> the uniform maximum; parry 60
-> a 19 % centre and a blow of 119; parry 2 -> the ceiling. THE CEILING IS
REACHABLE ON THE MONSTER'S SIDE in a way it never is on the player's, because a
monster badly out-rates a lightly armoured character -- pinned so nobody reads
the clamp as dead code.

**What moved:** the port is symmetric, round 377's parry pair has a consumer,

Round 378 (the damage centre ported, and two of my own expectations refuted by
the tests): ROUND 377 LEFT ZERO BLOCKERS and said what remained was arithmetic.
It was, and it is now shipped: combat.DamageCentrePercent, combat.RollCentred,
CharacterRate and MonsterRate, wired into attackerDamageOf. A blow's position in
the weapon's range is now the engine's, not uniform.

TWO EXPECTATIONS OF MINE WERE WRONG AND THE TESTS CAUGHT BOTH, which is the part
worth recording. (1) I asserted the centre-bias put ">30 % of blows in the middle
fifth, and comfortably". The measurement said 28.2 %. Worked out properly: the
excursion is min of three uniforms, CDF 1-(1-x)^3, so the true figure is 27.1 %
against a uniform roll's 20.8 %. THE BIAS IS MODEST -- this changes the SHAPE of
damage, not its scale -- and the test now pins the closed form instead of my
impression. (2) A fallback test expected a uniform mean near 150 and got exactly
200, because this package's TestMain NILS the damage generator and RollDamage's
documented nil convention is "rolls the maximum". The whole test is now exact
rather than statistical, which is strictly better.

AND THE EXISTING SUITE CAUGHT THE REAL RISK. TestCombatFullFlow failed with
damage 1 where it wanted 20: its fixture weapons carry no attack rate, so hra
fell back to the bare 10+level against a monster's 27 and every blow landed near
the floor. THAT IS EXACTLY WHAT ROUND 376 PREDICTED would happen if the centre
shipped without the equipment term. The fix is a second guard: a weapon with
HitRateMin == 0 is an item table imported before col 113 existed, not a weapon
that cannot hit, so it takes the uniform roll -- the same reasoning the unarmed
fallback beside it already uses.

WHAT THIS MEANS IN PLAY, from the scenario table now pinned in the tests: a
level-1 character with a Copper Sword (attack rate 24) against a level-1 monster
sits at a 65 % centre, better than the uniform 50 %; the same character bare
would sit at 20 %. So on real data the port is a modest BUFF for an armed player,
and the nerf case is exactly the case the guard excludes.

MINE IS THE FOURTH, AND I MEASURED IT. GetParam has 190 call sites through vtable
slot 0x104. Round 370's census matched 80 of them. THE OTHER 110 -- 58 % -- PASS
A COMPUTED ARGUMENT and were invisible to it. So "param 9 is read by exactly one
function in the whole binary, measured against all 45 params read by literal
across 78 sites" is an enumeration of a BIASED SUBSAMPLE, and round 370 presented

the formula DOES -- parry rate is an input to the damage centre. That was always
the real basis. The census added nothing and claimed more, which is the exact
shape of the failure it was imitating.

A STRUCTURAL FACT THAT MAKES THIS GENERAL, not a one-off: 58 % of this binary's
GetParam sites pass a computed id. ANY literal-argument param census in this
binary is therefore a minority sample by construction, and a negative taken from
one is worthless without resolving the computed sites. That is now measured
rather than suspected.

ALSO LEARNED, AND IT MATTERS FOR THE NEXT ROUND: params 13/14 and 190/191 are THE
SAME TWO FLOATS (2026-09-15). [WITHDRAWN round 375: THAT ENTRY IS SUPERSEDED four

DISTRIBUTION -- "true of the floats at publish time, false at evaluation time,
which is the only time that matters". 190/191 carry the weapon's flat range
alone; 13/14 carry that plus the Str term plus every buff and skill modifier. So
porting the centre is NOT a distribution change on numbers srrevamp already has,
and this paragraph's "obvious next step" was built on a superseded fact.]

DELIBERATELY NOT WIRED THIS TICK. Shipping a combat change on the back of a tick
that opened by finding my own evidence overstated is not the moment for it.

**What moved:** a claim I made three rounds ago withdrawn in every place it
appears, its conclusion re-grounded on the evidence that actually supports it,

Round 373 (THREE ROUNDS RETRACTED: "the hit chance" was the damage centre, and
the tool built last round found it in one command): RAN tools/known.sh FIRST, as
round 372 built it to be run, on "attack rate". It returned RE_COMPLETION.md:1488
-- "What 'attack rate' actually does, and the damage dice (2026-09-15)" -- whose
second sentence is "attack rate turns out NOT TO BE A HIT/MISS ROLL AT ALL". That
contradicts rounds 370, 371 and 372 outright.

WHAT WAS WRONG. Round 370 read FUN_0040fdd0 and reported a HIT CHANCE:
clamp((levelTerm + hra/era * 0.5) * 100, 10, 90). The formula and every constant
are RIGHT; the MEANING is wrong. The same expression is the CENTRE OF THE DAMAGE
RANGE: damage% = centre% +- p, where p = min of three uniform samples, and damage
= lo + damage%/100 * (hi - lo). The _rand() calls round 370 cited as proof "it IS
rolled" are the three samples for the excursion, not a hit test.

THE CASCADE, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. Round 371 computed a bare level-1
character's hra = 11 against a monster's era = 27 and called the resulting 20 %
"implausibly low for a starting fight". THERE WAS NOTHING IMPLAUSIBLE: 20 % is a
damage CENTRE, and a weak character landing blows near the bottom of the weapon's
range is exactly right. Round 372 then spent an entire tick hunting the equipment
term that would explain the implausibility -- chasing an artifact of the
misreading. A wrong meaning does not announce itself; it generates a plausible
puzzle, and the puzzle consumes the next two rounds.

WHAT SURVIVES, AND IT IS NOT NOTHING. (1) The six constants, read out of the PE
image in round 370, match the 2026-09-15 reading exactly -- an independent
re-derivation by a different method, at a width that reading had to get right.
(2) The enumeration: param 9 is read by exactly one function, measured against
all 45 params read by literal across 78 sites [WITHDRAWN round 374: that census
saw only 80 of 190 GetParam sites -- 110 pass a COMPUTED id], so there is no separate parry
roll. (3) ROUND 371'S PLAYER BASE RATES ARE GENUINELY NEW AND NOW MATTER MORE
than when they were filed: a bare character has hra = era = 10 + Level. The
2026-09-15 entry closed with "srrevamp has no attack-rate or parry-rate stat, so
porting the centre would mean INVENTING ITS ONLY INPUT" -- that blocker is gone.
With hr on weapons and er on armour (magic_options.md, itemdata col 114, and a
verified Copper Sword tooltip), the damage centre is portable.

THE TOOL WORKED, ON ITS FIRST USE, AGAINST ITS AUTHOR. tools/known.sh was built
last round after three ticks of re-deriving recorded work. Run first this tick it
did not find a re-derivation -- it found a three-round CONTRADICTION, which is

CORRECTED IN PLACE: damage_pipeline.md's two sections are replaced by a

**What moved:** three rounds of wrong meaning retracted before any of it was

Round 372 (a third re-derivation, and a tool so the rule stops depending on my
memory): SET OUT TO VERIFY ROUND 371'S PREDICTION that equipment hit-rate closes
the implausible 20 % hit chance. Ended up re-deriving magicoption.txt's packed
tag vocabulary, which this project recorded on 2026-09-16. THAT IS THE THIRD
CONSECUTIVE TICK of going to the data before the docs.

THREE PROBE FLAWS IN A ROW, EACH CAUGHT, AND THE NEGATIVE SURVIVED TWO OF THEM.
Grepping real itemdata for the tag 'hra' returned zero, which reads as "equipment
cannot modify attack rate". (1) The 'era' hits that DID appear were the word
"General" -- substring noise. (2) The tags are not strings at all: magicoption
stores them as PACKED MULTI-CHAR INTEGERS, so a string grep is structurally blind
to them. (3) After decoding, my printable-ASCII filter silently dropped every
NUL-padded THREE-character tag -- precisely the class being looked for. Only the
third fix surfaced 'hra' (6845025) and 'era' (6648417). A negative that survives
two flawed probes is not a finding.

THE FIX IS MECHANICAL RATHER THAN A PROMISE. tools/known.sh greps every
recovered-knowledge surface at once -- prose docs, the name and handler tables,
and the Go sources' own citations, since many findings live only in a comment
beside the constant they justify. It exits 0 when something is known, so it reads
the way the rule does. Two controls: a documented term returns hits (and in fact
surfaces "The stat-tag vocabulary is complete: magicoption.txt names every tag",
the exact entry this round re-derived), a nonsense term returns nothing and
exit 1. THE RULE WAS NEVER FORGOTTEN -- obeying it meant remembering which of ~60
docs to grep, and that friction is what the script removes.

ONE THING IS GENUINELY NEW, AND IT RETRACTS ROUND 371'S PREDICTION. The tags that
reach params 9 and 11 are hra -> MATTR_AVATAR_HR and era -> MATTR_AVATAR_ER --
AVATAR options, the cosmetic family, beside inta -> MATTR_AVATAR_INT and luca ->
MATTR_AVATAR_LUCK. The plain hr -> MATTR_HR carries NO PARAM ID (param_names.md
lists it as a skill code), and that same file opens by warning that 'hra' is
ATTACK rate rather than hit rate, a distinction that has already corrected this
project twice. So whether an ordinary weapon raises param 11 is UNESTABLISHED and
the 20 % figure is still unexplained. Round 371 called equipment "the obvious
source"; it is not obviously the source at all.

**What moved:** one prediction retracted before it could be wired, a repeated

Round 371 (the player's attack and parry rates, and TWO re-derivations of my own
documentation): ROUND 370 NAMED THE BLOCKER as "the player side has no hra/era".
That is true of srrevamp and MISLEADING ABOUT THE ENGINE: the player formula was
already recoverable from three facts this project recorded on 2026-09-15 and
never put together.

THE COMPOSITION, WHICH IS THE ONLY GENUINELY NEW PART: GObjPC_InitStats sets
param 11 (hra) and param 9 (era) each to a base of 10.0 at slot 0 -- the same
.rdata 0x00b45b44 that is the hit formula's floor -- and gives each a DIRECT
derived edge from param 0 (Level) at slot 0 with no intermediate node. Slot 0
sums. So a bare character has hra = era = 10 + Level, with equipment contributing
through Stat_ApplyTaggedModifier ('hra'->11, 'era'->9) and status effects through
AbnormalState_Apply13_p11, both already named.

TWO RE-DERIVATIONS OF ALREADY-WRITTEN WORK, AND THE RULE THAT WOULD HAVE
PREVENTED BOTH. I read GObjPC_InitStats out of the dump to find the bindings --
the 2026-09-15 stat-graph entry already stated "a character's innate attack rate
(param 11) and parry (param 9) are each 10.0, each with a level-derived binding
(0 -> 11, 0 -> 9)". I then read ParamKeeper_EvaluateParam to learn what a slot-0
edge does -- the 2026-09-15 combination-rules entry already gave the exact
formula and "slot 0 -> acc = entry + acc". THE STANDING RULE IS TO GREP THE DOCS
BEFORE THE DUMP, and this tick went to the dump first, twice. Recorded because
the cost is not the wasted reads: it is that round 370 presented a documented
fact as a newly-discovered blocker.

A CONSEQUENCE THAT SHAPES THE NEXT STEP RATHER THAN A RESULT TO SHIP. A bare
level-1 character has hra = 11 against a level-1 monster's era = 2*1+25 = 27,
giving about a 20 % hit chance -- implausible for a starting fight. So equipment
hit-rate must dominate early, and itemdata cols 16/17 (HitRateMin/HitRateMax,
which srrevamp's refdata ALREADY parses) are the obvious source. That is a
prediction to verify before wiring, and it is exactly the kind of number that
would have been promoted on a curve if the implausibility had not been computed.

**What moved:** the engine's player hit-rate formula stated for the first time by
composing three recorded facts, the contributors named, and a numeric sanity
check that flags equipment as the missing term. Against that, two avoidable

Round 370 (the hit chance, and an open assumption that was asking the wrong
question): WENT TO THE PROJECT'S OWN SCOREBOARD for the loop's stated goal --
GROUNDING_AUDIT.md's "what is genuinely still assumed" -- rather than another
protocol thread. Its largest live item was "parry and evade are still not
rolled". THE PARRY HALF WAS MIS-FRAMED: the engine has no separate parry roll to
be missing.

THE PROBE WAS AN ENUMERATION, NOT A GREP. 'era' (parry rate) is ParamKeeper param
9. Sweeping every IGObj::GetParam(<literal>) through vtable slot 65 gives 45
distinct params across 78 sites [WITHDRAWN round 374 -- 58 % of GetParam sites pass
a COMPUTED id and were invisible to this census], and param 9 is read by EXACTLY ONE FUNCTION in
the binary, FUN_0040fdd0 -- which sits in the Formulae.cpp translation unit
beside Formula_MitigatePhysicalDamage. So the absence of a parry mechanic is
measured against a population rather than asserted from a failed search, which is
the standing rule for negatives here.

THE FORMULA: hitPercent = clamp((levelTerm + hra/era * 0.5) * 100, 10, 90), with
levelTerm = clamp((atkLevel - defLevel) * 0.03, 0, 0.30), hra = param 11 (attack
rate) and era = param 9. It IS rolled: caller FUN_0040dce0 calls _rand() and
compares. All six constants read out of the PE image.

TWO CONTROLS ON THE CONSTANT READS. 0x00b45af0 came back 100.0 and 0x00b45ac0
came back 1.0, the two values this project had already recorded for the
mitigation formula. And levelTerm is FUN_0040fd60, which internal/combat had
ALREADY DISASSEMBLED ON A DIFFERENT DAY, recording the same 0.03 and 0.30 at the
same two addresses -- an independent re-derivation agreeing exactly.

A MISATTRIBUTION SUSPECTED AND DISPROVEN, which is the part worth keeping.
LevelAdvantagePerLevel/Cap in internal/combat are these same constants applied to
DAMAGE, and finding them here driving HIT CHANCE looked like srrevamp having
attached them to the wrong quantity. It had not: FUN_0040fd60 is a shared helper
with two callers and srrevamp's comment cites the other one. The shipped code is
right and the suspicion was mine.

NOT SETTLED AND SAID SO: the register order was not disassembled, so "hra is the
attacker's, era the defender's" rests on what the two stats ARE rather than on
which object sat in which register; the second caller FUN_0040dff0 is unread; and
EVADE is untouched, still vocabulary only.

**What moved:** an open assumption on this project's grounding scoreboard is
retired as MIS-FRAMED rather than answered, replaced by a fully grounded hit
formula with six constants and two controls, and the real blocker is named: the
player side has no hra/era at all, while monsters carry both in real data
(characterdata cols 75/77, 2*level+25). No behaviour changed, so no tag.

Round 369 (the broadcast class joined from both sides, and a 3x inflation caught
by my own rule): ROUND 368 ENUMERATED THE 0x3NNN BROADCASTS; this joins them to
the client handlers that receive them. message_handlers.tsv turns out to hold 151
rows for the class with its server_senders column EMPTY on every one, so round
368's table fills a column that had been sitting blank since 2026-09-17. Written
to docs/protocol/broadcast_join.tsv: 157 opcodes, 50 joined on both sides.

THE FIRST COUNT WAS WRONG BY 3x AND MY OWN RULE CAUGHT IT. A naive filter --
"named if it does not start with FUN_" -- reported 28 genuinely named client
handlers and 28 join candidates. But GObjPC::FUN_004b1630 passes that filter, and
this project's standing rule is that a MODULE IS NOT A NAME and neither is a
vslot_. Classifying on the LEAF after Class:: gives 6 named handlers and 9
candidates. THIS IS EXACTLY THE ROUND-334 FAILURE (the 57-of-57 "tell", where a
classifier scored a bare hex string as named) arriving again in a new sweep.

A SECOND DISQUALIFIER WAS NEEDED AND IS NEW. Of the 9, several senders are named
MsgHandler_38e9, GObjPC_HandleSiegeMsg_516 -- names that encode WHICH OPCODE, not
WHAT THE MESSAGE IS. A name is not evidence of purpose just because it is a name.
Excluding names ending in a 3-4 hex digit suffix leaves EIGHT rows whose server
sender actually says something.

THE CLIENT SIDE COULD NOT CORROBORATE ANY OF IT, and that is reported rather than
hidden. Reading 0x3026's handler for chat markers returned NOTHING: no named

join is therefore ONE-SIDED, evidenced by the server sender's own name.

THREE NAMES FILED AND APPLIED (applied 3, failed 0), the ones with multi-sender
or two-sided evidence. Chat_OnChatUpdate (0x3026): three server chat functions
compose it and the opcode is independently AGENT_CHAT_UPDATE on two agreeing

AGREEMENT -- the handler already sat in the client module UI_TC while round 368's

CTrainingCamp__MemberDeleted and MemberGraduated. Named OnMemberUpdate rather

NOT NAMED ON PURPOSE: the other five semantic rows (0x3054 SetLevel, 0x305c item

**What moved:** a blank column in a table this project reasons from is filled,

Round 368 (the third side of the message surface, and the broadcast class nobody
had counted): ROUNDS 363-367 FOUND 0x7021 AND 0x7005 BY HAND, one function at a
time. Both were invisible to every table this project holds, and noticing WHY
turned five rounds of hand-reading into a lever: client_senders.tsv is what the
CLIENT sends, and round 334's server_senders sweep swept `mov ecx,0xbXXX` and so
covers REPLIES only. NEITHER CAN SEE THE SERVER ORIGINATING A MESSAGE.

THE LEVER IS THE THREE CONSTRUCTION IDIOMS those five rounds taught: the opcode
field written directly at msgbuf+0x1050, the new-message vcall (*obj + 0x14), and
the begin-message helper FUN_00430a00. Sweeping all three gives 297 sites and 132
distinct opcodes, 231 of the sites (78 %) inside functions already named. Written
to docs/protocol/server_senders.tsv.

THE DISTRIBUTION IS THE FINDING. 159 of the 297 sites compose 0x3NNN opcodes --
the largest class by a factor of two, and the one with NO TABLE ANYWHERE in this
project. 0x3026 is AGENT_CHAT_UPDATE (S->C), so 0x3NNN is the server's BROADCAST
surface: what it tells clients unprompted. That is precisely the class round 362
identified as the blocker for monster movement ("the client half is a push, not a
poll"), and it now has 60-odd enumerated opcodes instead of a description.

THREE CONTROLS, RUN BEFORE THE TABLE WAS BELIEVED. (1) It must contain the two
rows read by hand, with the right functions -- it does: 0x7021 ->
AITactics_MoveAlongDirection, 0x7005 -> CMainProcess::FUN_00437e80. (2) 0x3026's
composing functions come back as CGObjCOS_Summoned::ChattingByProxy,
ChattingByProxyArg and CGObjPC::SendQuestNpcChat -- all chat, all named by
earlier rounds that this sweep never consulted, so opcode AND purpose agree
independently. (3) Against observed_opcodes.md's 13 cross-validated names, 5 of
11 S->C are found.

THE THIRD CONTROL'S SIX MISSES ARE THE MOST INFORMATIVE PART, and 5-of-11 would
have been the wrong thing to report. EVERY ONE OF THE SIX is a GATEWAY opcode --
0x2322, 0xa101, 0xa102, 0xa103, 0xa106, 0xa323 -- composed by GatewayServer.exe,
a DIFFERENT BINARY from the one swept. Their absence is the correct result. And
both nominally-C->S entries ARE present (0x7005, 0x6004), which is the real
finding underneath: the game server composes client-form opcodes when it talks to
another server, which is why the hand-found pair looked so odd in rounds 363-367.

STATED AS A LIMIT, NOT DISCOVERED LATER: a site that builds its opcode from a
variable rather than a literal is invisible to all three idioms, so this is not a
claim to be every message the server sends.

**What moved:** no shipped value. A message surface this project had described
only in fragments is enumerated with its provenance and three controls, the
broadcast class that blocks monster movement is counted for the first time, and
five rounds of one-function-at-a-time reading are generalised into a sweep. No

Round 367 (following one loose end lands on the logout opcode, and confirms it a
third way): ROUND 366 IDENTIFIED THE SOLE EMITTER of the movement payload's
optional extra byte -- CGObjMobile::vslot_292 -- and left what it means open.
Following its ONE call site terminates the thread completely.

THE CHAIN IS SHORT AND CLOSED. vtable slot 292 has exactly one caller,
CMainProcess::FUN_00437e80, and that function composes a message whose opcode
field at +0x1050 is the literal 0x7005. It appends an id and a state byte taken
from an object's +0x50 (4 is forced when there is no object or the flag argument
is 0); any other value goes to vslot_292, which re-emits the byte and, WHEN IT IS
3, appends the movement destination with the extra byte. So THE OPTIONAL EXTRA
BYTE IS EMITTED IN EXACTLY ONE MESSAGE IN THE ENTIRE SERVER.

AND THAT MESSAGE IS THE LOGOUT REQUEST. 0x7005 is already in observed_opcodes.md
as AGENT_GAME_LOGOUT_REQ, resting on two agreeing sources -- this project's own
binary opcode harvest and public community documentation. THIS ROUND ADDS A
THIRD, from the server's own code path, and it arrived while following an
unrelated thread rather than by re-reading either earlier source: one of
FUN_00437e80's two callers is CMainProcess::CharDataSavingCompleted, and a
character's data finishing saving is a logout step. A character logging out while
in motion reports where they were headed -- which is exactly why the movement
payload has an optional byte at all.

WIRED: OpLogoutRequest (0x7005) and OpLogoutResponse (0xB005) added to
opcodes.go. The reply comes from this project's OWN handler table
(server_handlers.tsv row 0x005: handler GObjPC::FUN_0050eff0, client handler
FUN_0086db40), not from the public list.

NOT CLAIMED: what the state byte's values mean. The only fact is that 3 is the
value that carries a movement destination; reading that as "moving" is the
natural inference and is recorded as an inference rather than promoted. The
byte's source object, and the id that precedes it, are also unidentified.

A FALSE START WORTH RECORDING: this round opened by treating vslot_292's byte as
an ACTION-KIND VOCABULARY -- the systematic param-code lever -- and went looking
for call sites with literal kinds. There are none: slot 292 has a single caller
and the value arrives as a variable. The vocabulary lever does not apply to a
slot with one call site, and the cheap check (count the call sites before
harvesting) would have said so first.

**What moved:** two real opcodes into opcodes.go with a three-way citation, a
loose end from round 366 closed rather than left open, and a cross-validation
table strengthened from two independent sources to three. No behaviour changed,
so no tag.

Round 366 (the response opcode earns its place, and a grep nearly invented three
states): ROUND 365 LEFT FOUR NAMED GAPS on 0x7021 and deliberately kept 0xB021
OUT of opcodes.go on the grounds that "conventional is not evidence". TWO OF THE
FOUR ARE NOW CLOSED FROM USE-SITES.

0xB021 IS REAL AND IS NOW IN opcodes.go. GObjPC::FUN_004b0ea0 begins a message
with it through FUN_00430a00, which writes the MsgBuf opcode field at +0x1050 --
the argument is dropped by the decompiler but is the literal at the call site,
the standing __fastcall trap. It then appends one leading field and THE SAME
movement destination this project already encodes, through the 0x0048bad0
serialiser with the optional extra byte absent. Added as OpMovementResponse.
WHETHER IT IS AN ACK, A BROADCAST, OR BOTH IS NOT READ, and the leading field is
not identified. Also: 0x3021 appears in the CLIENT and NEVER in the server, so
whatever it is, it is not the movement broadcast.

THE OPTIONAL EXTRA BYTE HAS EXACTLY ONE EMITTER. Every call to the destination
serialiser passes 0 -- the monster AI, the 0xB021 responder, the flag and
battle-arena handlers -- except CGObjMobile::vslot_292 (vtable slot 292, COMDAT
twin at 0x0048b570/0x004a9c60), which writes a one-byte ACTION KIND and appends
the movement with the extra byte only when that kind is 3. So the byte marks a
movement EMBEDDED IN AN ACTION message rather than a standalone move.

A USE-SITE CORROBORATES ROUND 361 FROM OUTSIDE. FUN_004b0ea0's first gate reads
chardata+6 and proceeds only when it is 0 or 1: a character may move while a
trade session is merely OPENED (1) and may not once it is ESTABLISHED (2). The
movement gate and the trade code agree without sharing any code, which is the
kind of confirmation the 1-versus-2 split needed.

AND THE ROUND NEARLY INVENTED THREE STATES. The same function compares a value
against 8, 0x10 and 0x12, and the filtered grep that surfaced them made them look
like three more chardata+6 values -- a tempting extension of a vocabulary this
project had just built. THEY ARE NOT: cVar6 is REASSIGNED between the two blocks,
and the later comparisons are against the return of vtable slot 0xfc, a different
getter whose identity is unread. Reading the whole body is what caught it. This
is the same failure mode as characterdata col 79, arriving by a different road.

**What moved:** one real opcode promoted from "conventional guess, withheld" to
"read, cited and in opcodes.go"; the extra byte's sole emitter identified; an
independent corroboration of the interaction state's 1-vs-2 split; and a
three-value misreading caught and recorded rather than shipped. No behaviour
changed, so no tag.

Round 365 (the first real payload layout gets implemented, and the orphan guard
earns its keep): ROUND 364 FINISHED 0x7021's SPEC; this implements it.
opcodes.go's own header said "payload layouts are documented in login.md, not
encoded here yet" -- that is now out of date, which is the point of the round.
server/internal/proto/movement.go carries OpMovementRequest,
EncodeMovementAngle, Movement.Encode and DecodeMovement.

THE TESTS ARE WRITTEN AGAINST THE SPEC, NOT AGAINST THE CODE. The layout cases
are hand-written byte strings taken from movement.md's table rather than
captured from Encode's output, and the angle cases were computed independently
before the implementation existed.

THEY ALL PASSED FIRST TRY, WHICH IS A REASON TO DISTRUST THEM, so both key
constants were MUTATION-CHECKED. Replacing 65535 with the "obvious" 65536 makes
a full turn encode to 0 instead of 65535 and fails two cases; substituting
full-precision 180/pi for the float32-widened constant the binaries hold fails
the constant test. Both mutations were reverted and the suite re-run green.

AND THE GUARD BUILT IN AN EARLIER ROUND CAUGHT THIS ROUND. internal/systems'
orphan detector failed the build: "DecodeMovement is exported and nothing calls
it. This is the shape that hid the HP-regen rule, the real drop tables and the
skill-reset cost formula." It is right -- the SENDING half is reachable
(Movement.Encode and EncodeMovementAngle are both called) but nothing decodes a
0x7021, because srrevamp's gateway still speaks the placeholder opcodes. Rather
than delete the decoder or wire a fake caller, it is recorded in knownOrphans
with the reason: a format recovered in ONE DIRECTION ONLY is how a layout gets
half-checked, so the matching half is kept deliberately, and the entry says to
delete the line the moment the gateway accepts a real 0x7021.

NOT CLAIMED: the reply opcode. 0xB021 is the conventional pairing for a 0x7021
request and NOTHING WAS READ TO CONFIRM IT, so it is not in opcodes.go.

**What moved:** the first real payload layout in internal/proto, with
byte-for-byte tests and two mutation checks; movement.md gains a Status section
recording what is implemented and what is still unread. NO TAG: no behaviour
changed and nothing player-visible moved -- the codec has no caller yet by
design, and the release rule here is to tag after visible fixes.

Round 364 (the movement opcode, finished from both binaries at once): ROUND 363
LEFT TWO NAMED GAPS in the 0x7021 payload -- the three .rdata floats that scale
the angle, and the +0x14 field in the heading form. Both are closed, and the
opcode now has its own page in docs/protocol/opcodes/, the third after handshake
and login.

THE WIDTHS CAME FROM THE OTHER BINARY. The server's destination serialiser
(0x0048bad0) appends through a helper whose argument type Ghidra drops, so the
field widths are unreadable there. The CLIENT has the same routine (0x009ebbf0)
and its append helper takes an EXPLICIT BYTE COUNT. Reading the twin gives the
whole layout: u8 kind; an optional u8 the caller may ask for (the monster AI does
not); then either a u8 at +0x14 and a u16 angle, or a u16 region followed by
three f32 when region & 0x8000 and three u16 otherwise. THE +0x14 FIELD IS ONE
BYTE -- its width settled, its meaning still unread and not named.

THE ANGLE CONSTANTS WERE READ OUT OF THE PE IMAGES, NOT INFERRED. Rather than
dirty the Ghidra project for three floats, the section headers were parsed and
the .rdata bytes read directly: 57.295780181884766, 360.0 and 65535.0, as IEEE
DOUBLES. So angle = round(rad * 57.29578 / 360 * 65535), and A FULL TURN MAPS TO
65535, NOT 65536 -- that is the constant the binaries hold.

THE CONTROL WAS FOUR ALREADY-KNOWN VALUES, read through the same address->value
mapping before the three unknowns were believed: 0xb46160 = 85.0 (the wander
leg's base), 0xb45e58 = 30.0 (the probe distance), 0xb45e68 = -1.0 (the reverse
multiplier) and 0xb45c84 = 1e-6 (the speed epsilon). All four match what the AI
reading had already recorded. That last one also settles WIDTH: the epsilon is an
f32 and reads as garbage as a double, while the angle constants read as garbage
as f32 and as exact round numbers as doubles.

AND THEN A SECOND, STRONGER CONTROL: the client holds its own copies at unrelated
addresses (0xdde8f0/0xdde7a8/0xdde7b0), and they are BYTE-IDENTICAL to the
server's. Two independently compiled executables agreeing to the last bit.

A PRECISION DETAIL THAT WILL BITE A REIMPLEMENTATION: 57.295780181884766 is NOT
180/pi (57.295779513082320). It is the FLOAT32 of 180/pi widened to double, so
the engine's degree conversion carries float32 precision and a reimplementation
using full-precision 180/pi disagrees in the low bits of the encoded angle.

FRAMING CORRECTED BY READING THE PROJECT'S OWN DECISION DOC: PROTOCOL_DECISION.md
(2026-08-22) sets the goal as a real WIRE-LEVEL reimplementation and names the
own-designed opcodes in internal/session as placeholder scaffolding. So 0x7021 is
not reference material for an own-design packet -- it IS the destination format,
and TODO.md's outstanding move packet is this opcode.

**What moved:** no shipped value, no code. Two named gaps closed, a fully
specified opcode page written with its controls, and the standing move-packet
item upgraded from "mirror this shape" to a finished spec. It still does not
unblock monster movement on its own -- that needs the server stepping positions
and a push to the client (round 362).

Round 363 (the WANDER speed question was mis-framed, and monster movement is the
CLIENT'S OWN packet): ROUND 362 LEFT ONE BOUNDED QUESTION -- which speed a WANDER
leg steps at -- and said to settle it from the mover. There is nothing to settle
IN THE AI: no state reads a speed to compute a step. Across every AI function the
walk and run fields appear ONLY as immobility gates (<= 0.0 in AI::CTactics::Init,
AITactics_CreditAttacker and five FUN_0054xxxx guards; <= 1e-6 in PickWanderLeg
and AITactics_Handler_110). WANDER picks a DESTINATION, never a speed.

A PROBE THAT LOOKED RIGHT AND WAS NOT, recorded because it nearly became the
finding. Grepping +0x16c/+0x170 scoped to the AI address range returns
CAIState_PATROL::OnEnter and CAIState_MOVING::OnEnter apparently "reading walk
speed", which would have settled the question as WALK -- the answer round 362
already leaned toward, so it would have confirmed a prior lean. Both are false
hits: PATROL copies 0x16c,0x170,0x174,0x178,0x17c,0x180 as a BLOCK into its
context at +0x38..+0x4c, and FUN_00549970 squares 0x16c and 0x170 together with a
third field as VECTOR COMPONENTS. The offsets mean walk/run only when reached
through the owner pointer, *(int *)(ctx + 4) + 0x16c. SCOPING A GREP BY ADDRESS
RANGE DOES NOT SEPARATE THESE; ONLY THE BASE OBJECT DOES.

HOW A MONSTER ACTUALLY MOVES. FUN_00540f70, the destination setter PickWanderLeg
hands its leg to, ends by composing a message with opcode 0x7021 and sending it.
0x7021 IS THE CLIENT'S OWN MOVEMENT REQUEST -- client_senders.tsv already records
the client sending it from FUN_009ebd10 -- so a monster moves by issuing the same
message a player's client issues, and player and monster movement share one path
rather than having two. The payload, read from GObjPC::FUN_0048bad0 where the
argument decides only whether a second byte is included (the AI passes 0): a kind
byte; then if kind == 0 a heading form (a u16 from +0x14 and a u16 angle), else a
u16 region followed by three coords -- f32 when region & 0x8000, else
region-local u16s. That last split is the same position encoding this project
recovered elsewhere (region span 1920, local [0,1920)).

NOT READ: the three .rdata floats that scale the angle, and the +0x14 field in
the heading form. Naming the angle scale would be a guess.

**What moved:** no shipped value, no code. A question this project had stated as
open is RETIRED AS MIS-FRAMED rather than answered, with the false probe that
would have answered it wrongly recorded beside it; monster movement is shown to
be the client's own 0x7021 request; and its payload is read, which gives
srrevamp's outstanding move packet (docs/TODO.md) a retail shape to mirror
instead of an invented one.

Round 362 (the monster speeds, and why the AI cannot be wired yet): THIS TICK
WENT AT THE BIGGEST PLAYER-VISIBLE GAP instead of another naming round --
internal/ai is 30 KB of tested, fully-specified state machine IMPORTED NOWHERE,
the fifth instance of the recovered-implemented-unwired class. It is still
unwired, and this round establishes why, plus the one piece of real data it was
missing.

THE DATA: all eleven roster species' WALK AND RUN SPEEDS, read from the retail
characterdata_5000.txt -- Speed1 (col 46) and Speed2 (col 47), published as
ParamKeeper params 23/24 from the common record's +0xe4/+0xe6, so world units per
second. Mangyang 8/22, Yeoha 9/20, Earth Ghost 11/75, the rest 12-15 walk and 55
run. Tabled in docs/protocol/monster_ai.md.

THE CONTROL WAS RUN BEFORE THE NUMBERS WERE TAKEN, and it caught a real error.
Col 57 (level) and col 59 (max HP) are values this project already holds per
species in monsterSpecs; all eleven rows match on both, and col 50 matches
BCRadius. Selecting the row by CODE NAME instead finds the wrong one:
characterdata_10000.txt holds a SECOND MOB_CH_MANGNYANG at level 90 with 676,983
HP whose speeds (8/22) look perfectly plausible. CODE NAMES ARE NOT UNIQUE ACROSS
THE CHARACTERDATA FILES; select by RefObjID. Without the control that row would
have shipped.
*Corrected in round 523:* that row is MOB_CH_STRONG_MANGNYANG (RefObjID 9383), a
different code, and code names ARE unique across the six data files (13,291 rows,
