## The naming figure overstated by fourfold, and the arithmetic reconciles (2026-09-17)

The loop prompt suggests `SymbolReport.java` as a way to see named-vs-`FUN_`
counts, so this tick ran it — and found the number it reports has been counting
the wrong thing.

### What it was counting

	boolean hasName = !(st == SourceType.DEFAULT || n.startsWith("FUN_"));

A function whose symbol is `vslot_395` is not `FUN_`-prefixed, so it landed in
**NAMED**. A `vslot_NNN` is what the RTTI plate pass produces: it says which
vtable slot a function occupies and nothing about what it does.

### The real figures

| | server | client |
|---|---:|---:|
| **NAMED** (a real name) | **1,825 (5.3%)** | **1,285 (3.0%)** |
| SLOTTED (vtable slot only) | 5,617 | 5,136 |
| ATTRIBUTED (module only) | 14,473 | 13,565 |
| UNKNOWN | 12,198 | 23,474 |
| — of those, real bodies | 11,495 | 21,270 |

against the **21.7%** and **14.8%** this project has quoted in five places.

### How the mechanism was confirmed rather than guessed

	server   1,825 named + 5,617 slotted = 7,442   (recorded: 7,386, 21.7%)
	client   1,285 named + 5,136 slotted = 6,421   (recorded: 6,432, 14.8%)

Both reconcile to within the handful of names applied since the old figures were
taken. That is what makes this a mechanism rather than a suspicion: the
overstatement is *exactly* the slotted count, in both binaries independently.

### Why it matters beyond the number

The plate pass added roughly 14,000 class prefixes and 5,600 slot labels in one
go. Under the old metric that is a jump from 7,386 to 21,919 "named" functions —
**a tripling with no additional function understood.** A metric that moves like
that cannot be used to steer work, which is the job a coverage number has.

`SymbolReport.java` now reports four tiers, because a slot number is the same
kind of knowing as a module name: **where a function lives, not what it is.**
Its own header already warned that folding attribution into naming "would
flatter the number" — the warning was right and was being applied to the wrong
tier.

This is the same failure `docs/SYSTEMS.md` was created to escape ("N% of
functions named measured the wrong thing"). SYSTEMS.md replaced the metric for
tracking *systems*; the metric itself was never fixed, and kept being quoted.

### An independent corroboration, noticed in passing

`absence_audit.md` already records `character` as "creation lives on the
AgentServer, already disclosed". The previous tick reached that conclusion from
the other end — no `INSERT INTO _CHAR`, no creation handler strings, no write to
the live inventory-size field — without knowing this line was there. Two
independent routes to the same answer.

### The honest read of 5.3%

11,495 functions in the server have a real body, no name, no slot and no module.
That is the work, and it is the first time this project has had a number for it
that is not flattered.

## A staleness fix that starved the loop, reverted (2026-09-17)

v0.1.288 changed `re_tick.sh` to record the project stamp taken **before** a
dump rebuild rather than after, to catch a rename applied while the dump was
building. The reasoning was wrong and the effect was severe.

`analyzeHeadless` touches the Ghidra project while it runs, even under
`-readOnly`. So the project's newest mtime always ends up **newer than a
pre-run stamp**, and every subsequent tick sees the dump as stale:

	re_server: stamp=1789628606   project newest=1789629504
	re_client: stamp=(none)       project newest=1789629507

Both dumps then rebuild on every 15-minute tick — about **nine minutes of every
tick** — which is exactly the failure the original post-run stamping existed to
prevent, and which its comment had warned about in those words. The tick log
shows 26 "dump stale" rebuilds.

**It starved this loop for four consecutive ticks**, each of which correctly
found a decompilation in flight and stood down.

### The fix, and where the responsibility belongs

Post-run stamping is restored. The mid-run window it cannot close is real but
narrow, and it belongs to whoever changes the project rather than to the
heartbeat: `ApplyRecoveredNames` is the only thing that meaningfully changes it,
so the apply step now deletes `PROJSTAMP` and the next tick rebuilds.
`docs/RE_LOOP.md`'s apply recipe carries the extra line.

That is a better division than either stamping choice on its own — the cache is
invalidated by the operation that dirties it, instead of being guessed at from
timestamps that cannot distinguish a rename from a read.

### What this cost, stated plainly

Four ticks of no progress, and the diagnosis took a fifth. The change that
caused it shipped with a confident commit message explaining why the previous
behaviour was wrong; the previous behaviour was right, and its own comment said
why. Reading that comment as a warning rather than as an obstacle would have
saved all five.

## Three named limits, from the engine's own asserts (2026-09-17)

With the heartbeat fixed and both dumps current, this tick went after naming
levers that had not been tried.

**Tried and exhausted first:** harvesting log strings shaped `Class::Method(` as
candidate function names. 56 such signatures exist, 46 name exactly one
function, and after removing those already named that way **6 remain, none with
a matching namespace**. The `## Illegal ##` pass had already taken this lever;
recorded so it is not tried a third time.

**The lever that paid** is the third argument of
`CGameServer::FUN_00964760(line, file, expr)` — the assert's **source text**, so
the engine states its invariants in its own words. Only **49 distinct
expressions across 19 files**, but where one names a `MAX_*` constant, the
comparison right above the assert gives its value:

| constant | value | how fixed |
|---|---:|---|
| `MAX_MAGPARAM_PER_ITEM` | **12** | `cmp BYTE PTR [esi+0x24],0xc ; jb` |
| `MAX_ITEM_PER_SHOP_TAB` | **240** | `cmp BYTE PTR [esi+0x48],0xf0 ; jb` |
| `MAX_LOCALOBJID_BITS` | **21** | `mov eax,0x15` as the `pow(2,N)` exponent **and** `and ecx,0x1fffff`, eight instructions apart |

The third is the one worth dwelling on: `CGObj::Create` inlines `pow(2, N)` by
square-and-multiply with the exponent as a literal, then masks the id to 21
bits. Two independent statements of 21 in one function — not a suggestive curve.

### Two readings that needed each other

`MAX_ITEM_PER_SHOP_TAB`'s assert has **two** clauses and compiles to **one**
comparison, because `m_btSlotIndex` is a byte and `0 <= x` is vacuous for an
unsigned one. The instruction alone under-reports what the engine checks; the
assert text alone over-reports what it compiles to. Both together are what makes
it safe — and it is a good reminder that a decompiled comparison is not the
whole predicate.

### Where they landed

`combat.MaxMagicOptionsPerItem` and `shop.MaxItemsPerShopTab`, each with the
citation and a test pinning it to the literal. **Neither is enforced**, and both
say so: srrevamp has the magic-option vocabulary but no per-item option list,
and no shop-tab model. `MAX_LOCALOBJID_BITS` has no home — srrevamp allocates no
live object ids — so it is documented only.

No number srrevamp computes with changed. Three engine facts are now grounded
and parked where they will be needed, which is the honest shape of this one.

`docs/protocol/engine_limits.md` also records the sixteen expressions that name
members rather than constants — `m_dwAvailableOPs`, `m_dwLink`, `m_btItemClass`
and more, each confirming a reading another spec reached from the other end.

## A second level-difference damage term, found and deliberately not wired (2026-09-17)

Followed the `__FILE__` attribution lever to its most promising name:
**`Formulae.cpp`**. Small — 49 source files and 155 functions carry a file
string, so this is not the 14,473-function ATTRIBUTED tier, which gets its
namespaces from RTTI rather than asserts — but the file names are the engine's
own module decomposition, and one of them is called Formulae.

Three functions live in it. One, `Formula_SkillPhysDamage`, was already named;
its two siblings turned out to be the EXP path, which this project has already
mined (`Formula_ExpScaleByLevelWindow`, `Formula_MonsterExpReward`,
`GObjPC_RecalcLevelDiffExpScale` are all cited in `internal/leveldata`).

### What is new

`Formula_SkillPhysDamage` carries a **second** level-difference term, opposite
in sign to the one this project already ships:

	scale  = 1 - 0.025 * d          (d = the level difference, when positive)
	floor  = damage * 10 / 100
	result = clamp(damage * scale, floor, damage)

**2.5% per level, floored at 10% of the base.** The constants are `2.5` at
`.rdata 0xb45e50` and `100.0` at `0xb45af0`; the `imul 0x51eb851f ; sar edx,5`
beside the floor is the compiler's division by 100, not a game constant.

The asymmetry with the known term is the interesting part:
`combat.LevelAdvantage` is **3% per level, capped at +30%**, from
`Formula_MitigatePhysicalDamage`. This one is **2.5% per level, floored at
10%**. Two different rates in two different directions, which is exactly why
neither could have been inferred from the other.

### Why nothing was wired

`Combat_ResolveDamage` calls it twice, and the two sites pass the object pair
**swapped**:

	58f4fc  push edi ; mov edx,esi ; call 0x40f5f0
	58fbab  push esi ; mov edx,edi ; call 0x40f5f0

so the argument order cannot say which participant is the attacker, and nothing
else read so far does. **Applied backwards, this term penalises the wrong
side.**

`LevelAdvantage` had the same ambiguity and was settled by an independent fact —
the same function reads the DEFENCE params off one of the two objects, and those
are known to be the target's. The equivalent probe here is identifying `esi` and
`edi` inside `Combat_ResolveDamage` (8,298 bytes, unread), and that is the
recorded next step.

So `docs/protocol/damage_pipeline.md` carries the term and
`server/internal/combat` carries nothing. **A cap or a floor can be parked in
code with "nothing enforces this yet"; a damage multiplier whose direction is
unknown cannot**, because the obvious way to use it is also the way to get it
backwards. That distinction is worth keeping — the previous tick parked two
constants in code quite happily, and this one should not.

## `+0xa30` named, and a tempting damage inference discarded (2026-09-17)

Took the probe the previous tick recorded: settle which participant is the
attacker in `Formula_SkillPhysDamage`, so its 2.5%-per-level penalty can be
wired.

### The inference that looked like it would settle it

The formula opens by looking something up in one participant's `+0xa30` and
**adding** the result to the base damage:

	40f607  lea eax,[esi+0xa30]
	40f60d  call 0x5a0330          ; an STL map find, keyed off the EAX argument
	40f616  add edi,[eax+0x4]      ; edi is the damage

A bonus added to damage is the attacker's. That would have settled the
direction, and it is wrong.

### `+0xa30` is on every character

It is the character's **active skill/buff container**, identified by its users:
`CMainProcess::CGame__EnterWorld` creates it, `AQ_SkillManager::vslot_007/008`
persist it, `CGSkillObject::Update` maintains it at five sites,
`Stat_ApplyTaggedModifier` reads it, the item-use paths consult it — and
`Formula_MitigatePhysicalDamage`, the function whose participant roles this
project *already* settled, takes `lea eax,[ebp+0xa30]` off its own.

Both sides have one, so having one identifies nobody. Written up in
`docs/protocol/igobj_vtable.md`, with the negative stated: its presence in a
damage formula does not tell you who is attacking.

This is worth recording as a trap rather than as a dead end. The lookup really
is a damage bonus; the inference "bonus, therefore attacker" really is unsound;
and the two facts feel like one.

### What did come out of it

The formula's calling convention, decoded:

	ecx   the damage struct   (caller: ebx->0x234; the formula reads *ecx)
	edx   -> the formula's `ebx`
	stack -> the formula's `esi`
	eax   the map key         (caller: ebx->0x538)

with the penalty firing when `level(ebx) > level(esi)`.

And the reason the call sites cannot settle it, now precise:

	58f4fc  push edi ; mov edx,esi   ->  formula esi = caller edi, ebx = caller esi
	58fbab  push esi ; mov edx,edi   ->  formula esi = caller esi, ebx = caller edi

The pair is passed in **opposite orders**, so site 1 penalises whichever way
site 2 rewards. One is presumably the reverse direction of the exchange — a
counter, a reflect, or a second damage type.

### The probe, narrowed

Identify what `esi` and `edi` hold at `0x0058f4ff` and `0x0058fbae`
specifically. That is a control-flow question about two addresses, not a reading
of all 8,298 bytes of `Combat_ResolveDamage`, which is what the previous tick's
note implied.

Still nothing wired into `internal/combat`, for the same reason as before: a
damage multiplier applied backwards is worse than one not applied at all.

## The skill level penalty settled and wired, and a two-instruction misreading (2026-09-17)

Took the narrowed probe the previous tick recorded — *what do `esi` and `edi`
hold at `0x0058f4ff` and `0x0058fbae`* — and it dissolved the blocker rather
than answering it.

### The two call sites were never swapped

The previous tick recorded this as the reason the direction could not be read:

	58f4fc  push edi ; mov edx,esi   ->  "formula esi = caller edi"
	58fbab  push esi ; mov edx,edi   ->  "formula esi = caller esi"

and concluded "the pair is passed in **opposite orders**", inventing a reverse
exchange — a counter or a reflect — to explain it.

Tracing the writes that feed those registers:

	58f4bc  mov edi,[esp+0x124]      58fb5d  mov esi,[esp+0x124]
	58f468  mov esi,[esp+0x28]       58fb64  mov edi,[esp+0x28]

**Both sites pass the same two operands.** `[esp+0x124]` is pushed at both;
`[esp+0x28]` goes to `edx` at both. The apparent swap is register allocation
across two branches of one `if`, and the two blocks are otherwise
instruction-for-instruction identical.

So the blocker was never a missing fact. It was reading two instructions without
tracing what fed them — and a plausible mechanic (a counterattack) invented to
explain the artifact. The mechanic does not exist.

### Whose level is subtracted from whose, three ways

`Formula_SkillPhysDamage(param_1 = pdmg record, param_2 = [esp+0x28],
param_3 = [esp+0x124])`, testing `level(param_2) - level(param_3) > 0`.

1. **`[esp+0x124]` is `Combat_ResolveDamage`'s arg0**, and its callers
   `FUN_005857b0` / `FUN_00586700` call
   `Combat_ResolveDamage(param_2, *(param_3+0x14), *(param_3+0x18))` where their
   `param_2` is the actor whose param `0x8d` they read, whose `+0x28c` block they
   maintain and whose `[0x302]` they clear: the **caster**.
2. **The same slot is `Formula_MitigatePhysicalDamage`'s `param_3`** at both of
   that function's call sites (`58f2f8`, `58f7e7`) — always the last push, i.e.
   the argument immediately before the damage float, which fixes the position
   without counting pushes. Inside, `param_3` is `ebp`: the object that gets the
   out-levelling **bonus** (`40e6b6`) and the **Str ratio** (`40e6cb`), both the
   attacker's, with stage 14's `cmp bl,al / jbe` stating the direction outright.
3. **`[esp+0x28]` is iterated, not passed in.** Written exactly once, at
   `58e908`, from a walk over the container the caller hands in as args 1 and 2
   (`cmp ecx,edx / je`, `cmp ecx,[eax+8] / jae`, `mov ecx,[ecx]`,
   `call FUN_00485d90`), each element filtered on vtable slots `0x18` and `0x28`
   before being damaged. One attacker, many targets.

A fourth reading fell out unasked: `FUN_0040f750`, the sibling on the other arm
of the same `if`, carries the **identical** level test with the roles in the same
slots (`this` = target, stack = attacker).

**`param_2` is the target, `param_3` the attacker.** The penalty fires when the
target out-levels the attacker — the mirror of `LevelAdvantage`, at a different
rate and with a floor instead of a cap.

### Where it applies

The result is **added into `[ebp+0x20]`** (`58f522`, `58fbd1`). The mitigated
weapon blow goes to `+0x28` (physical) and `+0x24` (magical), so this term scales
the **skill's own flat damage**, separately from the mitigation chain.

### Wired

`combat.SkillLevelPenalty(base, attackerLevel, targetLevel)` — `1 - 0.025*d`
truncated through `__ftol2`, clamped to `[base*10/100, base]` — applied in
`session.performAttack` to `damageBonus`, srrevamp's name for exactly that half,
before it joins the roll.

Two tests: `TestSkillLevelPenalty` pins the rate, the floor, the truncation and
the "0 means unknown" convention; `TestSkillLevelPenaltyIsNotTheLevelAdvantage`
fails if a later refactor collapses the two level terms, which differ in rate
(2.5% vs 3%), in bound (a 10% floor vs a +30% cap), in sign, and in source
function.

The floor is reached at exactly **d = 36**, where `1 - 0.025*36 = 0.10`, so the
penalty saturates 36 levels below the target. That is arithmetic on the two
recovered constants, not a third claim.

### What this closes

The ledger's standing refusal — *"a damage multiplier applied backwards is worse
than one not applied at all"* — was correct and is now discharged by proof rather
than waived. It cost four ticks of not-wiring, which was the right price.

## The stored-procedure catalogue was 39 of 71 (2026-09-17)

Set out to close `character.StartingStr`, and closed a different, larger thing
on the way.

### The Strength question, settled at the machine level

`character.StartingStr` has been own-design throughout, resting on four
measurements that no artifact holds a starting stat. A fifth was added, and it
is the strongest kind — an enumeration of writers rather than a search:

- `CInstancePC::CharData_BindDBColumns` binds `"Strength"` to charData `+0x74`
  and `"Intellect"` to `+0x76`, **literally**, in the engine's own code.
- Scanning **every word-sized store to those two offsets across the whole
  image**, the only ones touching charData are inside `GObjPC::SetStr` and
  `GObjPC::SetInt`. The other hits are unrelated structs — `CInstanceCOS`,
  `CGameWorldLayer`, quest handlers, `RTNavMeshTerrain`.
- Those two functions appear in **0 vtable slots**, so nothing reaches them
  virtually.
- Their **only** caller is `GObjPC_SpendStatPoints`, which refuses unless
  `str + int <= pool` and only ever **adds**.

So `SR_GameServer.exe` never assigns a starting Strength; it only increments one
it loaded from `_CHAR`. The value is unreachable from this binary as a matter of
structure, which is a *proven reason to disclose* rather than an unexplored gap.

Also re-confirmed the level-up economy directly from the disassembly rather than
from the note: `lea edx,[esi+edi*1] / lea ecx,[edx+esi*4] / mov [eax+0x84],cx`
then `push esi / mov eax,esi / call 0x511470` — grant `levels*5`, auto-spend
`levels` into each of Str and Int, leaving 3. Already shipped as
`leveldata.StatPointsPerLevel` and `character.StatGrowthPerLevel`.

### The number that did not match

`character.go` cited **75** stored procedures as the structural argument;
`persistence.Procs` and its test asserted **39**. Both were wrong, in opposite
directions, and the contradiction had been sitting in the repo unnoticed.

Harvesting every invocation form:

| form | distinct | example |
|---|---:|---|
| `{?=CALL _NAME (…)}` | 39 | the only one the original harvest matched |
| `{CALL _NAME (…)}` | 26 | `{CALL _STRG_ADD_EQUIP_NORMAL (?, ?, %d,…)}` |
| `EXEC _NAME …` | 7 | `exec _skill_manage %d, %d, %d, %d` |
| `trs_sm_*job` | 5 | `trs_sm_trainingcampjob` |

**71 procedures**, plus the five job wrappers. The catalogue was missing 32.

**This is the second time the same defect has shipped in the same file.**
`persistence.md`'s runtime-table count was 35 of 54 because its regex was
uppercase-only. One pattern, run once, reported as a complete enumeration. The
rule that would have caught both: *a harvest is complete only when its pattern
has been falsified — a second spelling found and a third ruled out — not when it
has been run.* Neither was caught by anything in that file; both were caught by
an unrelated probe noticing a number that did not match.

### What the 32 changed

- **Item creation was entirely absent.** The `_STRG_ADD_*` family plus
  `_STRG_SPLIT_ITEM` is every route by which an item comes into existence. The
  catalogue could describe moving an item but not making one.
- **A whole cash-shop subsystem**: `_STRG_BUY_CASHITEM_*` and five
  `_STRG_RESTORE_SOLDITEM_*` that undo a sale.
- **A false claim, now retracted.** `persistence.md` said "there is no procedure
  for gaining experience, taking damage, or changing a skill level" and drew a
  structural conclusion from it. `_skill_manage` and `_quest_manage` exist.
  Experience and damage genuinely do ride the character save, so half of it
  survives; the other half was an artifact of the regex presented as a finding
  about the engine.
- **Gold is read by procedure too**: `_GET_USER_GOLD`, `_GET_GUILD_GOLD`.

### Two are variadic, and one recount was wrong

`_STRG_ADD_ITEM_MAGIC` and `_STRG_RESTORE_SOLDITEM_ITEM_MAGIC` have literals
that end mid-list *in the binary* — `AQ_StorageUpdater::AddMagicItem` appends
`"%s,%I64d"` once per magic parameter, bounded by its own assert. Marked
`Variadic`.

And a caught mistake worth recording: the first recount of the arities counted
`%d` placeholders and reported `_Rent_Info_Manager` as 24 arguments. It takes
**10** — three of them are datetimes spelled `'%d-%d-%d %d:%d:%d'`, and a quoted
group is one argument. The original 39 arities were right; the recount was
wrong, and was checked against them before anything was changed. Had the recount
been trusted, this pass would have "corrected" 39 correct numbers into 39 wrong
ones while fixing the count.

## The error-code scan was widened, and it found the skill-use gate (2026-09-17)

Applied the previous tick's rule — *a harvest is complete only once its pattern
has been falsified* — to the project's other load-bearing enumerations. Two
survived, one did not, and the one that did not was the most useful.

### What survived falsification

- **The reference-table count (85)** already has a genuine cross-check: two
  probes sharing nothing (reading loaders, harvesting strings) agree.
- **The client's error dispatcher.** `error_codes.md` builds its table from one
  function, `UI_SILKMALL::FUN_007b8b40`, which is exactly the "one pattern,
  assumed to be the only one" shape that just failed twice. Counting switch
  cases on values ≥ 0x100 across the entire client: that function has **624**
  and the next-largest has **36** — and all five of the others switch on
  disjoint ranges (`0x01xx`–`0x0fxx`, opcodes) rather than error codes. The
  one-dispatcher model is correct.
- **The source-path lever is exhausted**: 153 functions carry a `.cpp` path and
  all 153 are already named. So is the self-naming-string lever — of 12,194
  still-`FUN_` server functions, exactly **one** carries a `Class::Method`
  string, and it has more than one candidate. 64.3% of the server is named
  strictly; further naming needs a different kind of lever, not another string
  harvest.

### What did not: the server-side scan

`error_codes.md` recorded, and never fixed, that its scan for where a code is
*raised* matched only `mov ax,0xNNNN` / `mov eax,…`. Widened to every constant
materialisation (`client/tools/re/errsites.py`):

| | narrow | widened |
|---|---:|---:|
| (function, code) pairs | 391 | 924 |
| functions carrying a named refusal | **157** | **362** |

**205 functions with a named refusal were invisible.** The missed shapes, by
yield: `mov WORD PTR [reg],CODE` (an out-parameter), `mov DWORD PTR [esp+N],CODE`
(a stack local — `Mastery_LevelUp`'s shape, the example the doc gave), `push
CODE`, `mov ebx/edi,CODE`, and `cmp ax,CODE`, which attributes a code's *handler*
as well as its raiser.

Two traps, both caught by checking the probe rather than the result:

- **Displacements are not constants.** `mov ecx,DWORD PTR [esp+0x3003]` is a
  stack access. Blanking bracketed expressions first drops the count from 414 to
  362 — 52 of the "new" functions were noise.
- **Some codes are computed.** The skill-use gate spells one refusal as
  `(-(ushort)(x != 0) & 0xfff1) + 0x3018`, giving `0x3018` or `0x3009` with
  neither present as an immediate. No immediate scan finds those.

### The richest function in the binary

`FUN_0058d8f0` (3,134 bytes) sits immediately before `Combat_ResolveDamage` and
returns **seventeen distinct refusal codes** — more than any other function in
`SR_GameServer.exe`; the next-densest manages twelve. It is the precondition
ladder every cast passes through, and it is now written up in full, in the
engine's own order, as `docs/protocol/skill_use_gate.md`.

**srrevamp already matches rows 1, 12, 14 and 15** — known skill, cooldown, then
HP cost, then MP cost, each gated on the cost exceeding zero. That is the
engine's order and gating, and it was not known to be when the handler was
written. Nothing changed; it is recorded because "we happen to agree" and "we
match a read" are different claims.

### The groggy threshold, and a vtable slot settled a third time

Row 9 refuses when `MaxHP * 0.3 < CurHP` — a skill that requires the caster at or
**below 30% health**. `.rdata 0x00b45ce0` is a **double** (the operand is
`QWORD PTR`; read four bytes wide the same address looks like the float 2.0),
holding `0.30000001192092896` = `(double)0.3f`, so the game's number is 0.3. The
direction comes from the flags — `fcomp` sets C0 on `ST0 < mem`, `test ah,0x5`
masks C0/C2, `jp` skips on even parity — not from the source order.

This is a **third independent witness** that vtable slot `0x110` is `GetMaxHP`
and not the `GetCurHP` its stub string says, and the first one that is a
reductio: under "both slots are current HP" the test reads `cur*0.3 < cur`, true
for every positive HP, and the branch is unreachable code the engine still pays
two virtual calls for. `igobj_vtable.md` had the correction in prose since
2026-09-16 but its **summary table still said `GetCurHP` for slots 68 and 69**;
both rows are fixed.

The useful shape, worth keeping: where two slots being identical would collapse
an expression to something with no free variable — zero for `GObjPC_SetLevel`'s
heal, always-true here — the expression itself decides, with no vtable evidence
needed.

### And a correction to this ledger's own reasoning

`error_codes.md` said the absent `0x38xx` family "is a property of the probe, not
of the game". **That was wrong**, and it conflated the server scan with the
client dispatcher walk. Measured: **no function in the client has a `0x38xx`
switch case at all.** Those codes are raised by the server and have no message in
the client's error dispatcher, so mastery refusals surface some other way or not
at all. Naming that family needs a different source, not a wider pattern.

## A whole system found by its vocabulary: skill withdrawal (2026-09-17)

The previous tick built the widened error-code scan and then used it to read
exactly one function. This tick used it the way it was meant to be used.

### The refusal vocabulary is a locating lever

Of the **362** server functions the widened scan attributes to a named refusal,
**291 are still `FUN_`**. Grouping those by the *system* each code belongs to
leaves **62 whose refusals all come from one vocabulary** — an unambiguous
attribution, by system:

	STRGERR 17   FORT 13   SKILL_USE 9   SOCKETERR 5   REINFORCERR 4
	WITHDRAW 4   TC_ERROR 3   GUILDERR 3   COSERR 1   JOB 1   PARTYERR 1   FRIEND 1

This is a different kind of lever from the ones already used up. It does not
need a string inside the function, a vtable slot, or a source path — only that
the function refuses something the client can name. Three of the clusters are
recorded open items: `FUN_005c6550` (guild alliance) and `FUN_005c6b60` (guild
war) are both listed as unrecovered in `guild.md`, and `AQ_Siege::FUN_006232c0`
is the fortress-dungeon probe.

### `WITHDRAW_SKILL_*`: four contiguous unnamed functions, one system

`0059f410`, `0059f610`, `0059f8b0`, `0059fd60` raise nothing else. That is the
**skill reset**, a system this project had no trace of. Written up as
`docs/protocol/skill_withdraw.md`; the cost formula is in
`server/internal/skill/withdraw.go` with tests.

**`0x7800` is the success value**, recovered from the server's own use
(`if (r != 0x7800) return r`). It is absent from `error_codes.md` and correctly
so — that table lists refusals, and the client has no message for success. Worth
recording as a shape: a family running `0x7801`–`0x7806` looks complete, and the
base of the range is exactly the value a client-side harvest structurally cannot
supply.

The validator's gold check is the same 64-bit `charData+0x78`/`+0x7c` comparison
as everywhere else — the **fifth** independent subsystem to confirm that layout.
And the charge is gated on `flags & 1`, so a free withdrawal path exists; what
sets the flag is not read.

### The cost, and what it is priced in

	cost per refunded level = goldMin * 100 * (1 + masteryLevel/10)

from `0x00410c80`, with `.rdata` 0.8, 80.0, 10.0, 1.0 and 0.5 all read. The
engine spells `* 100` as `(base / 0.8) * 80.0`.

`goldMin` is **the per-level gold table's minimum at the character's MaxLevel**
(vtable slot `0x128` = slot 74). That the `+0x268` array is the gold table was
already settled by this project from its *other* reader, `FUN_00724330`, which
rolls `rand()%101 <= entry[0]` then a range between `entry[1]` and `entry[2]` to
fund `ITEM_ETC_GOLD_03` — so `+4` is the minimum.

So a skill reset is priced in **hundreds of a level-appropriate gold drop**: the
cost tracks the economy's own curve instead of a hand-written table. The
consequence worth acting on is that the gold table is now load-bearing for two
unrelated systems, which raises the value of proving the `levelgold.txt` join —
still **inferred, not proven**, and said again here rather than quietly reused.

### A measurement instead of an assumption about rounding

`__ftol2(x + 0.5)` looks like round-half-up and is not a rounding rule at all:
with integer inputs the term is always an integer, `goldMin*100 +
goldMin*10*m`. Measured over 600,000 (goldMin, mastery) pairs, the `+ 0.5`
changes the answer in **27,435**, and in **every one of those** plain truncation
lands exactly one *below* the correct integer. It is a float-error guard, and
dropping it would be a systematic off-by-one on 4.6% of inputs rather than a
convention quibble. The test asserts the closed form across a sweep instead of
memorising the one case that happens to fail.

A wrong expectation of mine was caught the same way: I first wrote the test
expecting `WithdrawCost(7, 15)` to be 805, having read the divisor as 100. It is
1750 — the divisor is 10, so mastery 15 is `1 + 1.5`. The code was right and the
test was wrong, which is the good direction for that to happen in, and the
sweep-based assertion that replaced it cannot be written wrong the same way.

## The union cap is 8, read rather than assumed (2026-09-17)

Took two items off `guild.md`'s "What is not recovered" list, both located by the
refusal-vocabulary lever rather than by reading around.

### A claim this project had carried for a long time

`guild.md` recorded, verbatim: *"Unions holding eight guilds is a long-standing
note in this project that no read has confirmed."* That is the exact shape of
claim the loop's rules exist to stop — a number everyone knows, sourced to
nothing.

It is now read **four ways**, from the three functions that maintain the member
array at `alliance + 0x1c`:

1. `CMainProcess::FUN_005b8c70`, the slot setter: `if (7 < index)
   Assert_BreakIfDebugger();` before `alliance[+0x1c + index*4] = guildID`.
2. `FUN_005b8cf0`, the clearer: the same assert.
3. That function's loop, which runs `0 .. 7` inclusive and exits on
   `if (7 < i) return 1`.
4. `FUN_005b8e90`, the membership scan: `do { ... } while (i < 8);`.

**Two of the four are traversals rather than guards** — code the engine actually
walks, not an assert that merely fires in a debug build. That is the difference
between a bound and a convention, and it is why this is a confirmation rather
than a fourth restatement of the same folklore.

It is also a **fixed array, not a list**: the setter refuses an occupied index
with its own log line (`"Anohter Alliance guild is set in that index!!"`, the
engine's typo), so a guild holds a slot and leaving frees that slot rather than
compacting.

### Both guilds need level 2, and the error names are the second witness

`FUN_005c6550`'s ladder checks the same constant against two different guilds.
On its own, a symmetric pair of comparisons is exactly what a reader invents a
story about — so the direction comes from the client's names instead:
`TOO_LOW_CREATOR_ALLIANCE` (0x4c2a) for the requester and
`TOO_LOW_JOINER_ALLIANCE` (0x4c2b) for the target, each matching the object whose
`GetLevel()` was called. The error table did the work an independent binary
would otherwise have to.

### Two codes the engine never raises

`0x4c27 ALREADY_ALLIED` and `0x4c29 ALLIANCE_FULL` are in the client's message
table and appear **nowhere** in `SR_GameServer.exe`. The probe is known good on
this family — the same scan finds `0x4c2a` inside the very function being read.

The interesting part is what that means rather than that it is missing: the cap
is enforced by the **array bound**, structurally, and never by returning a code.
The client carries two messages it may never be sent. Both are kept in
`internal/guild/alliance.go` so the vocabulary is complete and the absence is not
re-derived by the next pass.

### The lever is doing what it was built for

Three ticks ago the error-code scan was one pattern that had never been
falsified. Widening it reached 362 functions; grouping the 291 unnamed ones by
vocabulary left 62 unambiguous; the first cluster gave the skill-reset system and
this one gives the alliance rules. Both were on documented "not recovered" lists,
and neither needed a function read speculatively to find.

## Guild war, and a decompiler artifact that would have shipped a wrong cap (2026-09-17)

`FUN_005c6b60` was the last combat item on `guild.md`'s "What is not recovered"
list. Located the same way the alliance was — one vocabulary, every code a
`GUILDWARERR_` or `GUILD*`.

### The cap is 50 and the decompiler says 49

Ghidra renders the check as `if (0x31 < (byte)guild[0x11]) return 0x4c3e;`, which
reads as a cap of **49**. The instructions:

	005c6ddd  mov eax,DWORD PTR [esi+0x44]
	005c6de0  cmp al,0x32                  ; 50
	005c6de2  jb  0x5c6dfe                 ; proceed only while count < 50
	005c6df5  mov ax,0x4c3e                ; GUILDWARERR_MAX_HOSTILE_GUILD

`0x31 <` is Ghidra's rewriting of `< 0x32`. I read the decompiled form first and
was about to write 49; the assembly was checked only because this project's own
note calls `limit-1 < value` an idiom to read constants off, and reading a
constant off an idiom is exactly when to look at the instruction.

**This is the second such bound in the same document.** The alliance array's
appears as `7 < index` for an array of **8**. So the rule is now general and
worth stating once: *when the decompiler shows a bound as `N < x`, the engine's
constant is `N+1`, and the assembly is what to quote.* Both constants shipped
this week; only one of them would have been wrong, and it is the one where the
array length did not independently corroborate the number.

### The two-sided check, and why it is safe to read

The cap is compared against the same offset on both guilds, with
`MAX_HOSTILE_GUILD` (0x4c3e) for the declarer and `TARGET_MAX_HOSTILE_GUILD`
(0x4c3f) for the target. That is the third time this week a symmetric pair of
identical comparisons has been disambiguated purely by the client's names for
the two refusals — the alliance level check and the skill-use gate being the
others. The error table is functioning as a second binary.

### The field, named by two refusals and honest about a gap

`guild + 0x44` is a byte, and two refusals pin it:

	FUN_005c6b60  count >= 50  -> GUILDWARERR_MAX_HOSTILE_GUILD
	FUN_005c6870  count != 0   -> GUILD_ERROR_BREAK_WAR

A state enum would not be compared against 50; a flag would not need a byte.
**No writer was found** — every access at that offset inside the guild module is
a comparison — so the count is maintained somewhere this pass did not reach.
Recorded as a gap. A probe that found only readers and concluded "therefore it
is constant" would be the `SetStr` mistake in reverse, and that one only came out
right because the enumeration was exhaustive; here it is not.

### A war is wagered and timed

`DB_Bind__GUILDWAR` binds `WarType`, `VictoryPointIndex`, **`LodgedGold`**,
`WarEndTime`, two `Guild` and two `PointGain` columns. Already in
`db_columns.md`, so not a new recovery — but reading it here changes what the
system IS: a war has a type, staked gold, an end time and a per-side score. An
implementation that starts from "a war is a boolean between two guilds" will have
to be undone, which is worth knowing before anyone writes it.

**An ally cannot be a war target**, so the two systems recovered this week are
mutually exclusive on the same pair of guilds — asserted in
`TestAllianceAndWarAreMutuallyExclusive` so a later pass cannot let both hold.

## An audit of every grounded bound, and the largest unclaimed constant in the damage path (2026-09-17)

The previous tick nearly shipped 49 where the engine says 50, because Ghidra
renders `cmp al,0x32 ; jb` as `0x31 < x`. That is a defect of a *class*, not of
one function, so this tick audited the class.

### The audit

Extracted every address this project cites — 161 functions across `docs/` and
`server/internal` — and re-read **every unsigned bound inside them in assembly**:
54 comparisons of the form `cmp <operand>, IMM` followed by `jb`/`jbe`/`ja`/`jae`.

**Nothing already shipped is wrong.** The audit confirmed:

| function | asm | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `CGItemEquip::CanBeEquipedAt` | `cmp al,13 ; jae` | `equipment.MaxEquipSlots` = 13 |
| `SiegeFortressMgr::HandleSiegeRequest` | `cmp al,3 ; jae` | fortress war needs guild level ≥ 3 |
| same | `cmp [ebp+0x24],7 ; jae` | …and ≥ 7 members |
| `FUN_0062f640` | `cmp cx,40 ; ja` | the −20…+20 tax range, biased by 20 |
| `FUN_005d0fb0` | `cmp bl,5 ; jb` | five entries in `MaxMembersByLevel` |
| `GObjPC_SetLevel` | `cmp di,65530 ; jb` | the stat-point overflow guard |

A negative result, and the right kind: the constants this project relies on were
read correctly the first time. The audit's value is that this is now **measured**
rather than assumed after one near-miss.

### What it found that nothing claimed

Four sites in `Combat_ResolveDamage` — `0058f2c1`, `0058f2d7`, `0058f97d`,
`0058f993` — all `cmp al,0x5a`, in the one function srrevamp reimplements most
closely. Following them:

**Stage 1 of the damage pipeline is mastery-scaled, and this project had the
argument wrong.** `damage_pipeline.md` recorded stage 1 as
`FUN_0040dce0(ctx, defender, damage)`. That function takes no damage argument:

	fVar9 = FUN_0040db50(ctx)              ; the weapon/skill roll
	fVar1 = (float)param_2 / 100.0 + 1.0   ; param_2 is a PERCENTAGE BYTE
	fVar3 = fVar1 * (float)fVar9

and the percentage is built by `FUN_0059e770` from the skill's two mastery slots
(`ctx+0xa0`, `ctx+0xa4` — the same pair the skill-withdraw cost reads), returning
the **character's** trained level in the higher of them via `FUN_0059e750`
(`record[+8] + 0x20`). A skill with a mastery the character never trained still
contributes **1**; only an attack with no skill record returns 0.

So **mastery adds up to +90% to base damage, before mitigation** — the largest
single multiplier in the pipeline, and srrevamp had none of it.

### The clamp is not a `min`, and that is the whole point of the four sites

	0058f2c1  cmp al,0x5a ; mov [esp+0x68],al ; jbe done   ; p1 <= 90 -> p1
	0058f2cd  mov [esp+0x68],0x5a                          ; else 90
	0058f2d7  cmp al,0x5a ; jbe done                       ; p2 <= 90 -> keep 90
	0058f2db  mov [esp+0x68],al                            ; else p2

The percentage is computed twice, off two different attack records: `p1` when it
is within the cap, otherwise `max(90, p2)`. **When both exceed 90 the result is
`p2`, above the cap** — precisely the case `min(pct, 90)` gets wrong, and the
only reason the engine spends four instructions instead of one.
`combat.ClampMasteryPercent` reproduces it, with a test that fails if it is ever
tidied into a min.

What the second record is has not been identified. srrevamp has one, so it
passes the same value twice and its clamp collapses to a cap at 90 — correct for
everything it can reach today, and recorded so the day that stops being true is
noticed rather than discovered.

### Wired

`combat.MasteryDamagePercent`, `ClampMasteryPercent`, `MasteryDamageScale` and
`ApplyMasteryScale`, threaded through `session.performAttack` as `masteryPercent`
and applied to the roll before mitigation. A plain attack passes 0 and is
unchanged, which is what the engine does too.

*Corrected in round 505: the engine does NOT pass 0 for every plain attack.
The swing is the weapon's base attack skill (`PrepareAction` 0x4ad030), and
`Skill_GetRequiredMasteryLevel` (0x59e770) returns the caster's mastery level
for any row whose `+0x574` is set by `getv MAAT` -- the CH base attacks and the
EU staff and wand ones. srrevamp still passes 0 because it does not export MAAT.*

srrevamp carries only `Mastery1` (`refdata.Skill` notes the real table has a
second), so the second slot is reported unoccupied and contributes the engine's
default of 1. That is a faithful reading of a table this project has half of,
stated as such rather than smoothed into "the formula uses one mastery".

## The `CRefSkill` field map: 2 offsets named, now 119 (2026-09-17)

Recent ticks kept reading raw `skill+0xNNN` offsets blind — `+0x4a4`, `+0x39c`,
`+0x49c` in the skill-use gate; `+0x240`, `+0x400`, `+0x3d0` in
`Combat_ResolveDamage`; `+0xa0`/`+0xa4` in the mastery scale. `docs/protocol/`
named exactly **two** `CRefSkill` offsets in total. That is the gap this tick
closed, systematically rather than one field at a time.

`SkillGlobal::RefSkill_ParseParams` (`0x00587630`, 7,509 bytes) walks a skill's
Param stream as `(code, values...)` runs and stores each value into a field of
the record — so it *is* the code → offset map. Vendored as
`client/tools/re/skillfields.py`; written up as
`docs/protocol/skill_fields.md`.

### The first extraction was wrong, and looked right

Pairing each store with the nearest preceding `cmp reg,CODE` produced a clean,
monotonic, plausible table. It was wrong: MSVC compiles a large switch on sparse
values as a **binary search tree**, so the last comparison before a store is
whichever tree node was visited on the way down, not the code that matched.

It was caught by the two anchors this project already had:

	pdm2 -> 0x234    but Combat_ResolveDamage's comment says 0x234 is pdmg
	resu -> 0x3a0    but skill_params.md says 0x3a0 is reqi's five-slot list

Both disagreed. Following `je` targets instead — the equality test, with `ja`/`jb`
ignored as tree navigation — gives `pdmg -> 0x234`, and the map then agrees with
all three independent anchors (`pdmg`, `da`, `pw`).

**This project's notes already called the binary-search-tree shape a trap**, when
reading the ParamKeeper tag dispatcher. It cost a first pass here anyway. Worth
recording as its own lesson: knowing a trap by name is not the same as
recognising it in a new function, and the thing that actually saved it was having
two previously-recovered facts to contradict.

### And a fabricated row, caught before it shipped

The first draft of the skill-use gate's update listed `+0x294` as `efr`. That
came from the **discarded contaminated extraction**, not the corrected one —
carried across while writing prose rather than re-checked. Grepping the corrected
map for `0x294` returns nothing.

Corrected to say `+0x294` and `+0x428` remain unnamed, and that their absence
means the extractor could not reach them rather than that nothing fills them.
Recorded because it is precisely the failure mode this project's hard rules name:
a value that was not read, presented as if it had been.

### What it grounds

| offset | code | was read blind by |
|---|---|---|
| `0x240` | `da` | `Combat_ResolveDamage`, after the magical mitigation |
| `0x39c` | `reqc` | the gate's stealth and musical-range flags |
| `0x400` | `lfst` | the branch to `FUN_0040f750` |
| `0x49c` | `qest` | the gate's computed `ITS_NOT_A_BATTLE_FIELD` code |
| `0x4a4` | `msch` | the gate's `EU_BAN_HAWN_TRANS` and `DUPLICATE` branches |
| `0x534` | `BSHP` | the bonus-map key in `FUN_0040f750` |
| `0x3d0` | `dtnt` | `Combat_ResolveDamage`'s target filter |

`da -> 0x240` is the satisfying one: `skill_params.md` had already decoded `da`
as "a conditional damage percentage" from the *other* side, and
`Combat_ResolveDamage` tests `[ebx+0x240] != 0` immediately after the magical
mitigation call. Two pages that never referenced each other, agreeing.

### Coverage, stated rather than implied

188 distinct printable codes are compared; 120 case bodies are reached by a `je`;
119 contain a direct field store. **Codes whose values go into a list are
absent** — `reqi` fills five slots and `att` is six words, both written by loops
past a conditional branch. Those two are the ones this project already knew
about, so the gap is *known* to be real rather than suspected, which is the only
reason it can be stated as a bound on the tool rather than a hope.

No value changed, so nothing was wired; this is naming, and `go test -p 1 ./...`
is green unchanged.

## The field map's most important row was missing, and my filter was the reason (2026-09-17)

Went back at yesterday's `CRefSkill` map to close the gap it shipped with —
list-valued codes absent — and found that one of the two examples given for that
gap was not an example of it at all.

### `att` was lost to a filter, not to a loop

`skill_fields.md` said `att` was missing because list-valued codes are written
by loops the extractor cannot follow. That was wrong. `att`'s case body stores a
pointer like every other:

	00587af3  add eax,0x4
	00587af8  mov DWORD PTR [ebp+0x0],eax

The store is via **`ebp`**, which the prologue set to `esi+0x230`, at offset
**0** — and the extractor's filter was `offset >= 0x20`. A guess dressed as a
rule, and it dropped the single most-read field in the record: `CRefSkill+0x230`
is the attack descriptor the **entire** damage pipeline reads.

Two failure modes — "the tool cannot follow a loop" and "the tool's filter
rejected it" — produce identical output, which is why the coverage claim needed a
*known-missing* example to rest on. `reqi` is one, from
`docs/protocol/skill_params.md`. `att` was cited alongside it on a guess, and the
guess was wrong. The claim now rests on `reqi` alone, which is the only one it was
ever entitled to.

### The real bound, and a structural check that did not exist before

The prologue is the answer to what the filter should have been:

	00587638  lea ebp,[esi+0x230]
	00587641  call 0x9e3520          ; memset(ebp, 0, 0x37c)

`esi` is the record; the param-field block is exactly `0x230`–`0x5ac`. Filtering
on that instead recovers `att` and takes the map from 119 to **120**.

It also gives the table something it lacked yesterday: **an independent check on
the map as a whole**. Every one of the 120 offsets falls inside the block the
parser clears. A row-by-row anchor (`pdmg`, `da`, `pw`) can only confirm the rows
it names; a block bound confirms that nothing drifted anywhere.

### Each field is a pointer, not a value

	005877ff  add eax,0x4
	00587802  mov DWORD PTR [esi+0x240],eax    ; a POINTER to da's values
	00587808  add ecx,0x2                      ; 2 words: code + 1 value

So `CRefSkill+0x240` is where `da`'s values start, not `da`. Reading yesterday's
table as "offset holds the value" would be wrong in all 120 rows, and the table
did not say which it was.

### A question I opened this tick, and closed against myself

I started from the premise that `att` had **six** values while
`skill_params.md` accounted for five, and that the sixth was an ungrounded value
srrevamp reads around. It is not. `ecx` counts words **including the code word** —
`da` consumes 2 (code + 1 value), `att` consumes 6 — so `att` has **five**
values, and `(type, percent, min, max, percent)` is complete.

The premise was wrong and the tick's stated reason for existing dissolved.
Recording it because the alternative — quietly pivoting to what did pan out — is
how a project ends up unable to tell which of its open questions were ever real.

Nothing srrevamp uses changed, so nothing was wired; `go test -p 1 ./...` green
unchanged.

## The `CRefSkill` map is a bijection now: 2 → 120 → 203 offsets (2026-09-17)

Set out to use yesterday's map as a whole-binary scanner — label every
`skill+0xNNN` read with the param it consumes — and the scanner turned out to be
invalid, which sent the tick somewhere better.

### The scanner does not work, and the reason is worth keeping

Scanning the server for reads in the param block's offset range finds **1,456
functions**. Most are not reading a CRefSkill at all: `CQSP_ALL_POTION_3`,
`CQEV_WINTER_EVENT_2009` and dozens of quest and event handlers have their own
fields in `0x230`–`0x5ac` and match on offset alone. A quest handler does not
consume 28 skill params.

**An offset does not identify an object type.** The map is a join key only where
the base register is independently known to be a CRefSkill. That is a real
constraint on how it can be used, and it would have produced hundreds of
confident false attributions if shipped.

### Where it IS valid, and what it says

In `Combat_ResolveDamage`, `ebx` is provably a CRefSkill — loaded as `[arg2+8]`
and the base of `+0x230` (`att`) and `+0x234` (`pdmg`), both confirmed. Scanning
only `[ebx+…]` there gives **38 distinct fields read**, of which 19 were mapped
and 19 were not.

The 19 unmapped ones clustered *beside* mapped ones — `0x238` next to `pdmg`,
`0x244`/`0x248` next to `da` — which is what sent the tick at the extractor
instead.

### Three more forms of one trap

Each expansion came from a different way MSVC spells "this code matched":

| shape | what it hid |
|---|---|
| `cmp reg,CODE ; jne DEFAULT`, body falls through | `pdm2` at `0x238` |
| `sub reg,K1 ; je` / `sub reg,K2 ; jne` — a chain compiled as a **running subtraction**, so the second test is `K1+K2`, not `K2` | `cr`/`ck` at `0x244`/`0x248` |
| a `je` target that is itself another comparison **sub-tree** | `getv` claiming `BLAT`'s field |

120 → 205 → **203** after the last was fixed.

### The collision check earned its keep

At 205 the map had 205 codes claiming 204 offsets: **one duplicate**. One
duplicate in 205 rows is easy to wave away as an alias, and it was not an alias —
it was a whole class of mis-attribution showing through a single row. `getv` is a
genuine code (`cmp edx,0x67657476 ; je 0x5882b5`) whose target compares four more
codes, so a linear walk from it ran into `BLAT`'s store.

The discriminator: **a real case body is straight-line up to its store.** `att`
branches, but only after storing. Abandoning a block whose first conditional jump
precedes any store drops `getv` and keeps `att`.

**The map is now a bijection** — 203 codes, 203 distinct offsets, none outside
the memset block, no code claiming two and no offset claimed by two. That is a
property that cannot hold by accident across 203 rows, and it is worth more than
any individual anchor: a row anchor confirms its own row, a bijection over a
known-size block (223 dword slots, 203 named) constrains everything at once.

### Honest about what is still missing

`reqi` and `getv` are real codes the tool does not place — one writes through a
loop past a conditional branch, the other is a tree node. Twenty slots are
unnamed. Their absence bounds the tool, not the binary, and the tool has already
been wrong about exactly that once: `att` was listed as list-valued yesterday
when it was a filter bug.

Nothing srrevamp uses changed, so nothing was wired; `go test -p 1 ./...` green.

## The damage resolution reads 37 named skill params; srrevamp models one (2026-09-17)

Three ticks went into the `CRefSkill` field map. This is what it was for.

### The inventory

`Combat_ResolveDamage` reads **38 distinct `CRefSkill` fields** through `ebx`,
and **37 now have names** — up from 19 before the map became a bijection. The
skill-use gate reads 15 and **14 are named**.

`ebx` being a `CRefSkill` is established independently (loaded as `[arg2+8]`, and
the base of `+0x230` `att` and `+0x234` `pdmg`), which is the whole reason this
scan is valid where the whole-binary version is not: an offset does not identify
an object type, and the unconstrained scan matches 1,456 functions, mostly quest
handlers.

Both lists are now in `damage_pipeline.md` and `skill_use_gate.md`.

### The number that matters

**srrevamp models one of the 37**: `att`, plus the mastery scale wired two ticks
ago. The other 36 are read by the engine and not by this project.

That is a measurement of scope rather than a defect list — most have no source
srrevamp can reach. But it is worth having, because *"srrevamp implements the
damage pipeline"* and *"srrevamp implements one of the pipeline's 37 inputs"* are
very different claims, and until this tick nothing in the project could tell them
apart. `damage_pipeline.md` reads as a fairly complete recovery; the input count
is the thing that puts it in proportion.

`da` is read **ten times**, more than any other field — more than `att` (6) or
`pdmg` (5). A page that describes the pipeline stage by stage and mentions `da`
once, at stage 12, is not wrong, but it is not weighted like the code.

### A temptation declined

The gate's newly-named fields include `hide`, `trap`, `tele`/`tel2`/`tel3` and
`cnsm`; its refusal ladder has stealth, trap-placement, teleport and ammunition
rows. Matching them up by theme would take about a minute and would look
convincing.

Not done, and recorded as not done. This project has twice promoted a meaning on
a resemblance (characterdata col 79) and once invented a mechanic to explain a
register allocation (the "reverse exchange" in `Formula_SkillPhysDamage`). The
join needs the offset each row actually tests, which is a separate read. What
shipped is the field list; the row-to-param join is an open item, stated as one.

### And a cwd bug caught by an implausible answer

A check for which params `skill_params.md` decodes returned **zero** — run from
`server/` against a relative `docs/` path that does not exist there. Zero of 37
being documented was implausible enough to re-check; the real answer is 36. The
recorded trap in this project is "`cd server && …` fails when cwd is already
`server/`"; this is the same trap from the other side, where the command
succeeds and silently answers about nothing.

Nothing srrevamp uses changed, so nothing was wired; `go test -p 1 ./...` green.

## The theme match would have been wrong (2026-09-17)

Last tick named the 15 `CRefSkill` fields the skill-use gate reads and
**declined** to say which refusal each guards, because matching `hide`, `trap`,
`tele`/`tel2`/`tel3` and `cnsm` to the stealth, trap, teleport and ammunition
rows by theme is the inference that produced this project's characterdata col 79
errors and the invented "reverse exchange" in `Formula_SkillPhysDamage`.

The join is now read, and it contradicts the theme match on three of four:

- **`hide` does not guard the stealth row.** It gates the *battle-state* block
  (`CANT_BATTLE_STATE`). Stealth is `reqc` bit `0x10`.
- **`trap` does not guard the trap rows.** It is an inner condition of that same
  battle-state block; the trap refusals are hundreds of bytes earlier.
- **`reqc` (`0x39c`) is one flag word driving three unrelated rows** — groggy
  (bit `0x4`), stealth (`0x10`) and musical range (`0x20`). No name-to-row
  mapping could have produced that, because the three share no theme.

`cnsm` before the ammunition row is the one case where position and theme agree,
and it is recorded as **positional only** — the field read sits immediately
before the refusal, and no decompiled condition was read for it.

So the general claim is now measured rather than asserted: **a four-character
param name says which skilldata column fills a field, not what the field means**,
and here it actively misleads for 3 of the 4 names a reader would have reached
for. `skill_use_gate.md` carries the table.

### A suspicion raised and then disproved

Spot-checking five map rows against the parser, four verified immediately
(`hide`, `cnsm`, `lnks`, the `tel*` family) and **`trap -> 0x4a0` looked wrong**:
its store sits immediately before `0x58933f`, the shared tail every case jumps
to, which is where a default handler would live.

It is correct. `cmp edx,0x74726170 ; je 0x589333` is the *only* jump to that
block, and the block stores `0x4a0` before falling into the tail. The suspicion
came from reading the window *before* the store instead of following the jump —
the same mistake in miniature that the whole binary-search-tree saga was about.

Recorded because a disproved suspicion is worth as much as a confirmed one here:
the alternative is a map with an unexplained asterisk nobody re-checks.

### Two things confirmed in passing

- **`cmp ecx,0x32` at `0x58934a`** is the parser's loop bound: **50 param
  slots**, which is exactly what `refdata.Skill`'s comment already claimed
  ("the 50 generic Param slots"). An independent confirmation of a number the
  project had from the client side.
- **`+0x428` is `hide`.** An earlier pass listed it as unnamed; it is read
  through `esi` like the rest and was simply missed.

Nothing srrevamp uses changed, so nothing was wired; `go test -p 1 ./...` green.

## The regen row's last open item, and a shipped test that was wrong (2026-09-17)

`docs/SYSTEMS.md` carried one caveat on the passive-regeneration row for as long
as the row has existed: *"the curHP\*0.5 bound at 0x004e2c00 is read but its
comparison is not."* A read constant with an unread comparison is exactly the
shape that has burned this project before, and it sat on a value srrevamp ships.

### The comparison

`0x004e2c00` is not a function; it is `CGObjPC::vslot_362 + 0x270`, and the
comparison is 0xb4 bytes earlier at `0x004e2b4c`:

	004e2afb  cmp ebp,0x1 ; jge ; mov ebp,0x1   ; floor the amount at 1
	004e2b05  fmul QWORD PTR ds:0xb45c50        ; cap = cur * 0.5
	004e2b0b  call 0x9fbb40                     ; __ftol2, so TRUNCATED
	004e2b4c  cmp ebp,edi ; jl ; mov ebp,edi    ; amount = min(amount, cap)

`.rdata 0x00b45c50` is the double `0.5`. `jl` keeps the amount when it is the
smaller, so the pair is a **min**, and — the part that matters — the cap is
applied **after** the floor at 1.

### Where it binds, which is the whole point

With `RegenPercentPerTick` at 4, the percentage term is 4% of the pool and the
cap is 50% of it, so the cap is inert everywhere except at the very bottom,
where the floor of 1 has pushed the amount above what the pool can afford:

	cur = 0  ->  cap 0, amount 0   (srrevamp gave 1)
	cur = 1  ->  cap 0, amount 0   (srrevamp gave 1)
	cur = 2  ->  cap 1, amount 1

**A character at 1 point does not passively regenerate at all.** That is a
mechanic rather than a rounding artifact: the engine spends four instructions
making the floor of 1 conditional on the pool being able to support it.

### A shipped test was asserting a partial reading

`TestRegenPerTickFloorsAtOne` asserted `RegenPerTick(1, 1000) == 1` and
`RegenPerTick(0, 1000) == 1`, with the comment *"The engine floors the amount at
1 **before anything else**"*. Those are precisely the two inputs the cap
overrides.

The floor is real and still applies. What was wrong is "before anything else" —
and the two rows were asserting a *consequence* of the unread comparison, not a
behaviour anyone had observed. The floor is now pinned where it is still
observable (pools of 2–24, where 4% rounds to zero and only the floor makes them
regenerate), and the two overridden rows assert 0 with the reason attached.

Worth stating plainly: a test can encode a gap as confidently as it encodes a
fact, and this one had been green for as long as the caveat had been open. The
caveat was the only thing that flagged it.

### Two mistakes of mine, caught by the tests

I wrote the new cap test expecting `RegenPerTick(4, 100) == 2`, having confused
the cap with the amount — 4% of 4 is 0, the floor lifts it to 1, and the cap of 2
never binds, so the answer is 1. And my first edit to fix that row silently did
nothing, because `gofmt` had realigned the struct literal and my exact-string
replacement no longer matched; the test kept failing with the same message until
I checked the line rather than assuming the edit had landed.

### Confirmed in passing

`vslot_362` opens with `if (slot0x110() == slot0x108() && slot0x114() ==
slot0x10c()) return` — "both pools are full, nothing to do". That is a fifth
independent witness that slot `0x110` is **MaxHP** and not the `GetCurHP` its
stub string claims: comparing a value to itself would make the guard
unconditional.

`docs/SYSTEMS.md`'s regen row now has no caveat.

## Sweeping the tracker's caveats, and a tool trap (2026-09-17)

Last tick a caveat in `docs/SYSTEMS.md` led straight to a shipped test that
encoded a gap as a fact. That generalises, so this tick swept the whole caveat
column — 23 rows carry one.

### Two caveats were stale and one was wrong

- **Guild** still listed the alliance rules (`FUN_005c6550`) and guild war
  (`FUN_005c6b60`) as open. Both were recovered this session (v0.1.317,
  v0.1.318).
- **Persistence** said "the interface and the **39** procedures are whole" and
  "none of the **35** runtime tables" — both numbers this project corrected
  itself (71 and 54). The tracker had drifted from the pages it points at.
- **Teleport network** said to "read the `_REFTELELINK` consumer at
  `0x0082d770`". That address is the table **loader** — it binds the name
  `"_REFTELELINK"` and walks rows, exactly like `_REFCHARGEN`'s loader. No
  consumer has been located, and the caveat now says so instead of sending the
  next reader to the wrong function.

A tracker that tells you a solved thing is open is worse than one that says
nothing, because it costs a tick to find out.

### `refRecord[0xa4]` is `_RefObjCommon` field 28

Two caveats — durability and alchemy — both said they were blocked on
"`RefObjItem::ExtractData` counted through". **That premise was wrong.**

`RefObjItem::ExtractData` (7,052 bytes) makes only 23 direct stores across 19
distinct offsets, and **every one is `≥ 0x198`**. It does not write `+0xa4` at
all. The field belongs to the **common** record, and running the scanner on
`RefObjCommon_ExtractData` resolves it positively: **field 28 → `+0xa4`**.

So the durability caveat has moved from "needs a function counted through" to a
specific, positive identification.

### What it still does not give, and why that is the doc's own rule

A field index is **not** a text column index. `refobj_binary_format.md` says it
outright — the binary tables are self-describing, carry a per-column schema of
`(index, width)` records, and the parser **skips** columns it does not want, so
"binary field 57 and text column 57 are different fields". That page exists
because this exact inference was made and corrected before.

So `refRecord[0xa4]` is field 28 and its itemdata column is still unknown, and
mapping it needs the per-column schema rather than a field count. Recorded in
`repair.UnitPrice`, where `priceBasis` stays a caller-supplied input for that
reason rather than for a vague one.

### A tool trap worth more than the finding

`/var/tmp` holds both `fields.py` and `fields2.py`. Running the obvious one:

	fields.py  RefObjCommon_ExtractData ->  42 fields,  4 offsets resolved
	fields2.py RefObjCommon_ExtractData ->  58 fields, 20 offsets resolved

## I misread my own source page, and the correction opened a conflict (2026-09-17)

Last tick I identified `refRecord[0xa4]` as `_RefObjCommon` field 28 and then
said the field index gives **no** text column, citing
`refobj_binary_format.md`'s line that "binary field 57 and text column 57 are
different fields".

**That misread the page.** Read in full, it says the opposite for the range that
matters:

> The two agree on field order — four independent anchors land exactly (ID at
> index 1, Country at 14, the four requirement pairs at 32..39, the five asset
> strings at 52..56) — which is why treating "consumed field N" as "text column
> N" **has worked**. It stops working at the last common field.

The break is at 57, where the binary carries the link to the type-specific
record and the denormalised text table does not. **Field 28 sits inside the
anchored range**, bracketed by the anchors at 14 and 32..39. So field 28 is text
column 28.

I quoted the one sentence that supported the cautious answer and did not read
the paragraph it sits in. Being wrong in the conservative direction is still
being wrong: it parked a solved question as blocked.

### And then the answer did not fit

Measured on the real table — `itemdata_1000`, 837 rows, **UTF-16LE** (a first
read with latin-1 produced plausible-looking garbage) — columns 28 and 29 are a
**paired range**: `c29 ≈ 1.5 × c28` on every row, and `c28` climbs monotonically
with weapon tier, 198 → 2020 across `SWORD_01_A` … `SWORD_05_B`.

That is the shape of a durability or stat pair. It is not the shape of a price.
And `repair.go` cites the engine as

	price = (float)refRecord[0xa4] / (float)item[0x194]

A durability divided by the instance's max durability is ≈ 1, which would make
`UnitPrice` a constant.

**So something is wrong and this tick does not know which.** Either the
field-to-column identification fails here in a way the four anchors do not
catch, or `refRecord[0xa4]` is not the price basis that comment has called it
since it was written.

**Not resolved, and deliberately not guessed.** The shape of a column is a
curve, and this project's rule is that a use-site settles meaning — the rule
exists because characterdata col 79 was promoted on a curve twice. The probe is
named instead: read what writes `_RefObjCommon+0xa4`, and what `item[0x194]`
actually holds.

`priceBasis` stays a caller-supplied input, now for a stated reason rather than
a vague one, and `SYSTEMS.md`'s durability caveat carries the conflict.

Nothing srrevamp uses changed; `go test -p 1 ./...` green.

## The repair basis is itemdata column 28, and the conflict was mine (2026-09-17)

Took the probe the previous tick named — read what fills `_RefObjCommon+0xa4`
and what `item[0x194]` holds — and it dissolved the conflict rather than
deciding it.

### The formula, re-read

`GItemEquip::ComputeRepair` (`0x00496e60`) reaches the ref record through **two**
dereferences, which the old comment glossed as one:

	00496e94  mov esi,[eax+0x34]      ; the instance's data block
	00496e97  mov ebx,[esi+0x38]      ; current durability
	00496eaf  mov edi,[eax+0x194]     ; max durability
	00496ee6  mov edx,[esi+0x18]      ; -> THE REF RECORD
	00496ee9  mov ecx,[edx+0xa4]
	00496eef  fild [edx+0xa4] ; fild [eax+0x194] ; fdivp
	00496f1b  fld1 ; fcom             ; clamp at 1.0

So `price = refRecord[0xa4] / maxDurability` is exactly right, and
`item[0x194]` really is max durability — it is the minuend of the "anything to
repair?" test.

### The conflict was an off-by-one of mine

The previous tick reported columns 28/29 as a 1.5-ratio pair climbing with tier
and called that "durability-shaped", concluding something must be wrong.

**The pair is 27/28, not 28/29.** My column dump printed `r[2], r[6], r[7],
r[26]…` under a header that labelled them `name, c6, c7, c26…`, and the long name
string in the `r[6]` slot made the printed columns look shifted by one. Column 26
is **Price** — `export-refdata`'s own `fPrice = 26`, and the values 890/1500/2250
are exactly that. Durability is **63/64**, confirmed by the same map and by that
tool's test fixture (`62/76`, which is literally `ITEM_CH_SWORD_01_A`'s row).

So nothing about the binary was inconsistent. I built a conflict out of
mislabelled output and then correctly refused to resolve it by guessing — which
was the right call for the wrong reason, since the thing to check was my own
probe.

### What column 28 is, from the use-site

`price = basis/maxDurability` and `cost = price * units`, so repairing from zero
to full buys `units = maxDurability` and costs **exactly `basis`**. Column 28 is
therefore **the item's full-repair cost in gold** — an identification from the
arithmetic, not from the column's shape.

Against the real table:

| item | col 28 | durability | gold/unit | col 26 (Price) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `ITEM_CH_SWORD_01_A` | 297 | 62/76 | 3.9 | 890 |
| `ITEM_CH_SWORD_03_A` | 1426 | 71/87 | 16.4 | 15,250 |
| `ITEM_CH_SWORD_06_A` | 3718 | 87/107 | 34.7 | 40,000 |

`TestFullRepairCostsExactlyTheBasis` pins the identity on five real items.

### What this closes and what it does not

`SYSTEMS.md`'s durability caveat loses the conflict and gains a column number.
`priceBasis` is still a caller-supplied input to `repair.Estimate` — the value is
now *known* to be itemdata column 28, but `refdata.Item` does not carry that
column yet, so wiring it is a schema change rather than a constant.

The reading of the tick: **"the answer does not fit" is a claim about the probe
at least as often as about the binary.** The previous tick's instinct not to
promote a curve was right, but the next step should have been to re-check the
dump's column labels, not to write the conflict up as a property of the engine.

## The suite was red and I reported it green (2026-09-17)

Wiring `RepairCost` through, the full suite failed — and the failure had nothing
to do with the change.

`TestRecoveredNamesFileIsWellFormed` allows `origin` to be `engine` or
`descriptive`. **191 of `recovered_names.tsv`'s 302 rows use a third value,
`reading`**, which neither the test nor the file's own header documented. So the
test has been failing on the file's *dominant* origin for as long as those rows
have existed — and it is verified failing at **v0.1.325**, with the file
unchanged across this whole session.

I reported `go test -p 1 ./...` as green on that tick and on several others.
**Those reports were wrong.**

### How

The command was

	go test -p 1 ./... 2>&1 | grep -v "^ok\|no test files" | head; echo "EXIT=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"

`head` closes the pipe after ten lines, which SIGPIPEs `grep` and then `go test`.
A run killed part-way through does not report the failures it had not reached
yet, and the status read back is not a completed run's. The truncation I added to
keep output short is what hid the failure.

The second form I reached for was no better:

	go test ... | grep -vE "^ok|no test files"; echo "REAL_EXIT=$?"

`$?` after a pipeline is the **last** command's status, so that printed *grep's*
exit — 1 meaning "no lines matched", i.e. **success reported as failure**. Two
different wrappers, two different wrong answers, in the same tick.

What actually works, and what this loop should use:

	go test -p 1 ./... > log 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"; grep -E "^(FAIL|---)" log

Run to completion, status from the command itself, output inspected separately.
Verified green that way: exit 0, 52 packages, no FAIL lines.

### The fix

`reading` is a real origin — it appears in applied Ghidra names too
(`origin=reading` on `GItemEquip::ComputeRepair`) and means *read off the
function's behaviour rather than off a string*: stronger than `descriptive`,
still not the engine's own word. It is now documented in the file's header and
accepted by the test, with the set stated as closed so a fourth value is a typo.

### What this costs

Every "`go test -p 1 ./...` green" in the entries above this one was produced by
the truncating form. The *code* changes in them are fine — each tick also ran the
specific package it touched, unpiped — but the suite-wide claim was not
established. It is established from here.

## The academy membership check, read in assembly (2026-09-17)

`academy.md` carried an open question with a wiring target already built: two
level floors, 41 and 61, sharing one refusal, with "which branch is which role"
unread. The read settled the mechanics and corrected two recorded facts; it did
not settle the roles, and the entry says why.

**The refusal code was wrong.** `academy.md`, `academy.go` and the function's
Ghidra comment all gave it as `0x6818`. **`0x6818` is not in the client's error
table.** The branch pushes `0x6822`, which *is* `TC_ERROR_POSIBLE_41L`: the name
was right and the number beside it was not. No Go code used the wrong value; it
lived only in prose, which is how it survived three copies.

**The predicates were vague.** They were recorded as `a != 0` and `b() != 0`.
In assembly they are two tiny functions comparing a **class byte at
`member[+0x34][+0x50]`** against `2` and `1`, and the level is a **byte at
`[+0x53]` of the same record**, the looked-up member's stored level rather than
the caller's. Class 2 needs level ≥ 41 (`cmp dl,0x28 ; jbe refuse`); class 1
needs ≥ 61 (`cmp dl,0x3c ; ja pass`). Ghidra's `extraout_DL` naming made it look
like each helper returned a level; neither touches `DL`. The level is loaded
once, before either call.

**Wired**: `MembershipLevelFloor`, `MeetsMembershipLevel`, `MemberClass1/2` and
`ErrMembershipLevel = 0x6822`, with boundary tests at 40/41 and 60/61, and a test
that fails if the two classes' floors are swapped, which a test checking only
the set {41, 61} would never catch.

**Roles not named.** `FUN_005e0790` and `FUN_005e0a30` both skip `class == 1`
members inside a loop over the camp, which looks like "everyone except the
master", and 61 is one above the founder level of 60. Two suggestive readings
agreeing is still not a use-site. This loop's rule exists because a column was
promoted on a curve twice, and "two hints agree" is how a curve feels from the
inside. The probe that would settle it is a refusal whose *name* says master or
apprentice, gated on the class byte; none was found in the functions read.

Suite verified unambiguously: `go test` exit 0, 52 packages, no FAIL lines.

## Academy roles settled — and the reading I declined to promote was wrong (2026-09-17)

The previous tick left one question open with a named probe: *a refusal whose
name says a role, gated on the class byte*. It worked, and it proved the
suggestive reading the previous tick declined to promote was wrong.

**The engine's roles are student and guardian.** `academy.md` framed the camp as
"a master and apprentices". That came from outside knowledge of the game, not
from any read; the refusal vocabulary uses `STUDENT_COUNT_OVER` and
`SECOND_GUARDIAN_COUNT_OVER`.

**Each role reaches the class byte by use-site alone.** `STUDENT_COUNT_OVER` is
raised by cap `FUN_005e44d0`, which calls count `FUN_005e4460`, which counts
members for which `FUN_005e36e0()` holds, i.e. class byte `== 2`. The
second-guardian chain goes `FUN_005e4450` → `FUN_005e43e0` → `FUN_005e36c0()` →
`== 1`. So **class 2 is a student, class 1 a second guardian**.

**Caps, from assembly:** `cmp eax,0x5 ; sbb eax,eax ; add eax,1` gives full at
**5 students**, and `cmp eax,0x2` gives **2 second guardians**. Ghidra renders
them `4 < count` and `1 < count`. Equivalent, but the engine's literals are 5 and
2, and a decompiler-rendered bound has been read one too few before in this
project.

**The invite routine assigns the role by the invitee's level**: ≤ 39 student,
40–59 second guardian, ≥ 60 a third branch whose refusal was not read and is not
named.

### The wrong reading

Last tick recorded that two functions skip `class == 1` members inside a loop
over the camp, "the shape of 'everyone except the master'", and that 61 is one
above the founder level of 60: two suggestive readings agreeing on class 1 being
the master. **Class 1 is the second guardian.**

Neither reading was promoted, and that restraint is the only reason no code
shipped the wrong role. This is the characterdata-col-79 rule demonstrated
inside two ticks rather than cited: *two hints agreeing is how a curve feels from
the inside*, and the thing that settled it was a chain of calls ending at a
refusal the engine named.

### Wired

`MemberClassStudent = 2`, `MemberClassSecondGuardian = 1` (the old
`MemberClass1/2` kept as aliases), `MaxStudents = 5`, `MaxSecondGuardians = 2`,
`StudentMaxInviteLevel = 39`, `SecondGuardianMaxInviteLevel = 59`, `RoleFull`
and `InviteRole` (which returns `ok = false` for 60+, the unread branch).
`TestMembershipLevelsAreRecordedByValueNotRole` existed to make exactly this pass
change the constants deliberately; it is replaced by
`TestMembershipLevelsByRole` and `TestRoleClassCodes`, the latter pinning the
swap a "class 1 is the master" reading would have shipped.

Suite verified unambiguously: `go test` exit 0, 52 packages, no FAIL lines.

## The academy's "third branch" was a refusal (2026-09-17)

Last tick left one branch of the invite routine unnamed: invitees of level 60 or
more jump to `0x0051937f`, recorded as "a third branch, NOT read".

**It is not a role.** The block is `push 0x3 ; call send(0xb472) ; ret`, and
`00519305 ja 0x51937f` is its only entry. Invitees of 60+ are refused outright.
The academy has exactly **two** invitable roles, student (≤ 39) and second
guardian (40–59).

Result `3` is generic: the same routine sends it when the target fails vtable
slot `0x1c`, `IsPC`, so it means "cannot invite this character" rather than
anything about level. Not a `TC_ERROR_` code, so it has no client name.

**A boundary with both sides read.** The founder floor is 60 and the invite
ceiling is 59: no level can both found and be invited, and none can do neither.
Both constants were recovered independently, from `FUN_004e4680` and this
routine, and `TestFounderFloorMeetsInviteCeiling` holds them together. That is a
structural claim about two read numbers, not a claim about what the founder's
role is. Whether "second" guardian implies the founder is the first is unread and
stays unwritten.

Recorded because it is the cheap version of an expensive mistake: leaving a
branch as "a third role, unread" invites the next pass to go looking for a role
that does not exist. Reading the branch took one disassembly.

Suite verified unambiguously: `go test` exit 0, 52 packages, no FAIL lines.
