## 2026-09-18 — auditing every recovered vocabulary for the same decoder bug

A length assumption in a decoder has now silently dropped codes twice — the stat tags published
with four-character codes truncated to three, and `skillparam` published without its two- and
three-character codes, losing `'att'`. Both times nothing downstream could see the gap. Rather
than move on, this tick audited the other vocabularies for the same fault.

**The stat-tag vocabulary is complete.** Re-extracted with variable-length decoding,
`Stat_ApplyTaggedModifier` compares **43 distinct tags** — 6 two-character, 10 three-character,
27 four-character — and all three lengths are present in what was published. That artifact was
sound.

**And the shipped tables are correctly partitioned by source**, which was the real question:

	ParamFor           24 keys, every one a tag the dispatcher compares
	SecondParamFor      1 key,  likewise
	ResistCategoryFor   5 keys, likewise
	LabelFor           16 keys, one ('dura') the dispatcher never sees
	BonusUnit           9 keys, two ('er', 'hr') the dispatcher never sees

The three tables claiming dispatcher provenance hold **nothing** that the dispatcher does not
compare. The outliers are all in `LabelFor`/`BonusUnit`, which are read from the *item dumper* —

## 2026-09-18 — what a skill parameter actually does: 47 codes mapped to the params they drive

The skill vocabulary gave code -> field. The open half was what a code *means*, and the answer
is the same one this project keeps arriving at: **the use-site settles it.** For a skill
parameter the use-site is `ApplySkillParamsToChar`, the function `EngageSkill` calls to turn a
skill's parameters into the character's stats.

It is a run of guarded blocks — `if (skill+off) { … ParamKeeper_SetParam }` — so the pairing is
local. The param id travels in EDI and is invisible in the C, so this was read from the asm with
each block bounded by the next skill-field reference. **47 codes drive a ParamKeeper write**, 20
of them exactly one param. Now in `skillparam.DrivesParams`.

**Being inside that one function is what makes it safe.** A binary-wide sweep of these offsets
was tried earlier and was useless — `CQNO_RM_MEETROC_6::PayQuestReward` appeared to read sixteen
skill fields, because quest structs have fields at the same offsets. `ApplySkillParamsToChar` is
provably a skill consumer, so an offset it reads is a skill offset by construction. The
collision problem is dissolved rather than filtered.

**Six entries validate the table against work done before it existed:**

	'stri' -> 1        Strength, the param combat.ParamFor gives 'str'
	'inti' -> 2        Intellect, likewise for 'int'
	'hpi'  -> 3        the MaxHP chain head, likewise for 'hpa'
	'mpi'  -> 4        the MaxMP chain head, likewise for 'mp'
	'bgra' -> 27..32   exactly combat.ResistParams, the run 'rals' writes
	'luck','alcu' -> 173, 172   the two params the enchant success-rate readers consume

The `'bgra'` one is the strongest: a skill parameter and an item tag, recovered weeks apart from
different dispatchers, writing the same six consecutive params. A test now asserts it, so if
either table moves without the other, one of them fails.

A code driving several params is not an error — `'defp'` writes both the physical and magical
flat absorbs, `'bgra'` the whole resist family. **What is not claimed is the arithmetic**: how a
parameter's value becomes the param's, which slot it lands in, or how contributors combine. Only
which params a code touches is read.

Full suite green, 53 packages.

## 2026-09-18 — half the arithmetic: which slot each skill parameter writes

Last tick mapped 47 skill parameters to the params they drive and said plainly that the
arithmetic was not claimed. The most tractable piece of it is the **slot**, because
`ParamKeeper_EvaluateParam` combines a param's four accumulators as

	value = base * (1 + pct/100) * mult * (scale/100)

so the slot says whether a skill parameter adds a flat amount, a percentage or a multiplier.
It is the first visible argument to `ParamKeeper_SetParam` — the last pushed immediate before
the call — read from the same bounded blocks. **47 codes, 107 contributions: 70 base, 20 pct,
16 mult, 1 scale.** Now `skillparam.Contributions`.

**The table validates itself structurally, and nothing in the extraction set that up.** The
binary pairs a flat code with a ratio code over the same params:

	'apau' -> 13, 14, 15, 16  in the BASE slot
	'apru' -> 13, 14, 15, 16  in the PCT  slot
	'defp' -> 5, 6            in the BASE slot
	'defr' -> 5, 6            in the PCT  slot   (plus 7, 8, 12 in base)

Two codes covering one set of params through different slots is exactly an absolute/percentage
pair. The slots were read and the pairing fell out of them; a misread slot would break it. A
test asserts both pairs, so the invariant guards the reading rather than decorating it.

Other structure is visible and deliberately left unnamed: `'hide'`, `'hst2'`, `'hst3'`, `'hste'`
and `'STSP'` all multiply params 23 and 24, and `'dru'`/`'dru2'` write the same four params —
coherent families, but the mnemonics are not evidence and no meaning is assigned.

**Still not claimed**: how a parameter's own value becomes the number written, and how several
contributors to one slot combine. The slot is read; the arithmetic inside it is not.

Full suite green, 53 packages.

## 2026-09-18 — re-deriving a shipped formula, and one reading of mine that was wrong

Taking "stop inventing, be grounded" at the largest invented value: skill damage. Re-derived
`Formulae::Formula_SkillPhysDamage` from the asm without looking at what the repo already had,
then compared.

**The shipped implementation is right on every point.** `combat.SkillLevelPenaltyPerLevel` and
`SkillLevelPenaltyFloorPercent` already carry 2.5% per level and a 10% floor, gated on the level
difference being positive, and an independent reading agrees: the gate at `40f643`, the factor
`1 - (d * 2.5)/100`, the `imul 0x51eb851f ; sar edx,5` divide-by-100 making the floor 10% of
base, and the clamp to `[floor, base]`. The two constants were additionally read **out of the
binary's data** rather than off the disassembly — `0x00b45e50` is the double `2.5` and
`0x00b45af0` is `100.0` — which is a second confirmation of the numbers themselves.

**One reading of mine was wrong and the repo was right.** I called the conversion at `40f671` a
rounding helper, because Ghidra renders it `ROUND(in_ST0)`. The repo's comment says `__ftol2`,
truncating toward zero. The instruction settles it: `cvttsd2si` — `tt` is truncate — with an
`fnstcw`/`fldcw` fallback for non-SSE2. **Ghidra's `ROUND()` is its generic float-to-int
operator, not a statement about rounding mode**, and taking it as one is exactly the kind of
inference from a rendering rather than an instruction that this log keeps recording.

**What is new is where the formula's inputs come from.** Reading its call site inside
`Combat_ResolveDamage`:

	58f4e2  cmp DWORD PTR [ebx+0x234],0x0   ; the branch is gated on the base being non-zero
	58f4f0  mov eax,[ebx+0x538]             ; the bonus selector
	58f4f6  mov ecx,[ebx+0x234]             ; the base
	58f4ff  call 0x40f5f0

`skill+0x234` is `'pdmg'` and `skill+0x538` is `'SAAA'` in the recovered table, so the base is
the **pdmg** parameter and the bonus is keyed by **SAAA**. That is a third independent
confirmation that `'pdmg'` is 0x234 — the branch walk that built `Field`, an annotation written
in an earlier session from a different function, and now the call site. Both are wired as
`skillparam.PhysDamage`/`PhysDamageBonus` with a test pinning the offsets.

**What stays invented, stated plainly**: `skill.Catalog`'s flat `DamageBonus` (15 and 10 for two
made-up skills). It is a fallback used only when no real skill refdata is loaded; with refdata
the damage comes from the skill's own parameters. Grounding the fallback is not possible — there
is nothing to ground it *to*, because the skills themselves are invented.

Full suite green, 53 packages.

does *not* implement is the one tried first. Named `Formula_SkillDamageCappedByHP` for what
distinguishes it structurally: its base is the `'lfst'` record, with `'BSHP'` keying a bonus and
`'mwhs'` adding a term, it applies the same positive-level-difference gate as the physical
formula, and then **clamps its result against a participant's current HP** — virtual slot 66,
`GetCurHP`, called twice.

The three inputs are wired as `skillparam.AltDamage`/`AltDamageBonus`/`AltDamageExtra` with a
test pinning their offsets and asserting the two formulas do not share a base — if they did,
one of the reads would be wrong.

**The names say structure, not meaning.** `'lfst'`, `'BSHP'` and `'mwhs'` read like abbreviations
for things, and none of that is claimed: they are named for their role in this formula. The
project's own rule is that a mnemonic is not evidence, and it has been wrong about exactly this
before.

**The gap is recorded in the code, not approximated.** `grep` confirms srrevamp has no `lfst`
path anywhere — a skill carrying that parameter takes the other branch in the real engine and
does not here. That is a missing branch rather than a wrong constant, so it is written into
`skillparam` where the next person to implement skill damage will see it, instead of being
patched over with the formula that is implemented.

Full suite green, 53 packages.

## 2026-09-18 — 'pmdg' is not magical damage, and the flag that caught it

The previous tick's own note flagged a doubt: a grep for reads of `skill+0x340` ('pmdg') found
it used mostly as a **bit field** (`test BYTE PTR [reg+0x340],0x1`), which is not what a damage
base looks like. That doubt was right to raise and it resolves in two parts.

**The table row is correct.** Reading the parser's leaf settles it: `'pmdg'` stores a pointer
into `[esi+0x340]`, the same shape as `'pdmg'`. The bit-field sites are a different structure
sharing the offset -- the collision this log has now hit six times. Checking the leaf rather
than the grep is what separates them.

**But the interpretation was wrong, and it was mine.** Two ticks ago I wrote that `'pmdg'` is
"its magical counterpart" to `'pdmg'`, on the strength of the mnemonic and the two sitting near
each other in the struct. **No damage formula reads it.** Its only readers are
`ApplySkillParamsToChar` and `FUN_00596960`, and that second one shows what it actually is.

`QueueTimedSkillEffect` (`0x00596960`) tests eight of a skill's parameters -- `'pmhp'`,
`'pmmp'`, `'pmdg'`, `'pmdp'`, `'php1'`, `'pmp1'`, `'pao'`, `'pcdu'` -- and if any is set,
allocates a record, copies all eight pointers into it, **stamps `GetTickCount()`** and queues
it. The tick stamp is the evidence: an effect applied immediately has no reason to record when
it started; one that pays out on a clock does.

All eight begin with `p`, which is suggestive and is deliberately **not** the reason they are
grouped -- the grouping is the function reading and copying them as a unit. What the `p` stands
for is not read.

Wired as `skillparam.TimedEffectCodes` with a test pinning each code to the offset the function
reads it from, and asserting `'pmdg'` is not either damage formula's base -- so the claim I got
wrong cannot come back.

Full suite green, 53 packages.

## 2026-09-18 — the skill query reply group, and a new flavour of the offset trap

Following the timed-effect record to where it is paid out: `QueueTimedSkillEffect` hands it to
`0x0059ec10`, which is a small **list insert** — the record joins a list at `object+0x278`. So
the payout is elsewhere, and finding it means finding what walks that list.

**That search was contaminated in a way this log has not recorded before.** Sweeping for
`+0x278]` returned 338 functions, and the first one read turned out not to touch the list at
all: `AQ_SkillManager::FUN_0059edc0` uses `*(code **)(*obj + 0x278)`, which is a **vtable slot**,
not a struct field. The sweep mixed struct-member reads with virtual-call slots at the same
numeric offset. Every previous instance of this trap was one struct's field colliding with
another's; this is a field colliding with a *slot*, and the two are not even the same kind of
thing.

**The wrong turn was still worth the read.** That function is the reply builder for completed
asynchronous skill queries: it switches on the query type and sends one of four messages, with a
success flag selecting the failure path.

	case 0 -> 0xb0a1     case 1 -> 0xb0a2     case 2 -> 0xb202     case 3 -> 0xb203

All four are acks of real dispatch indices, and **index 0x0a2's handler was already named
`Skill_HandleMasteryLevelUp`** — which is what grounds the whole group as skill and mastery work
rather than leaving it a guess. Named `AQ_SkillManager_SendQueryReply` and the three unnamed
handlers `GObjPC_HandleSkillMsg_0a1/202/203`; applied 4, and the handler table's reply column
now carries the three acks it was missing.

The names say only what is read: each handler is one of the four the skill manager answers. The
specific operation behind 0x0a1, 0x202 and 0x203 is **not** read and is not inferred from the
company they keep.

**The timed-effect payout is still open**, and the next attempt needs a discriminator that
separates a struct field from a vtable slot — the offset alone cannot.

## 2026-09-18 — the timed effect pays out on elapsed milliseconds

The payout was found by **behaviour rather than offset**, which was the point: the previous
tick's `+0x278` sweep failed because an offset cannot tell a struct field from a vtable slot.
The consumer had to read the tick stamp the queue wrote and touch the eight pointers it copied,
so that is what was searched for — functions calling `GetTickCount` and referencing four or more
of `+0x14..+0x30`. Sixteen matched; `FUN_00596a40` matched on **all eight** and sits immediately
after `QueueTimedSkillEffect` in the same translation unit.

Named `TickTimedSkillEffect`. Its expiry test is the whole finding:

	if (param[0] <= GetTickCount() - record[+0x8])   -> expired

**That comparison is what makes `param[0]` a duration in milliseconds** rather than a count or a
magnitude — it is measured against elapsed time from the stamp the queue recorded. Nothing about
the name or the position says that; the arithmetic does.

The record layout falls out of the pair:

	queue record   +0x08  the GetTickCount() when the effect began
	               +0x14  the eight parameter pointers, stride 4, to +0x30
	parameter      [0]    duration, milliseconds
	               [1],[2] values used by mode 1
	               [3]    mode -- 0 and 1 are handled, and the QUEUE REFUSES mode 2

Mode 2 being refused at queue time is worth recording: a third mode exists and this path is not
it, which is a fact about what is *not* here.

Wired as constants in `skillparam` with a test that the eighth pointer lands exactly where the
queue writes it, so the layout cannot drift.

**Left unresolved and said so**: what modes 0 and 1 mean, what virtual slot `0x4fc` does with the
value, and why the apply path is gated on the same byte the expiry sets — that control flow reads
oddly and is not explained rather than being smoothed over.

Full suite green, 53 packages.

## 2026-09-18 — the effect-application slot is a forwarder, and the slot number proves nothing

Resolving virtual slot `0x4fc`, the call `TickTimedSkillEffect` applies its effect through.

**Slot 319 has two implementations, not one.** `FUN_004a7500` sits there in the seventeen
character and COS classes, `FUN_0048f6d0` in the seven `CGItem` classes. Both are now named
`Char_ForwardToAttachedObject` and `Item_ForwardToAttachedObject`. That is worth recording
beyond the names: **a slot number is not an identity**. Two unrelated object families share
index 319 with different code, so "slot 319" answers nothing until the receiver's class is
known — the same lesson the vtable-propagation pass arrived at by measurement, now from a
single concrete case.

**The character one is a forwarder, not the implementation.** It asserts the object at
`this+0xd8` is non-null and passes all six arguments to *that* object's slot 10. So the effect
does not land on the character; it lands on something attached to it.

`CGObj::EnterWorld` installs that attachment: `this+0xd8` is filled from slot 23 of the object
at `this+0x98`, with an assert if it comes back null. So whatever receives skill effects exists
from world entry onward and is reached through two further indirections.

**What the attached object is, is not read**, and the name says so. Three hops from
`TickTimedSkillEffect` — slot 319, then `+0xd8`, then its slot 10 — each hop is an indirection
whose receiver class has to be established separately, and guessing at the end of that chain is
how a wrong name gets into the record. It stops here with the chain documented.

Applied 2.

## 2026-09-18 — the effect attachment comes from the game world, not the character

Continuing the chain from skill timed effects, using the route that worked for the manager
singletons: follow the thing that *produces* the object rather than the offset it sits at.

`CGObj::EnterWorld` fills `char+0x98` two statements after **asserting the `CGameWorldMgr`
singleton** (`DAT_00d6a9a4`, identified in the singleton pass), by calling `0x005f6b80`. That
function is now `GameWorldMgr_FindByID`: a 16-bit id in AX, bounds-checked against the count at
`this+0xc`, returning the matching entry or asserting.

**The receiver was confirmed from a different call site than the one that prompted the read** --
at `0x0040375a` the singleton is loaded into EDI, an id into AX, then `mov ecx,edi` immediately
before the call. Taking the receiver from `EnterWorld` alone would have been an inference from
adjacency; a second site with the singleton explicitly in ECX settles it.

So the chain behind a skill's timed effect is:

	char+0x98  = GameWorldMgr_FindByID(id)      -- an entry of the game world manager
	char+0xd8  = slot 23 of that entry          -- installed by CGObj::EnterWorld
	apply      = char slot 319 -> char+0xd8 slot 10

**Skill effects are applied through an object obtained from the world the character is in**, not
through the character directly. That is the shape; what the world entry's class is, and what its
slot 23 returns, are not read. The chain is recorded so the next hop starts from a fact rather
than from this tick's guess.

Applied 1.

## 2026-09-18 — the world entry is a CGameWorld, and the chain stalls one hop later

Continuing from `GameWorldMgr_FindByID`: what class is the entry it returns?

**Answered by RTTI rather than by the offset.** Sweeping the world manager's address
neighbourhood for vtable installs and resolving them through `vt_server.json` finds
`CGameWorld_Chins_Floor5` and `CGameWorld_Chins_Floor6` built there, alongside `CGameWorldMgr`
itself. So the manager's entries are **`CGameWorld` objects** -- a thirteen-class family:
`CGameWorld`, `CGameWorld_BattleArena`, `CGameWorld_Chins`, `_Chins_Floor5`, `_Chins_Floor6`,
`_Default`, `_Flag`, `_RocFront`, `_Siege`, `CDataDrivenGameWorld`, `CGameWorldLayer`,
`CGameWorldMgr`.

That settles `char+0x98`. With the class known, its slot 23 can be read off the vtable index
instead of guessed: **one shared implementation across eleven of the thirteen**, four
instructions long --

	8240b0  mov eax,DWORD PTR [ecx+0x38]
	8240b3  ret

Named `GameWorld_GetAttachedObject`, for the role that is read: `CGObj::EnterWorld` calls it on
the world entry and stores the result on the character at `+0xd8`, which is where
`Char_ForwardToAttachedObject` sends a skill's timed effect.

**The chain stalls at the next hop and the reason is recorded.** What the member at
`CGameWorld+0x38` *is* remains unread: no function whose name contains `GameWorld` writes that
field, so its installer is somewhere else and the offset alone cannot find it -- `+0x38` is far
too common. Guessing the type from the getter would put a wrong class into the record, which is
how `pmdg` went wrong.

What the whole trace has established, and what it has not, now reads cleanly:

	QueueTimedSkillEffect -> record with a tick stamp and eight parameter pointers   READ
	TickTimedSkillEffect  -> expiry on elapsed ms, mode at param[3]                  READ
	char slot 319         -> Char_ForwardToAttachedObject                            READ
	char+0xd8             <- GameWorld_GetAttachedObject = CGameWorld[+0x38]         READ
	that object's class, and its slot 10                                             NOT READ

Applied 1.

## The skill Param block, end to end, and an off-by-one that cost half the table (2026-09-18)

The skill parameter vocabulary was an open lead in `docs/protocol/skill_params.md`: *"whether the
vocabulary is really ~105 or ~145 is open."* It is **209**, and closing it turned up a bug in the
document's own alignment that mattered more than the missing codes.

**What was done.** `SkillGlobal::RefSkill_ParseParams` (`0x00587630`) was walked structurally --
the decompiled dispatch tree parsed as a tree -- rather than by collecting `cmp` immediates. The
tree has four branch shapes, and each earlier pass matched some of them:

| shape | body is | count |
|---|---|---|
| `if (uVar1 == C) { … }` | the block | most |
| `if (uVar1 != C) goto <error>;` | the **fall-through** | 20 |
| `if (uVar1 != C) { …more tests… }` | the **else** | 2 (`spda`, `trap`) |
| `if (uVar1 == 'getv')` then switch on the **second word** | a two-word code | 1, 40 sub-codes |

**169 top-level codes and 40 `getv` sub-codes.** Classified: 146 fixed-run, 20 variable-length, 2
arrays (`setv`, `reqi`), 1 prefix.

**What makes it credible rather than a fourth guess.** It reproduces **all 131 rows of the
existing fixed-run table with zero disagreements**, including the five the document nominated as
its own controls (`att`, `defp`, `defr`, `spda`, `odar`). Three structural invariants hold that
would fail loudly otherwise: every field lies inside the parser's own `memset(skill+0x230, 0,
0x37c)`; no two codes share a field; and the tree is exhaustive, since the last code tested is
`trap` and its miss path is the parser's error string `"unknown skill param!!!"`.

**The off-by-one.** The document said the Param block starts at **column 69**. It starts at
**70**. Measured over all 33,632 rows of the seven skilldata shards in a real `Media.pk2`:

| first column | walks to the end | stops on a non-code |
|---|---|---|
| 69 | 21,385 | **11,907** |
| **70** | **32,367 (96.2%)** | **0** |

At 69 the walk reads a neighbouring column's value -- `1`, `3` or `4` -- as a code on a third of
the table. The remaining 1,265 rows at column 70 stop at a variable-length code, which is
expected: the parser does not state those run lengths. **No row hits an unrecognised code.**

**Three corrections to things this repo already asserted.**

- `efr` was "the most common stopper (9,534 rows)" and classified variable-length. It is a
  **fixed run of 7** whose first value picks which of three fields it fills (1 → `0x28c`,
  2 → `0x290`, 3 → `0x294`; anything else parsed and discarded). That is also why `skillparam.Field`
  and a second reading of the same branch disagreed about `efr` -- both offsets are real.
- `skillparam` said three codes could not be resolved to a field. It is **one**: `getv`, which
  genuinely has none because its second word selects among 40. `att` stores through the `_Dst`
  pointer the prologue sets to `skill+0x230`, and `setv` scans a five-slot array at `0x388`;
  a per-leaf reading could see neither. `refdata/skill.go`'s claim that `att`'s "branch loops
  instead of storing once" was wrong and is corrected.
- `skillparam.Codes` was 187 and is **209**; `Field` gained 24 entries.

**A structural fact that changes how the table is read.** A code's field does not receive the
parameter's value -- it receives a **pointer into the stream**, just past the code word. So
`Field[code]` and `Run[code]` are both needed to read anything, and until now only the first
existed.

**Wired through, and measured rather than argued.** `cmd/export-refdata` found `att`, `mc` and
`reqi` by scanning the whole row for the code literal -- a heuristic whose own comment spends
thirty lines arguing it is safe. It now walks the block with `skillparam.Walk` and falls back to
the scan only for the 1,265 rows the walk cannot finish. Running both binaries over all seven real
shards produces **byte-identical CSVs** (`md5 8aee684a…`, 33,632 rows). So this is not a fix:
it replaces an argument that the scan is safe with a method that does not need the argument.

The one case that looked like a live bug is not one. Skill `MSKILL_FW_HYEONGCHEON_ATTACK03_013`
has **28003 as its id** in column 2, which is the `mc` code, so the whole-row scan does find it
there first -- but `hitCountParam`'s selector guard (`cols[i+1] == "2"`) rejects it and the loop
goes on to the real one. Worth recording because the first measurement flagged it, and checking
the probe rather than the finding is what showed the shipping code was already right.

Applied 0 names; this was a format recovery, not a naming pass.

## What a skill parameter is FOR: the engine's own combat test, and a sized gap (2026-09-18)

With the Param vocabulary complete (previous round), the question stopped being "what codes exist"
and became "which ones does the engine read". A census over the 32,367 real skill rows that walk
cleanly answers the first half and re-orders the work queue:

| code | skills carrying it | status in srrevamp |
|---|---|---|
| `att` | 29,884 | read (AttackPercent/DamageMin/DamageMax) |
| `mc` | 27,543 | read (HitCount) |
| `efr` | 10,403 | **not read** |
| `getv` | 3,768 | not read |
| `pdmg` | 74 | not read |
| `lfst` | 43 | not read |
| `pmdg` | 23 | not read |

**This retired the step that was queued.** The plan was to implement the `lfst` branch, since
`Formula_SkillPhysDamage`'s caller tries it before `pdmg`. It is carried by **43 rows, 0.13%**.
Measuring before implementing is what stopped that; the mnemonics gave no hint of the sizes.

**Combat_ResolveDamage (`0x0058e5f0`) contains the engine's own definition of a combat skill.**
The function opens with a 33-term test, every term `*(int *)(skill + <field>) == 0`. Read through
`skillparam.Field` it is a list of parameter codes:

	att pdmg pdm2 ck fz fb es bu ps zb tant tnt2 dtnt lfst dttp se rt sl fe my
	bl dn st ds ca cssr csit cspd csmd cshp csmp tb   (+ efr, see below)

	if (!att && !ck) {
	    if (none of the other 31) {
	        if (!efr)                return;   // no blow at all
	        if (efr.values[1] != 6)  return;
	    }
	    local_d0 = 1;
	}

**32 of the 33 offsets resolve against `Field`, and the 33rd is `efr` at `0x28c`** — which `Field`
records under a different one of efr's three fields. Combat_ResolveDamage played no part in
building that table, so this is a second function agreeing with it on 33 offsets at once. Three
smaller agreements fall out of the same read: `skill+0x230` is dereferenced and masked with 4,
the physical bit `combat.AttackType` already takes from `att` value[0]; `skill+0x288` is read as
the pair `(2, N)`, exactly what `export-refdata`'s `hitCountParam` takes from `mc`; and
`skill+0x230`'s value[4] is read, so `att` carries five values and not four.

**The sized gap.** A skill carrying none of the 33, with no `efr` whose second value is 6, makes
the function **return before resolving anything** — no blow, not a blow of zero. Measured:

	carry none of the 33        1,813
	  rescued by efr[1] == 6       16
	  EARLY RETURN, no blow     1,797   (5.6% of walked rows)

srrevamp gives every one of those 1,797 `DisclosedSkillDamagePerLevel * level` instead, because
`session.skillDamageBonus` falls back to the disclosed bonus whenever `AttackPercent` is zero. So
an own-design constant is standing in for a case the engine settles outright. Closing it needs
`export-refdata` to emit whether a skill carries any combat parameter — a new CSV column, through
import and schema — which is the next step and is deliberately not rushed into this round.

**What is NOT claimed.** `local_d0 = 1` gates the `Formula_MitigatePhysicalDamage` call as well as
the damage floor, and the branches taken instead have not been read. So "a skill with no attack
parameter deals nothing" is proven for the early-return case ONLY, and is not asserted for the
rest. `combat.go`'s note, which described `local_d0` as picking the floor, has been extended to say
both of these.

Applied 0 names.

## Buffs stop dealing damage: the first behaviour change out of the Param block (2026-09-18)

The previous round established that `Combat_ResolveDamage` (`0x0058e5f0`) **returns before resolving
anything** when a skill carries none of its 33-parameter test and no `'efr'` whose second value is
6, and sized it at **1,797 of the 32,367** real rows that walk cleanly. srrevamp gave every one of
them `DisclosedSkillDamagePerLevel * level`, because `session.skillDamageBonus` fell back to the
disclosed bonus whenever `AttackPercent` was zero. Using a buff on a monster hurt it.

This round wired it through, end to end:

	skillparam.CarriesCombatParameter   the predicate, where the evidence is
	  -> export-refdata column 34       NoCombatParam
	  -> refdata.Skill.NoCombatParam    CSV + schema migration + both selects
	  -> session.UseSkillHandler        no blow at all for such a skill

**Verified on real data.** The exporter run over all seven skilldata shards from a real `Media.pk2`
flags **exactly 1,797** rows, matching the independent measurement, and **zero** of them carry an
attack percent — the consistency check, since a skill flagged non-combat must not have `'att'`.
The flagged rows are the right shape: `SKILL_CH_SWORD_SHIELD_D_01..04` (shield buffs),
`SKILL_ETC_TRANS_MONSTER_01` (a transform).

**The column is negative on purpose.** Skill CSV columns are a strict suffix, so an export made
before this one loads with the Go zero value. `false` means "this skill does resolve a blow", which
is exactly what every older export already meant — an operator who has not re-exported keeps
today's behaviour instead of silently muting a twentieth of the table. There is a test for that.

**Undecidable rows answer "does resolve a blow".** 1,265 rows stop at a variable-length code, which
hides whatever follows, so nothing can be concluded about them. They keep the damage they have
rather than being silenced on evidence that does not exist, and `CarriesCombatParameter` returns a
`decided` flag so the caller cannot read "none found" as "has none".

**The test was checked for being a test.** With the guard disabled,
`TestNoCombatParamSkillDealsNoDamage` fails reporting **20 damage** — a level-5 skill times the
disclosed 4 per level, which is precisely the old behaviour it is there to catch.

**What is still NOT claimed.** What such a skill does INSTEAD of a blow is not modelled: srrevamp
has no buff or heal system, so the cast succeeds, pays its costs and records its cooldown, and does
nothing else. And `local_d0 = 1` — the other branch, for a skill with no `'att'` that DOES carry
some other combat parameter — still gates `Formula_MitigatePhysicalDamage` in ways that have not
been read. Those skills keep the disclosed fallback, which is now the only place it applies to real
data.

Applied 0 names.

## `local_d0 == 1` reads: a skill with no `att` and no `ck` deals zero (2026-09-18)

The previous round left this open: `local_d0 = 1` gates the
`Formula_MitigatePhysicalDamage` call as well as the damage floor, and "the branches taken instead

	case 0:                                   // the ordinary damage kind
	  if (local_d0 == 0) {
	      result[0x28] = Formula_MitigatePhysicalDamage(...);   // physical
	      result[0x24] = Formula_MitigateMagicalDamage(...);    // magical
	  } else {
	      result[0x28] = 0;
	      result[0x24] = 0;
	  }
	  result[0x20] = result[0x28] + result[0x24];               // total

Both halves are written zero and the total is their sum, so **`local_d0 == 1` means zero damage**.

	carry 'att'                       29,884
	carry 'ck'                             1       <- one skill in the whole table
	carry NEITHER  (local_d0 = 1)      2,482
	  ...of which carry none of the 33   1,813     (the earlier return; 1,797 after 'efr')
	  ...of which carry some other         669     (resolve a blow, of zero)

## Every real skill row now has a grounded damage class (2026-09-18)

The previous round left `DisclosedSkillDamagePerLevel` on **1,526** real rows and named the two
causes. Both are closed, and the result is a partition with nothing left over.

**1. A zero percent is a real zero.** 440 rows carry `'att'` with a percent of 0, and srrevamp read
that as "no percentage": `combat.ApplySkillPercent` returned the blow unchanged for `percent <= 0`,
and `skillDamageBonus` added the disclosed bonus on top. The engine does neither.
`Formula_MitigatePhysicalDamage` (`0x0040e450`) and its magical twin (`0x0040e830`) both do

	pbVar1 = *(byte **)(skill + 0x230);
	damage = ((float)*(int *)(pbVar1 + 4) * damage) / 100.0;      // no guard around zero

and every later term is proportional to that damage, so the mitigated blow is zero.
`Combat_ResolveDamage` then floors a COMPUTED zero:

	if (total == 0) {
	    if (local_d0 == 0) { total = 1; }
	    else               { ...flag bit 0x10 on the result; the total stays 0... }
	}

So the blow is **exactly 1** — and the `else` is a third, independent site agreeing that a skill
with no `'att'`/`'ck'` deals zero. The flat min/max cannot rescue a zero percent (they join the
roll *before* the multiply), and in the data the question never arises: **all 440 carry a zero min
and max.** 420 of them are the mall pets' cold, fire and lightning skills.

Two sibling cases are identically zero for reasons the same formulas settle: `'att'` with neither
damage bit (each formula returns 0 at its own bit test — 5 more rows) and `'ck'` with no `'att'`
(both formulas open with `if (skill[0x230] == 0) return 0` — the 1 row). **446** in all, exported as
`FloorBlow` and carried to the blow as `combat.SkillPercentZero`, a sentinel that is negative
because the engine reads the percent unsigned, so no real value can collide with it. Berserk does
not boost a floor blow: its multiplier is a term inside the zeroed formula, and the floor lands
after it.

**2. The "undecidable" rows were decidable, soundly.** 1,265 rows stop at a variable-length code,
and the walk proves nothing past it. But one inference needs no walk: **a code word that appears
nowhere in the whole row cannot be in the block.** Only absence is proof — presence is not, since
the same integer can be another column's value, and there is a test pinning that direction. It
decides 1,085 of the 1,265 as zero-damage (872 of them as no-combat), and the other 180 all carry
the `'att'` literal.

**The partition, measured by running the exporter over a real `Media.pk2`.** Every count below was
predicted before the run and hit exactly:

	computed blow ('att', percent > 0, a damage bit)   29,619
	floor blow of 1                                       446
	zero                                                3,567      (2,669 of them no blow at all)
	                                                   ------
	                                                   33,632  of 33,632

	rows still reaching DisclosedSkillDamagePerLevel        0

30,064 rows carry `'att'` — the same figure `export-refdata`'s own comment recorded on 2026-09-16
from a different measurement. The disclosed constant now reaches no real row on a fresh export; it
survives for an export predating these columns and for the own-design `skill.Catalog`.

**Scope, unchanged from the previous round and still the honest limit:** all of this is the
ORDINARY damage kind, case 0 of the hit-record switch. Cases 1–4 compute damage by other means and
what selects them is unread. That is now the named next probe on the Skills row of
`docs/SYSTEMS.md`.

**Caught on the way.** The SQL store test caught a malformed `ON CONFLICT` clause — a substring
replace had matched inside it — that compiled fine and would have failed only at import. And an
existing test pinned `-1` as a "neutral" percent; nothing ever passed a negative to mean "none"
(two callers, both fed by `skillDamageBonus`), so the test now says what is true.

Applied 0 names.

## The four other damage kinds, named from the binary AND the data (2026-09-18)

The last two rounds scoped every skill-damage rule to "the ORDINARY damage kind, case 0 of the
hit-record switch" and left the other four unread. They are read, and the scope limit is now a
closed statement: **none of the four is reachable with the content srrevamp spawns.**

	kind 1   the attacker is under the monster transform     Formula_RollLevelDamage
	kind 2   the target is the hard-coded event monster      the list's value: 1
	kind 3   the target is a fortress structure or flag      FUN_0040f990 (unread)
	kind 4   the attacker wields a fortress weapon           exactly 1

All four require `attacker->IsPC()`. The full selector, its order and the evidence are in
`docs/protocol/damage_pipeline.md`; what is worth recording here is the METHOD, because it is the
one this project's rules ask for and it worked four times in a row: **the binary gives a pattern,
real data names it, and neither is taken alone.**

- Slots 244/248 turned out to be TID bit tests with a single implementation shared by all 30 object
  classes. A bit pattern is not a name. Tabulating real `characterdata` by TypeID gave
  **5 rows, all `STRUCTURE_*_FLAG`** and **71 rows, all `STRUCTURE_*`**, zero exceptions — and those
  are the names.
- `(weaponTID & 0xf800) == 0x8000` is only "TypeID4 == 16" because the weapon gate had already
  proved `TID >> 11` is TypeID4, and only "a fortress weapon" because `skill_params.md` had already
  tied code 16 to `SKILL_*_FORTRESSWEAPON`. Two earlier findings, neither made for this.
- The kind-2 list looked like a DB-loaded table. It is not: there is ONE record builder in the
  binary and its monster is a string literal, `"MOB_EV_WINTER_SNOWMAN"`. Real data: level 1,
  MaxHP 11, and the builder stores 1 as the damage — an event you win by hitting it eleven times.
- Kind 1 gates on `'msch'` value[0] == 1. Of 25 real skills carrying `'msch'`, exactly one
  qualifies: `SKILL_ETC_TRANS_MONSTER_01`.

**The TID layout falls out of the two predicates** and is recorded in `damage_pipeline.md`. Bits
1–15 are each confirmed (bit 1 against all 17,868 rows, TypeID4 independently by the weapon gate);
bit 0 is only *consistent with* column 7 and is marked unconfirmed. **(Confirmed in round 501:
`RefObjCommon_ExtractData` packs column 7 into bit 0, and `CGObj::IsCashItem` tests it.)**

**Wired, not just written down.** `combat.SelectDamageKind` reproduces the selector in the engine's
order, and `session.performAttack` applies kinds 2 and 4. Both end-to-end tests fail without the
wiring, reporting 40 — the ordinary kind's answer for the same cast.

Applied **7 names** to the server project: `CGObj::IsFortressFlag`,
`CGObj::IsFortressStructure`, `Equip_GetWeaponTID`, `EventMobList_Contains`,
`EventMobList_GetFixedDamage`, `EventMobList_BuildWinterSnowman`, `EventMobList_AddWinterSnowman`.

## The Param walk now finishes every real row: 19 markers, 1 terminator (2026-09-18)

The last three rounds scoped skill-damage rules to "rows that walk cleanly" and decided the 1,265
that stopped by a sound literal-absence fallback. This round removes the stopping: reading each of
the 20 "variable-length" codes' branches in `RefSkill_ParseParams` shows 19 are **run-1 markers**
(advance one word, point the field at the following runs, continue) and one, `ssou`, is a
**terminator** (its branch is the only one that `return`s). Reclassified, **all 33,632 real rows
walk to completion** with zero unrecognised codes — up from 96.2%.

This was pure format understanding, but it changed exporter output on 134 rows, and each change was
verified to be a CORRECTION rather than a regression before shipping:

- **123 rows: `NoCombatParam` 0 → 1.** These carry `efr` in a mode ≠ 6 and no other combat
  parameter, so the engine returns without a blow. The old literal-absence fallback saw the `efr`
  code word present and conservatively left them "resolves a blow"; it could not evaluate the mode.
  The complete walk can. Verified by walking three of them (`SKILL_ETC_DETECT_01_01`,
  `SKILL_QNO_EU_EASTEU_14_02_01`, `SKILL_CH_WATER_HARMONY_D_01`) and reading their `efr` values —
  all mode 1.
- **11 rows: `HitCount` 1 → 0.** Monster skills (`MSKILL_SD_CHIEF_HYENA_*`,
  `MSKILL_MOB_EV_WINTER_PRINCESS_*`) whose Param block is `ssou` at the first column — empty and
  immediately terminated. The whole-row `mc` scan was reading a coincidental `28003` in a column
  *past* the terminator. `HitsFor` maps 0 and 1 alike to one hit, so no behaviour change; the value
  is just correct now.

Both are the scan's documented failure mode — a code's integer appearing as data — which a walk
that finishes does not have. The exporter keeps the scan as a fallback for input the walk cannot
finish; no real row is such input any more. The invariants hold on the new output: NoCombatParam
(2,792) ⊂ ZeroDamage (3,567), disjoint from FloorBlow (446), and the computed/floor/zero classes
still partition all 33,632 rows.

`skillparam.Walk`/`Find` are now reliable on every real row, and `KindVarLen` is gone, replaced by
`KindMarker` and `KindTerminator`. Applied 0 names.

## The heal formula, read (2026-09-18)

"What a non-damaging skill DOES" is the frontier the last several rounds kept naming. The heal case
is now grounded, from `Skill_ApplyHealToObject` (`0x005a0850`) and its getter
`ParamKeeper_GetParamChecked` (`0x004b3740`):

	if 'nmh' (skill+0x598):  hp = target.MaxHP * hp / 100        # percent-of-max mode
	dHP = round((1 + GetParam(170)/100) * hp) + mwhhTerm
	dMP = round((1 + GetParam(171)/100) * mp) + mwmhTerm
	ApplyHPMPDelta(target, dHP, dMP, 0x40)

The base amount is the skill's `'heal'` value[0] (333 real skills carry it). `'nmh'` (10 skills)
switches HP to a percent of the target's MaxHP via `GetMaxHP` (slot 68). Params 170/171 scale each
half; they are read from **the healed object's own keeper** — confirmed from the call site, where the
same pointer feeds both `ApplyHPMPDelta`'s target and the `GetParam` reads, so no caster/target
guess is needed — and each has **exactly one writer**, the skill applier `FUN_00594ac0`, so they are
skill-granted buffs (a "healing received" stat). `'mwhh'`/`'mwmh'` (107/44 skills) add an Int/level
term via `FUN_00411080`, whose exact magnitude is **not read** and is flagged.

Full spec, with the grounded/not-read/not-wired split, in `docs/protocol/heal.md`. srrevamp has no
heal system, so this changes no behaviour — `'heal'`/`'nmh'`/`'mwhh'`/`'mwmh'` and params 170/171
are in `internal/skillparam` but read by no game code. Applied **2 names**:
`Skill_ApplyHealToObject`, `ParamKeeper_GetParamChecked`.

## `mwhh`/`mwmh` read: a percent of the caster's weapon damage (2026-09-18)

`heal.md`'s last open item was the exact `'mwhh'`/`'mwmh'` heal term, computed by a helper flagged
"not fully read." Read now, from disassembly (the decompile lost its `this`):

`Formula_WeaponAvgDamagePercent` (`0x00411080`), thiscall `(this, value)`:

	weapon = this->GetItem(6)                 # slot 6 = weapon, via GObjPC_GetItem (vtable slot 350)
	if weapon == 0: return 0
	avg = (weapon+0x1c0 + weapon+0x1c4) * 0.5 # 0.5 at .rdata 0xb45c50 -> average of two damage bounds
	return trunc( avg * IntLevelDamageRatio() * value/100 )

So `'mwhh'`/`'mwmh'` add a heal term equal to their percent of the healer's **average weapon damage**,
scaled by the Int/level ratio, and nothing when the healer holds no weapon. The `*0.5` of a summed
pair is what identifies it as an average; that the two floats are specifically the weapon's damage
bounds is a reading from the weapon slot and the `*0.5`, flagged as such rather than a proven field
identity.

The helper is **general, not heal-specific** — the cross-check that settles its meaning. Its five
call sites pass different skill values: `Combat_ResolveDamage` passes `'mwhs'` (skill+0x404,
`AltDamageExtra`), `Skill_ApplyHealToObject` passes `'mwhh'`/`'mwmh'`, and three more. All are
"percent of weapon damage" terms filed under different codes.

Two names applied: `Formula_WeaponAvgDamagePercent`, `GObjPC_GetItem` (the slot-350 forwarder to
`CGStorage::GetItem`, one implementation across 17 classes). This closes `heal.md` to two small
unread items (`ApplyHPMPDelta`'s `0x40` flag; the exact identity of weapon `+0x1c0`/`+0x1c4`). Not
wired -- srrevamp has no heal system and does not implement the `'mwhs'` alt-damage branch either.
Applied 0 Go changes.

## The alchemy reinforce offset is a 20-element strided array (2026-09-18)

`alchemy.md` carried an open probe: the reinforce base rate is read at
`refObjItem + (tier+21)*32` (`0x2c0`/`0x2e0`/`0x300`), "looks like a strided array" but "what the
offset means is not settled -- counting fields through 7,052 bytes of ExtractData is this system's
next probe." Settled, and not by counting fields.

`RefObjItem::ExtractData` fills `0x2a0..0x520` with **one loop**, not sequential fields:

	local_104 = 0
	do {
	    element = param_1 + (local_104 + 0x15) * 0x20     ; (tier+21)*0x20, base 0x2a0, stride 0x20
	    *(uint32*)element     = next 4-byte token          ; the dword LookupPackedRate reads
	    RefData_ReadStringField(element + 4)               ; a per-element string
	    local_104 = local_104 + 1
	} while (local_104 < 0x14)                             ; 20 elements

So the region is a 20-element array of `[dword, string]` (0x20 each). `(tier+21)*32` is
`element[tier]`; `CEnchant_Reinforce::LookupPackedRate` reads the dword of elements 1-3. This is why
no field count maps these to text columns -- they are array indices, which the doc had concluded but
now has the mechanism for.

It also cross-checks fields.py: its resolved offsets run `0x198..0x294` then jump to `0x524..0x570`,
and the gap `0x298..0x520` IS this array -- so the "unresolved" span was array data, not missing
work. And it qualifies the reinforce reading: element 0 (`0x2a0`) is read as a TimeSpan and
ExtractData's error calls the array "item cooltime", so it is a general per-index array (cooltimes,
and packed reinforce rates in elements 1-3), not a reinforce-only table. `LookupPackedRate` is one
consumer, not its definition.

Docs only; `CEnchant_Reinforce::LookupPackedRate` was already named. Not wired -- srrevamp's alchemy
uses its own rates and has no real per-item reinforce table loaded. Applied 0 names.

## Item reuse cooltime is minutes-scale, at record+0x2a0 (2026-09-18)

Following the strided array, element 0 (`item+0x2a0`) is the item's **reuse cooltime in minutes**,
settled from the asm rather than the mnemonic. `GObjPC::FUN_00440120` (the item-use result builder)
at `0x4402ea` calls `TimeSpan_SetDaysMinutesSeconds(days=0, minutes=item[0x2a0], seconds=0)` --
`push 0 / push [esi+0x2a0] / xor ecx,ecx` -- so the span is `item[0x2a0] * 60s`, copied into the
use-result packet at `+0x170`. The unit matters: it is minutes, not seconds (so NOT the HP/MP-potion
cooldown, which is seconds and category-based) and not days (a mid-read error the asm corrected --
the `TimeSpan` helper's first arg is days, but the call passes the cooltime as *minutes*). It is the
long reuse delay a scroll or special consumable carries.

**srrevamp gap, grounded and honest:** `session.useitem` enforces NO item cooldown -- a consumable
can be used as fast as the client sends. Wiring the real one needs the itemdata column that feeds
`item+0x2a0` imported into `refdata.Item`; the column is not identified (it is inside the
loop-populated strided array, not a sequential field), so this is recorded as a grounded gap with
its anchor, not a guessed constant. **SUPERSEDED, round 263 (2026-09-19):** the array is the
itemdata Param/Desc128 block and the REUSE DELAY is the element whose descriptor reads
`COOLTIME:<group>` (`ref+0x520` group, `ref+0x524` ms; `Item_HandleUseItem` -> `0x185b`). No potion
carries one, so "no cooldown on potions" is the engine's rule; the 148 rows that do are exported
(item columns 64-65) and gated in `UseItemHandler`. Two leads this tick -- teleport cost/level (cols 3/8/9) and the
item cooltime -- were run down; teleport's consumer was not located and is unbuilt in srrevamp, and
the cooltime is minutes-scale as above. Docs only, applied 0 names.

## The floor band uses a tenth of the BASE, not the damage — a shipped bug fixed (2026-09-18)

Re-deriving the minimum-damage rule from asm (chasing the "ResultDamage is under PhyAttackPoint's
5%" string) turned up that `combat.ApplyFloorBand`, shipped and cited, had it wrong. Stage 16 of
`Formula_MitigatePhysicalDamage`: a blow mitigated below 5% of its pre-mitigation base is reshaped
to `1 + (band-1) * rand()/32767` where **`band = base * 10 / 100`** — a tenth of the BASE. The
shipped code computed `band = damage * 10 / 100`, a tenth of the already-mitigated damage.

The FPU trace settles it: at `40e6f9` `fmul st,st(1)` forms `0.05*base`; `40e6fb` `fcomp st(2)`
compares it with the damage and pops; `40e6ff` `fstp st(1)` pops the damage and leaves the base on
the stack top; `40e706` then multiplies THAT (the base) by 10 and divides by 100. `[esp+0x28]` (the
base) is the same operand the 5% threshold uses, confirmed by the compare direction.

The bug was degenerate in the direction that matters: since the branch only runs when damage < 5% of
base, a tenth of the damage is always ~1 — the constant-1 the stage exists to replace. The function's
own doc said it makes a hit "land for a small RANDOM amount rather than a constant 1", which only the
base reading achieves. So the code contradicted its own stated intent, and three tests encoded the
degenerate values (40→4, band top ~40); all three now assert the base reading (40→100, band top
~10000) and fail under the old `damage` version.

Effect on play: heavily out-geared hits (high-defence targets) now land for a random 1..10% of the
attacker's attack instead of ~1 — a meaningful minimum, as the engine intends. Fixed in
`combat.ApplyFloorBand`, wired already through `ResolveBlow`. `go test -p 1 ./...` green.
Applied 0 names (the functions were named).

## Combat-formula audit: the rest hold (2026-09-18)

Prompted by the floor-band bug, the shipped combat formulas were re-derived from asm and their
constants re-read from `SR_GameServer.exe`'s `.rdata`. Result: the floor band was the only error.

- **Level advantage** (`FUN_0040fd60`): `clamp(diff * 0.03, 0, 0.30)`, with 0.03 the double at
  `0xb45dc8` and 0.30 the float at `0xb45b8c` — exactly `LevelAdvantagePerLevel`/`LevelAdvantageCap`.
- **Core mitigation** (`0x0040e450`): `attack/(1+red/100) - flat`, one float rounded once. srrevamp
  rounds the quotient then subtracts integer `flat`; subtracting an integer commutes with rounding,
  so it agrees (≤1 residue from rounding a stage early, not a bias).
- **Critical** ×2 and **berserk** ×2 both trace to `0xb45f30 = 2.0`.

One low-impact divergence disclosed rather than fixed: the engine folds crit+berserk into one
multiplier applied *before* the floor band; srrevamp applies berserk after `ResolveBlow` (after the
band). Only reachable on a berserk hit into a high-defence target. See `damage_pipeline.md`.

Net for the two ticks: one shipped bug found and fixed (floor band), every other shipped combat
constant and formula re-verified from the binary. Docs only this tick; 0 names.

## MaxHP/MaxMP formula re-verified from asm — correct (2026-09-18)

Continuing the audit the floor-band bug prompted, the most impactful shipped value — the
every-character `MaxHP = Str * 10 * 1.02^(level-1)` (and MaxMP with Int) — was re-derived from
`GObjPC_InitStats` (0x4e3200) asm at the two points a floor-band-style misread could hide:

- **Exponent is level-1, not level.** 0x4e35f6 calls `GetLevel` (vtable 0x124), 0x4e3601 is
  `sub eax,0x1`, and that feeds the 1.02 square-and-multiply at 0x4e35f8. So the growth term is
  `1.02^(level-1)`, matching `character.StatGrowth` used with `level-1`.
- **The 1000 is a scale (÷100 → ×10), not a ×1000.** 0x4e32ca/0x4e32e0 push the f32 1000.0
  (`.rdata 0xb462ac`) into `ParamKeeper_SetParam` with `edi=3` -- slot 3, the SCALE slot -- which
  `ParamKeeper_EvaluateParam` divides by 100. A point of Str is worth ten of the pool. Had it been a
  direct multiply, srrevamp (which uses `HPPerStr=10`) would be 100x low; it is not.

Both constants read straight from the exe: `0xb462ac` = 1000.0 (f32), `0xb45ea0` = 1.02 (f64).
`character.derivedStat` = `round(stat * 10 * 1.02^(level-1))` matches exactly. No bug.

So the audit pass (this tick + the last two) stands at: **one shipped bug found and fixed (floor

## What consumes durability (2026-09-18)

`SYSTEMS.md`'s durability row said consumption was "entirely unread". It is read
now, by following the field's writers rather than a name: the item record's
`Data` (`+0x38`, dirty bit 4) is only ever moved by `GItemEquip::AddDurability`
(`0x00496d90`, clamp `[0, this+0x194]`, broken flag at 0), whose one caller
`CGObjPC::ChangeItemDurability` (`vslot_312`, `0x004e7100`) removes a broken
item's stats from the ParamKeeper and tells the client with `0x3052 [u8 slot]
[s32 durability]`. Every loss is **-1**, rolled by `GObjPC::RollDurabilityLoss`
(`0x004a9a90`) at `min(2*rate, 100)`% -- weapon slot 6 for kind 0, the first of
slots 0..7-except-6 to pass for kind 1, shield slot 7 for kind 2 -- and the
**rates are hit counters** written by `Combat_ResolveDamage`: the attacker's
`action+6` +1 per landed hit, a target's `+0x15` +1 per landed hit, `+0x14` +1
per blocked hit. A timed skill effect (`0x004a9a10`) can also drain the weapon
or shield one point a tick. Full spec: `docs/protocol/durability.md`.

Two things this settled by use-site rather than by name: the skill parameter
`'dura'` is a **duration in ms** (`CGSkillObject::Update` clocks it), not
durability; and `GObjPC::FUN_005a1a20` is the percentage dice (`RollChance`),
which is why it gates the block roll and both drains alike. Six names added to
`recovered_names.tsv`. Not wired: srrevamp still has no per-instance durability,
so nothing in the server changes until that exists; the row stays PARTIAL with
that as its next probe.

## Max durability, and the item's white-stat factor (2026-09-19)

`GItemEquip+0x194` is built by `Char_BuildAggregateStats` (`0x00495d60`) run with
the **item** as `this`: `round(Dur_L + q*(Dur_U - Dur_L) + inc*plus)` from the
ref row's triple at `+0x1b0/+0x1b4/+0x1b8` (text columns 63/64 for L/U; the
increment's column is not identified), with `q = Item_VarianceFactor(0)`
(`0x00495d10`): `((Variance >> 5*group) & 0x1f) / 31.0` on the instance's
64-bit `Variance` at `record+0x30`, durability being group 0 (`xor esi,esi`
before the call, `lea ecx,[esi+esi*4]` for the shift, `fdiv [0xb45e28]` = 31.0
read from .rdata). Then `GItemEquip::ApplyDurabilityAndRateOptions`
(`0x00496a70`) nets the `'duru'`/`'dura'`/`'nrep'` options into a percent and
applies `max += round(max*pct/100)`, floored at 1 (100.0 at `0xb45af0`, read).
Two names added. Spec in `durability.md`. srrevamp still carries no per-instance
durability or variance, so no value changed; the row's next probe stands.

## The durability increment is zero by construction, and the item stat block counts (2026-09-19)

The one unvalued term in max durability, `inc * plus` from `ref+0x1b8`, is valued:
`RefObjItem::ExtractData` (`0x006a3d50`) consumes two dwords into `+0x1b0/+0x1b4`
and then writes **`+0x1b8 = 0` without advancing the stream** -- there is no
durability increment column, and the loader says so. So `maxDurability =
round(Dur_L + q*(Dur_U - Dur_L))`, nothing else.

Reading that loader's store sequence showed the item half is an array of
`(L, U, Inc)` triples from `+0x1b0` in text-column order, with `Inc` synthesized 0
exactly where the schema has no increment column (durability, block rate,
`PDStr`, `MDInt` -- four for four), the triple index being the variance group.
Anchored at both ends without counting: 63/64 by the `+0x194` store and the
repair use-site, 93 (`TwoHanded`) by `CGObjPC__AttachEquipItem` testing
`ref+0x223 == 1`. This nuances `refobj_binary_format.md`'s dead end: counting
consumed reads does convert inside 63..93; the seven unconsumed text columns
live elsewhere in the row. No srrevamp value changes.

## The white-stat roll, and a fresh item's durability (2026-09-19)

The one thing that kept per-instance durability from being buildable honestly
was `q`: srrevamp has no item variance and could not invent one. The creation
path reads cleanly. `GObjPC::InitItemVarianceAndData` (`0x007286c0`) rolls the
twelve 5-bit groups as `round(RollWhiteStatUnit() * 31)`; `RollWhiteStatUnit`
(`0x00729280`) is **the minimum of three `rand()/32767` draws** -- density
`3(1-x)^2`, mean 25%, a 31/31 group about 1 in 250,000 -- which is the skew
every player knows, now read off the binary. `WhiteStatOffset` (`0x00728ed0`)
is `round(U-L) * v/31`, so a new item's `Data` is its own max durability, and
`RefItemDrop::SetInitialItemData` (`0x00728470`) back-derives group 0 from the
`Data` it wrote so the two can never disagree. Five names added; the durability
row's every value is now grounded and its next step is construction, not
reading. The item-stats row gains the instance field map (plus level is
record+0x2c, a byte, not a column).

## The NPC interaction session, and a premise that was wrong (round 449)

Round 447's helper census is a worklist; its next entry, `FUN_005107c0` (7
callers, 447 bytes), turned out to sit at the centre of the NPC interaction
session, and pulling on it corrected a filed doc.

**Four names, all server, all applied.** `GObjPC::EndInteraction` (`0x5107c0`)
ends a session and replies `0xb04b{1}`; `GObjPC_HandleEndInteractionMsg_04b`
(`0x510660`) is the `0x04b` handler that calls it; `GObjPC_HandleTalkMenuSelectMsg_0d4`
(`0x516670`) walks the same `pc+0x2198` menu list `CGObjPC::ShowFirstTalkMenu`
builds; and `CGObjChar::HasAvailableInteraction` (`0x50cd80`) tests the
per-object interaction set.

**The correction.** `character_state.md` recorded INTERACTMODE 5 and 6 as coming
from "a switch on an NPC type byte", and concluded that naming them would be a
guess because no NPC type vocabulary is grounded here. Ghidra had rendered the
switch over a stack slot it never tied to the message read, so the client's byte
and the switch value looked like different things. They are the same slot —
`lea ecx,[esp+0x14]` feeds the `u8` read at `0x510320`, and `movzx eax,BYTE PTR
[esp+0x14]` is the switch at `0x510565`. **The discriminator is an id the client
chooses**, validated against the NPC's own set first.

That set is the lever, because **the engine names it**:
`CGObjChar::SetAvailableInteractionPerGObj` inserts into `obj+0x1c78..0x1c7c`
and `IGObj`'s base stub logs `## Illegal ##  IGObj::SetAvailableInteractionPerGObj
Entered!`. `HasAvailableInteraction` is its membership test, and the decompile
loses the comparison — `setne cl` on `find() != end` had to be read from
instructions.

**The jump table, read out whole**, gives ids **2..35** with only four bespoke
arms: id 2 → mode 5 and vtable offset `0x28c`, id 10 → mode 5, id 12 → mode 6,
id 35 → no mode at all, and every other id → the default, mode 6. So **mode 6 is
just the default**, which is why it never looked like a coherent service.

**Interaction id 2 is the talk menu, on a use-site.** Offset `0x28c` is vtable
slot 163, and slot 163 is `CGObjPC::ShowFirstTalkMenu` — named independently
from `IGObj`'s own assert, with the dump's RTTI plate stating `0x28c` itself.
The two handlers that require mode 5 are that menu's follow-ups.

**Also recovered:** `0x1c0b` / `0x1c0d` are a complementary pair ("already
busy" / "not busy"), and the `msg+0x103c := msg+0x103e` idiom, ~300 sites and
never reversed, is a cursor rewind — which shows the server **discards** the
`u32` the client sends with `0x04b`.

**Nothing to wire.** srrevamp has no NPC interaction session — no
`InteractMode` exists in `server/`— so no value moved and no tag was cut. Tests
green (`go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...`, 58 packages).

**Still open, with the probe named.** What ids 3..34 denote: they share the
default arm, which reveals nothing, so the answer is on the *writer* side —
whoever populates an NPC's available set knows the ids by name. A controlled
negative blocks the obvious route: **no call of slot 156 (`+0x270`) on an IGObj
exists in the decompiled server at all.** The only two `+ 0x270))` hits are
`ApplySkillParamsToChar` using it as a data offset and `CQSP_ALL_POTION_1::vslot_002`,
a different hierarchy where that slot number means something else (round 433's
rule). The probe control passed, so the negative is real and the set is filled
by an inlined or differently-shaped path.

## The interaction vocabulary, and a probe aimed at the wrong side (round 450)

Round 449 closed with a named open probe — what interaction ids 3..34 denote —
and said the answer had to come from the *writer* side, blocked by a controlled
negative. **Both halves of that were wrong, and finding out why is this round.**

**The negative was checked with the wrong instrument.** Round 449 grepped the
decompiled C for `+ 0x270))` and found two hits, neither a virtual call. An
instruction-level sweep of the whole binary finds **8** loads of `+0x270` — and
still not one virtual call, because every one of the 8 is an
`or DWORD PTR [reg],imm` bitmask write on an unrelated object. Control: the same
pattern finds **64** loads of `+0x144`, a slot known to be called. So the
conclusion survived, but it had been resting on a four-times-undercount, and the
decompiled-C form could not have distinguished a missing call from a call the
decompiler reshaped.

**The writer side was a dead end for a reason round 449 never tested.**
`CGObjChar::SetAvailableInteractionPerGObj` (`0x4a9550`) has **0 direct
callers** as well as 0 virtual ones — control, **41** direct calls to
`HasAvailableInteraction` in the same sweep — so it is **dead code in this
build**. The live writer is `CGObj::AddAvailableInteraction` (`0x484e40`), and
the raw set-insert it wraps is inlined into `CGObjNPCNPC::Create` and
`CGObjStruct::Create`: **an NPC or structure registers its interactions when it
is built**, from a **byte at `record + 0xc`** in a container it walks, not from
literals.

**The vocabulary came from the readers instead, and was cheap.** The 41 direct
callers of `HasAvailableInteraction` each push a literal id, and most enclosing
functions already carry recovered names:

| id | required by |
|---:|---|
| **0x0f** (15) | `CGuildManager::HandleCreateGuild` **and** `GObjPC_HandleGuildMsg_0f1` |
| **0x17, 0x18, 0x19, 0x1a, 0x1b, 0x1f, 0x28** | `SiegeFortress_DispatchCommand` (13/3/5/4/4/1/1 sites) |
| **0x02** | inlined in `CGObjNPCNPC::UseItem` — the talk menu, agreeing with round 449 |
| **0x01** | three functions, all still unnamed |

**Id 15 is the guild NPC on two independent named readers** and is the one to
trust. The siege ids all come from a single dispatcher, so what separates them
is *not* settled — reading that dispatcher's command switch is the next probe.

**A correction to round 449's own text.** It wrote "the valid range is 2 through
35", conflating the jump table's extent with the id space. Ids outside the table
take the `default` arm like any other unlisted id, and **id 40 is observed at a
real call site**, which proves it. Fixed in `character_state.md`.

**A coincidence named before it bites**: id `0x0f` is required by
`GObjPC_HandleGuildMsg_0f1`, whose opcode index is `0x0f1`. An id and an opcode,
unrelated, digits aligned by accident — the trap `jobs.md` records for job kind 1
sitting beside a minimum level of 20.

**Nothing to wire**, no name filed (the two functions this round leaned on were
already named), no tag. Tests green (`go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...`, 58 packages).

## How the client learns an NPC's interactions — and round 450 retracted (round 451)

Round 450 named `CGObj::AddAvailableInteraction` as the live writer of the
interaction set and had `CGObjNPCNPC::Create` and `CGObjStruct::Create` filling
it. **That is wrong and is retracted.** The evidence was the shared insert
helper `0x486fe0` being inlined into those constructors — but that helper is a
`set<byte>::insert` instantiation used by *several different sets*, and
attributing its sites to one of them is the COMDAT/shared-helper trap this
project already has on file. Reading the container pointer actually pushed at
each of its 11 sites splits them cleanly: three into `obj+0x130`, three into
`obj+0x90`, three into a stack local, and **only two into `obj+0x1c78`**.

**The correct model is two sets, and it explains the whole loop.**

`obj+0x130` is the object's **own offer list**, filled at construction from the
NPC's ref record (a list at `record+0x94`, one byte at `node+0xc` per entry) —
so the offer list is table-driven, which is the part round 450 got right.

`char+0x1c78` is the **per-character** set the 41 readers test, and the engine's
name for it says exactly that: `SetAvailableInteractionPerGObj`. Only two
functions write it and one is dead code, so the live writer is
**`CGObjChar::PublishAvailableInteractions` (`0x4a95a0`), vtable slot 227** —
declaring class by the round-418 LCA rule, with 13 vtables holding the address
and `CGObjChar` a base of every other. It clears `+0x1c78`, walks `+0x130`,
inserts each id, **and appends the count and every id to the outgoing message**.

**Its two callers both reply `0xb045`**, the select-entity reply. So the loop
closes: the server publishes the id list when you select an NPC, the client
picks one and sends it with `0x7046`, and the server checks it back against the
same set. It also sets `requester+0x728` — the flag `GObjPC::EndInteraction`
clears — which is why ending an interaction that was selected but never opened
succeeds rather than refusing `0x1c0d`.

**The siege split, which round 450 named as its next probe.** The dispatcher's
switch maps every fortress sub-command to its required id, and the per-id counts
come out **13/3/5/4/4/1/1 — reproducing round 450's raw-instruction census
exactly**, two readings with different failure modes agreeing. `0x16` and `0x17`
are the only arms with no interaction check, and they are also the two the
function special-cases before the switch. Recorded in `docs/protocol/siege.md`.

**The ids are grouped but still not named.** Only three of the seven have a
named callee (`0x17` tax ratio + both dungeons, `0x18` siege request, `0x19`
structure repair) and one callee is not enough to name a role. Next probe: the
log strings in the four unnamed manager blocks.

One name filed (`CGObjChar::PublishAvailableInteractions`), **held unapplied** —
one row is not worth the ~9-minute rebuild per the round-411 batching rule.
Nothing to wire, no tag. Tests green (`go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...`).
