The blocks turned out to carry something better than logs: each one **calls an
`AQ_Siege::QUERY_SIEGE_*` function** to issue its database work, and those
symbols are the binary's own names. Verified they are functions rather than
constants mentioned in passing — at `0x62f7c0`,
`AQ_Siege::QUERY_SIEGE_TAX_COLLECT(a,b,c,d)` sits on the success path with a
refusal code on the failure path.

| id | role | the engine's words |
|---:|---|---|
| 0x17 | fortress administration | `TAX_ACCUMULATE`, `TAX_COLLECT`, `HIRED_NPC` + tax ratio, dungeon create/enter |
| 0x18 | siege registration | `REQUEST_REMOVE` + `HandleSiegeRequest` |
| 0x19 | fortress structures | `STRUCT_ADD`, `STRUCT_UPGRADE` + `HandleStructureRepair` |
| 0x1a | item forge, instance 0 | `ITEM_FORGE_ADD` / `_REMOVE` / `_COLLECT` |
| 0x1b | item forge, instance 1 | the same three |
| 0x1f | structure update | `STRUCT_UPDATE` |
| 0x28 | **still unnamed** | no query at all |

**0x1a and 0x1b are the same forge twice, read rather than assumed.** The two
blocks are pairs of functions with matching sizes and matching query calls —
the COMDAT-twin shape this project has on file — so all three pairs were
diffed line by line. Each differs in **exactly two semantic places**:
`FUN_0061dac0(0)` vs `(1)`, and a flag test on bit `8` vs bit `0x10`. And
`FUN_0061dac0` opens `if (2 < *(uint *)(in_EAX + 0x38)) Assert`, **bounding the
collection at two**. So the ids index two instances of one forge; what tells
instance 0 from instance 1 is not claimed.

**Id 0x28 resisted and is recorded as such.** Its handler issues no query: it
reads a `u32`, requires `GetLifeState() == 1` (alive, round 411), and ends in a
slot `0x378` call — live state, not database work, so this lever cannot reach
it.

**One block was deliberately left unnamed.** `FUN_0062f4e0` issues
`QUERY_SIEGE_TAX_ACCUMULATE` while its own logs say
`"Before COLLECT_TAX DB work 2"` and `"Failed Update Accumulated Tax[COLLECT_TAX] 2"`.
The query name and the log name disagree, and a conflicting signal is exactly
when not to name.

**Thirteen names applied** (`applied 13, failed 0`) — the twelve siege handlers
plus `CGObjChar::PublishAvailableInteractions` held from round 451. One row came
back `KEEPOWNER`, keeping a `GObjPC` module attribution on
`HandleItemForgeRemove_0` while its identical twin took `SiegeFortressMgr`; it
was re-filed with `force` and re-applied in the same window, so the pair is
consistent and the rebuild was paid once.

**Nothing to wire** — srrevamp has no siege — so no value moved and no tag.
Tests green (`go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...`).

## The three job guilds are three interaction ids (round 453)

`jobs.md` has long recorded that the job-guild join handler maps a kind byte
`1/2/3` to `0x14/0x15/0x16`, and noted that kind 1's `0x14` equalling the level
floor of 20 is a coincidence. **What the mapped value IS was never read.** It is
an NPC interaction id, in the same vocabulary rounds 450–452 recovered, and it
goes straight into the gate:

	if (kind == 1) id = 0x14; ... else -> 0x4828
	if (CGObjChar::HasAvailableInteraction(npc, id) == 0) -> 0x480f

| interaction id | job guild |
|---:|---|
| 0x14 (20) | Trader |
| 0x15 (21) | Thief — the engine's word is "Robber" |
| 0x16 (22) | Hunter |

**Three independent readers agree**: `CInstanceCharTrijob::HandleJoinJobGuild`
and `JobGuild_HandleWithdraw` both map the client's kind byte, and
`GObjPC_HandleAliasMsg_0e3` maps **the player's own job type** (read with
`GObjPC::FUN_0060e040`) at three separate sites that jump to one shared gate.
The third is the strongest — it trusts no client byte at all. The kind names
themselves were already recovered from the engine's own two spellings, so the
chain from id to job name is grounded end to end.

**`0x480f` gains a meaning.** `error_codes.md` had it only as "pushed by
`JobGuild_HandleWithdraw`". It is **"this NPC is not your job's guild"**.

**The id space turns out to be organised.** These three sit directly below the
siege block, so **0x14–0x1b is one contiguous run of NPC roles**: three job
guilds, then the five fortress roles. That is a structural fact worth having —
it says the ids are allocated by role in blocks, not scattered.

**Id 1 is the item-sale gate**, narrowed but deliberately not promoted to "the
shop NPC". Its three readers are not dispatch handlers but entries in the
storage operation table `FUN_0050ce80` fills, beside the already-named
`CGStorage::TradeOfferItem`. `FUN_005267f0` is a validator returning the
client's own code names — `SPECIFY_POSITIVE_NUMBER_ONLY` for a count below 1,
`CANT_SELL_EQUIPED_ITEM` for a slot below the equipment boundary — and refusing
code 3 when the target does not offer interaction 1. **The sale guard is what
identifies it**; concluding from that alone that id 1 names the shop role in
general would be the step this project keeps getting wrong, and the function
serves two operation codes with only one carrying the sell check.

**No name filed this round, on purpose.** The one candidate (`FUN_005267f0`)
serves two operations and only one is identified, which is not enough. Nothing
to wire — `server/internal/jobs` has no NPC interaction model — and no tag.
Tests green (`go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...`).

## An NPC interaction, end to end — and the ids turn out to be data (round 454)

Rounds 449–453 recovered the interaction machinery in pieces. This round closed
the last link and the whole path now reads without a gap:

	refdata boolean column
	  -> the table's loader inserts an id into the associated REF OBJECT's set
	     at record+0x90                                              (load time)
	  -> CGObjNPCNPC::Create copies it to the object's own set, obj+0x130
	  -> CGObjChar::PublishAvailableInteractions (slot 227) refills char+0x1c78
	     and APPENDS the ids to the 0xb045 select-entity reply
	  -> client sends 0x7046 {entity, id}
	  -> GObjPC_HandleShopMsg_046 checks it with HasAvailableInteraction and
	     sets INTERACTMODE from its jump table
	  -> the service handler re-checks the id (41 such gates)
	  -> 0x704b -> GObjPC::EndInteraction resets INTERACTMODE and replies 0xb04b

**The finding is that the ids are DATA.** `teleportdata.txt` (`_RefTeleport`,
13 columns, `dd S d wwwww bb w b`) has its `bb` pair — **columns 9 and 10** — as
booleans that register **interaction ids 7 and 9** on the gate object, after a
lookup that fails with `"can't find associated ref obj with this teleport"`. A
second loader registers **id 8** the same way from a byte at its row's `+0x34`.
So which services an NPC offers is a table, and srrevamp can read the same
columns instead of hardcoding a list.

**What ids 7, 8 and 9 mean is NOT claimed.** None of the three has an explicit
gate anywhere in the server — they all fall to the `default` arm of the `0x046`
switch and no reader distinguishes them. The columns are settled; the services
are not.

**The gap is stated rather than hidden.** Only three registration sites exist,
covering 7, 8 and 9 — and ids 1, 2, 0x0f and 0x14–0x1b, every id whose *meaning*
rounds 450–453 recovered, have **no located registration**. The probe was a
census of direct calls to the `set<byte>` insert helper, and it would miss an
inlined insert, which this binary demonstrably does elsewhere
(`CGObjNPCNPC::UseItem` inlines the matching *find*). So that negative is weak.
Next probe: find the insert by shape — the tree-insert tail, or a `+0x94` write
in the same function as a `lea reg,[... + 0x90]`.

**One discrepancy left open.** The id-8 registrar reads its record at `+0x30`,
`+0x34`, `+0x38`, but `refdata_tables.md` lists its caller as the inserter for a
**0x1c-byte** record, which those offsets overrun. Either the recorded size
belongs to a handle or the attribution is wrong, so **id 8 is not attributed to
a table**.

One name filed (`CGameServer::RefRow_AddInteraction8`), **held unapplied** — it
needed the disassembly, because Ghidra renders the record reads against an
`in_EAX` it cannot tie to the call before them. Nothing to wire; srrevamp has no
NPC interaction model to carry the columns yet. No tag. Tests green.

## The interaction-id vocabulary, from the NPCs themselves (round 455)

Round 454's next probe was "find the insert by shape, not by the helper's name".
Run first, it **confirmed** the earlier census rather than overturning it: a
census of the containers passed to the `set<byte>` *find* helper at all 39 of
its sites — which catches an inlined find-then-insert — returns 27 on
`char+0x1c78`, 3 on `obj+0x130`, 3 on `record+0x90`, matching exactly. No hidden
inserts.

**The registrations were virtual calls all along.**
`CGObj::AddAvailableInteraction` is **vtable slot 89** (offset `0x164`),
computed from table `0xaec0a4` and checked against that table's slot 227 holding
a known address. `CGObjNPCNPC::Create` calls it **32 times with literal ids**,
each behind a comparison against the NPC's own **CodeName** — so the whole
vocabulary is named by the engine's own NPC names. 25 distinct ids, full table
in `docs/protocol/character_state.md`.

**Ten independent agreements make it trustworthy.** The attribution is a
heuristic (strings between one registration and the next), but ten of these ids
were already named from the *reader* side by unrelated evidence and every one
agrees — 0x0f `NPC_*_GUILD`, 0x14 `MERCHANT`, 0x15 `THIEF`, 0x16 `HUNTER`,
0x17 `FORTRESS_MANAGER`, 0x18 `FORTRESS_OFFICIAL`, 0x19 `FORTRESS_BATTLEAIDE`,
0x1a `FORTRESS_SMITH`, 0x1f `STRUCTURE_GATE_PULLEY_*`, 0x0c `THIEF_BUY`/`SPECIAL`.
Ids 0x15 and 0x16 are the strongest: the codenames literally read THIEF and
HUNTER, matching names round 453 derived by a completely different route.

**Three earlier items closed or corrected:**

- **Id 0x28 is named** — `NPC_SIEGE_DUNGEON_TELEPORT`. Round 452 could not reach
  it because its handler issues no database query; the codename fits a handler
  that reads a `u32`, requires the player alive, and ends in a slot call.
- **Round 452's "forge instance 0 and 1" is corrected.** The two are different
  NPCs, not two forges: **0x1a is the fortress SMITH, 0x1b the fortress TRAINER.**
- **Round 450's declined data point is vindicated.** It saw the client send id 3
  from an `IFStorageRoom` context and refused to use it. Id 3 is `WAREHOUSE`.

**Id 1 is a capability, not a role**, which retroactively justifies round 453's
caution. It is registered on **five unrelated families** — warehouse, stable,
guild hall and two fortress NPCs — so "id 1 is the shop NPC" would have been
wrong in exactly the way that round declined to be.

**A lead on a long-standing gap.** Round 361 recorded that nothing directly
writes INTERACTMODE **9** (open market) although six handlers require it. Id
`0x23` is `NPC_OPEN_MARKET_JUEL`, and `case 0x23` is the one arm of the `0x046`
switch that returns **without setting any mode**. The open-market NPC takes its
own path to mode 9 — a lead, not a finding; the path was not traced.

No name filed (both functions this leaned on were already named); one name still
held from round 454. Nothing to wire, no tag. Tests green.

## INTERACTMODE 9's writer, and a ninety-five-round gap half closed (round 456)

Round 361 recorded that "nothing writes 7 or 9" to `chardata+6` and carried it
as an open gap ever since. Round 455 left a lead. **Half the gap was a probe
defect.**

Redone at instruction level — every direct byte store to `[reg+0x6]` — the
census reads 0×13, 1×9, 2×4, 4×1, 5×2, 6×2, **9×1**, 7×0. **Value 9 is
written**, at `0x51b5bd`; the old grep missed it because that site stores in two
steps (`iVar2 = in_EAX[0xc]; *(iVar2 + 6) = 9`) while the grep wanted a one-step
`chardata + 6`.

**`OpenMarket_BeginSession` (`0x51b580`) is the writer**, on three independent
signals: it is reached only from `GObjPC_HandleShopMsg_046`'s `case 0x23` — the
one arm that returns *without* setting a mode itself; id `0x23` is registered on
`NPC_OPEN_MARKET_JUEL` (round 455); and mode 9 is what all six
`COpenMarketMgr::On*Req` handlers require (round 361). Round 455's lead is now
the finding.

**Value 7 survives, and the obvious escape route is closed too.** The natural
hypothesis was the dispatcher — `CGObjPC::SetCharacterState`'s **kind 2** arm
writes `chardata+6` from its argument, so any value could arrive there. A census
of all 98 call sites of slot 171 by *(kind, value)* finds only kinds `0x0d` and
`0x0f` as literals; **kind 2 is never used**. What remains are three
register-sourced writers, headed by round 361's own candidate
`AJStateChanger::vslot_002` (which writes the byte from a *job* field). **7 stays
open** — but its negative is now a measurement, not a grep.

**A probe defect caught before publication.** The first run of that census
reported "kind 2, ×2" and would have closed the question wrongly.
`SetCharacterState` is `ret 0x8` and its written value comes from `[esp+0x14]`,
which is **arg2** — so the kind is the *last* push, not the first, and those two
sites are really `(kind 0x0f, value 2)`. Reading the callee's own frame fixed
it. This is the same class of error as round 447's bare-name caller matching:
a census is only as good as the column it thinks it is reading.

One name filed (`OpenMarket_BeginSession`), held with round 454's — two rows is
not worth the ~9-minute rebuild. Nothing to wire; srrevamp has no open market.
No tag. Tests green.

## INTERACTMODE 7: read everywhere, written nowhere (round 457)

Round 456 left 7 as the last unnamed INTERACTMODE and named three
register-sourced writers as what remained. **Two of the three were false
positives** — that census matched any struct with a byte at offset 6, not only
chardata. `CGObjPC::FUN_004de300` is `CGObjPC`'s own constructor and
`FUN_0050fda0` is a copy constructor copying byte 6 of an unrelated record. Only
`AJStateChanger::vslot_002` was genuine, and this round traced it.

**The reads are real.** `AttachEquipItem` / `DetachEquipItem` do test 7, checked
at instruction level — `mov eax,[esi+0x30]; mov al,[eax+0x6]; cmp al,0x7`, ten
sites, two of them debug asserts and the rest real refusals.

**No literal path writes it.** All four routes into `chardata+6` were measured:
no direct byte store (0 sites); `SetCharacterState` kind 2 is **never passed as
a literal** at any of slot 171's 98 call sites; **no `mov BYTE PTR [reg+0xd],0x7`
exists anywhere in the binary**, so no `AJStateChanger` job carries it; and the
remaining indirect writers are the two false positives above.

**What this does not license.** It does not say 7 is dead. A computed or copied
value can still reach the byte, and this project has a standing rule against
exactly that inference. The established claim is narrower: **no code path in
this binary sets INTERACTMODE to 7 from a constant.**

**A bonus finding: `AJStateChanger` is the deferred `SetCharacterState`.** The
job counts down a float and on expiry switches on `+0xc` and applies `+0xd`,
using **the same kind vocabulary** — kind 2 → `chardata+6`, kind 3 →
`chardata+7`, kind 6 → `chardata+8`, kind 0 → vtable `0x1f0`, which round 411
independently named `SetLifeState`. That last agreement is what shows it is one
enum and not a coincidence, and it corroborates round 361's kind table from a
second function.

No name filed; two still held. Nothing to wire, no tag. Tests green.

## The guild NPC list, wired into the client (round 458)

The first round in this arc where a recovered value **changed shipped
behaviour**. `client/scripts/npc/npc_service_reader.gd` decided which services
an NPC's talk window offers, and for the guild it tested `codename.contains("GUILD")`.
Round 455 recovered what the server actually does, and the two disagree in both
directions.

**A premise I had to throw away first.** The plan was "the engine uses exact
codename comparison, the client uses substrings, so the client is wrong". Then
`FUN_009dddc0` — the comparison helper in `CGObjNPCNPC::Create` — turned out to
be **`strstr`**, confirmed by reading it (it walks four bytes at a time and
returns a pointer into the haystack). The tell was already visible in the call
sites: they branch on `result != 0` as a *match*, which is backwards for
`strcmp`. So the engine matches substrings too and the client's *kind* of rule
was right all along.

**The real defect is which substring.** The server tests **seven specific
patterns** for interaction `0x0f`; the client tested one short generic token:

	NPC_CH_GENARAL_SP   NPC_WC_GUILD   NPC_KT_GUILD   NPC_EU_GUILD
	NPC_CA_GUILD        NPC_SD_M_AREA_GUILD           NPC_SD_T_AREA_GUILD2

- **It missed a guild NPC.** `NPC_CH_GENARAL_SP` heads the server's own list and
  has no `GUILD` in its name, so the Chinese guild NPC showed no Guild option.
- **It invented three.** `NPC_SD_GUILD_AGENT`, `_AGENT2` and `_AGENT3` contain
  `GUILD` but the server gives them interaction `0x0c` — specialty goods — not
  the guild service. They offered a Guild button that does not belong to them.
  *Correction (round 520):* no codename test in the server gives them **any**
  interaction id. Their `strstr` chain ends in `IGObj::SetBodyMode` (slot 198,
  `0x4c6ddd`), and 0xc is the next chain, the `NPC_*_SPECIAL` literals. Removing
  their Guild button was still right.

Id `0x0f` is safe to act on because it has a **reader**:
`CGuildManager::HandleCreateGuild` gates on it, so it is the guild service and
not merely a number registered on guild-looking NPCs.

**Wired, with tests.** `GUILD_PATTERNS` now carries the server's seven with the
citation, and `npc_service_reader_test.gd` asserts all seven offer the service
and that the three agents do not — four assertions that each fail against the
old code. Green on the render box (17 ok, ALL PASS); `go test -count=1 -p 1
./...` green.

**Two things deliberately not changed.** The bare `WAREHOUSE` token stays,
because the server's own pattern for storage is the bare word too — checked, not
assumed. And `SMITH` → Repair stays as-is although the server groups
`NPC_*_SMITH` **and** `NPC_*_ARMOR` under interaction `4`: id 4 has **no reader
anywhere**, so nothing ties it to repair, and adding armour merchants to the
repair list on that basis would be the unproven leap this project keeps having
to retract.

*Correction (round 512):* the `SMITH` → Repair talk line was itself unproven,
and it is gone now. "No reader anywhere" holds for the **server** only. On the
client, the talk-menu builder `FUN_00700440` looks id 4 up at `LAB_00700b10`
and then adds nothing for it: there is no membership branch and no item. But
the client does have an id-4 reader. The NPC-select reply handler
`FUN_0088b200` tests id 4 at `0x88b8c5` and uses the result to show or hide
the store window's `GDR_STORE_BTN_REPAIR` / `GDR_STORE_BTN_REPAIRALL`. So
srrevamp's town smith now lists Buy and the end line only, and repair stays in
the store window's buttons. No NPC gets a repair talk line, `ARMOR` included.
The armour merchants carry id 4, though, so in the real client their store
window probably shows the repair buttons. The sentence above ("nothing ties it
to repair") is wrong for the client. See round 512.

*Update (round 514):* no longer "probably". The server registers id 4 on
fourteen town `SMITH`/`ARMOR` literals and eight fortress smiths, read directly
from `CGObjNPCNPC::Create` (`0x4c677f`, `0x4c736f`). The client hides the two
buttons at every NPC select and shows them again only for id 4, and vtable
`+0x5c` is show/hide. srrevamp now does the same. See round 514.

## The capability flags word, assembled — and a control that refused (round 459)

Started from round 458's open item: interaction id 4 groups `NPC_*_SMITH` and
`NPC_*_ARMOR`, but has no reader, so nothing ties it to repair. `CGObj::CanRepair`
looked like the link. **It is not** — it reads bit 6 of a flags word on the
*item's* ref row, so it answers "can this item be repaired", not "does this NPC
repair". Id 4 stays unnamed and the armour merchants stay out of the repair list.

What the detour found instead is worth more:

**Four capability readers the table had been missing.** A census of every
function reading `refobj + 0x8c` as `>> N & 1` finds accessors for bits **11,
12, 13 and 14** as well as the documented 0–10. Like bit 10 they have no
`## Illegal ##` stub, so the engine offers no name and none is invented.

**The flags word's construction, read out.** Each predicate has its own source
field, except three that share:

- **bits 12 and 13 come from ONE field**, tested `& 0x80` and `& 0x40` — a
  bit-packed value, not a boolean;
- **bit 14 shares a field with `CanDrop`** (bit 0 is `CanDrop`, bit 1 is 14);
- and **`CanDrop` is forced off when `CanTrade` is off** —
  `if (trade == 0 && dropf == 1) dropf = 0;` — an untradeable item is also
  undroppable regardless of its own column.

**A control refused, so no column numbers were published.** The natural payoff
was to turn those fields into `itemdata`/`characterdata` columns, since this
file's own header says srrevamp "cannot [model any of this] until the columns
are found". Walking the parser while tracking its own column counter yields
**47 columns with 5 strings — exactly the signature `refdata_tables.md` records
independently**, so the walk is sound. But feeding that 47 into the same walk of
`RefObjChar_ExtractData` puts the `+0x198` field at column **48**, and `+0x198`
is Level, grounded as characterdata column **57**. Off by nine.

`refdata_tables.md`'s own caveat explains it — *"the client's textdata files
carry more columns than the server reads"*. **The parser's read index is not the
file's column index**, and the offset is not constant. The bits-10/11 recovery
on file got its columns by anchoring against a real characterdata table, not by
counting reads. So the fields are identified here by *what they feed* and by
nothing else, and the column hunt stays open with the reason now known.

No name filed; two still held. Nothing to wire, no tag. Tests green.

## The capability columns, anchored — and round 459's conclusion retracted (round 460)

**Round 459 concluded "the column hunt stays open". It was already closed.**
`server/internal/refdata/item.go` carries `CanTrade`, `CanSell` and `CanDrop`
with their itemdata columns (16, 17, 20), and `shop.Sell` already refuses on
`CanSell`. The answer had reached the **code** and never reached
`item_capability_flags.md`, whose header still said srrevamp "models none of
this yet, and cannot until the columns are found" — and round 459 believed the
header. My own notes say to grep the repo's own code before a dump dig; not
doing that cost a round. Header corrected.

**The remaining columns are now anchored anyway**, by a method that does not
depend on counting reads. The parse needs one field tested `& 0x80`/`& 0x40`
(bits 12, 13) and one tested `& 1`/`& 2` (`CanDrop` and bit 14), adjacent and in
that order. A real itemdata has exactly one such adjacent pair in the region —
column **19** reads `0/128/223/255`, column **20** reads `0/1/3`, every
neighbour a plain `0/1`. That pins the run: 21 `CanPick`, 22 `CanRepair`,
23 `CanRevive`, 24 `CanUse`, 25 `CanThrow`.

**Two are confirmed by MEANING, which a shifted mapping could not fake:**
column 22 is `1` on **676/676** armour rows and `0` on **1,339/1,339**
potions/etc; column 24 is the **exact inverse**, zero on every armour row.
Armour is repaired but not used; a potion is used but not repaired.

**`CanRepair` is measured redundant and deliberately not wired.** Across three
itemdata parts — 3,879 rows — column 22's set is *exactly* the non-zero set of
the repair-cost columns, with no exception in any file, and `RepairHandler`
already skips items with no durability. Adding the flag would change no
behaviour, so it is recorded instead of implemented.

**`CanRevive` is a genuinely different flag**: column 23 matches 22 exactly in
two parts and diverges in the third, so they coincide only for ordinary
equipment.

No name filed; two still held. Nothing wired (measured redundant), no tag.
Tests green.

## The payload blocker was a register (round 461)

`SYSTEMS.md`'s Packet-protocol row has asked for one named handler's payload for
many rounds, on the grounds that "a real opcode number without the real layout
is worse than a placeholder". 93 of the 162 real request handlers are already
named, so the work was never *finding* the code. **The blocker was mechanical
and is now removed.**

	MsgBuf_AppendBytes (0x404090):  length in AX, source in arg 2

**AX is a register Ghidra drops.** Every append in the decompiled C reads
`MsgBuf_AppendBytes(&uStack_19)` and says nothing about whether that is one byte
or four, which is exactly why payloads resisted bulk reading. The sizes are
plain `mov eax,N` in the disassembly.

`tools/payload_layout.py` takes an address range and lists every append with the
length set before it, marking `VAR` when an intervening call clobbers eax. **It
declines rather than guesses**, which is what makes the output usable.

**Two controls, each a packet documented by a different route, both reproduced
exactly:** `Msg_SendTwoFieldReply` → `{u8, u16}` (round 443) and
`CGObjPC::FUN_004f0a00` → `{u8, u32}` (round 448).

**`0xb045`, the select-entity reply, is recovered** — the packet a client gets
on selecting an NPC or monster, and the carrier of the interaction ids rounds
449–455 recovered: `u8 status`, `u32 entity id`, then either a single byte or
the interaction block that slot `0x38c` appends in its place (`u8 count` +
count × `u8 id` + two conditional trailers).

**A trap the address ordering invites.** Two appends sit *after* the slot call
and look like trailing fields. They are past a `ret 0x4`, on a separate branch,
writing `{u8 = 2, u16}` — the standard two-field refusal inlined rather than
called. The `ret` is what rules them out; nothing in the decompiled C would.

This turns the row's next step from a dig into a sweep: the same tool runs over
the other 92 named handlers. No name filed; two still held. Nothing wired, no
tag. Tests green.

## The payload sweep: 312 senders mapped (round 462)

Round 461 removed the blocker (the append length lives in AX, which Ghidra
drops) and named the next step as a sweep. `tools/payload_sweep.py` does it.

**Finding the senders needed no reading.** A message is opened through vtable
slot `0x278` with the opcode as a plain push — `mov eax,[edx+0x278]; push
0xb045; call eax` — so opcode and sender fall out of the disassembly, and the
append lengths attach to whichever function they sit in.

**312 senders, 296 with at least one field, 264 fully fixed**, written to
`docs/protocol/payload_layouts.tsv`. The protocol is mostly small: 52 senders
carry a single byte, 25 carry `1,1,2`, 25 `1,1`, 17 `1,2`, 14 `1,4`.

**Four controls, each hand-read in an earlier round, reproduced exactly** —
`0xb045` `1,4,1,VAR,2` (461), `0xb04b` `1` (449), `0x3405` `1,4` (448), `0xb046`
`1,1,1` (449). And `1,1,2` turns out not to be 25 coincidences: all seventeen
`SiegeFortressMgr::Handle*` functions end in the same `{u8, u8 = 2, u16 code}`
refusal on `0xb05e`, which round 452 read by hand in the dispatcher.

**Four limits are recorded with the table rather than left for a reader to
discover.** `VAR` marks where a call may have clobbered eax and the tool
declined (32 senders); 23 senders open two opcodes and cannot have their appends
attributed; the appends are the function's own, so a payload continued in a
callee is missing — `0xb045`'s interaction block is exactly that case; and a
`mov eax,N` could in principle be setting a value rather than a length, which
the controls rather than the pattern are the reason to discount.

So it is a **map, not a spec**: field counts and widths, which is what was
missing, and no claim about meaning. The next step is the client side, whose
readers give the field *types* the server's `memcpy` cannot.

No name filed; two still held. Nothing wired, no tag. Tests green.

## The client sweep, and a cross-validation across two binaries (round 463)

Round 462 mapped every server sender's field widths and named the client as the
next source. It is, and the asymmetry between them is the point.

**`MsgStreamBuffer::Read` (`0x4f7220`, client)** takes its size as an **explicit
argument** where the server's writer takes it in **AX**. So the client side
reads straight from the decompiled C — `tools/client_read_sweep.py`, 391
functions, `docs/protocol/client_read_layouts.tsv`. Its bounds assert names the
binary's own `MsgStreamBuffer.h`, which is where the class name comes from.

**Joined through `message_handlers.tsv`: 151 pairs with both sides fully fixed.**

	agree on the first field's width   145 / 151  (96 %)
	one is a PREFIX of the other       118 / 151  (78 %)
	disagree on field 1                  6

Two binaries, two mechanisms, and they agree. **Exact equality is the wrong
test** — only 38 of 151 match exactly, but the disagreements are overwhelmingly
prefix relations, which is what the limits recorded in round 462 predict: a
server payload continued in a callee, several senders writing variants of one
opcode, client handlers that branch. Prefix containment is the metric the data
supports.

**Six pairs disagree on the very first field**, listed in PACKET_FORMAT.md. Each
is a wrong sender attribution or a real variant, and each is cheap to settle.

**A column I read wrong, caught by a loud failure.** The first join used
`message_handlers.tsv` column 2 as the client handler and matched **nothing** —
391 client functions against 3 names. Column 1 is the handler, column 2 the
registrar. The zero is what made it obvious; a join that had matched 20 of 151
would have been believed and published. (Round 449 quoted the registrar as the
client handler for `0xb04b` in passing; nothing depended on it.)

One name filed (`MsgStreamBuffer::Read`), three now held. Nothing wired, no tag.
Tests green.

## The cross-validation, corrected and settled (round 464)

Round 463 reported six field-1 disagreements. **The unit was wrong.** Counting
*pairs* makes an opcode with several senders look like several disagreements —
`0xb0c5` has **six** senders and one of them matches the client exactly. Counted
per **opcode**, over 128 of them:

	some sender agrees on field 1   121 / 128  (95 %)
	some sender is a prefix-match    99 / 128  (77 %)
	some sender matches exactly      38 / 128  (30 %)

close to round 463's per-pair figures, so those numbers were not far wrong — but
the *disagreement list* was contaminated, and the corrected one is **seven**
opcodes, two of which the per-pair view had hidden.

**A hypothesis tested and mostly refuted.** If the server writes one `u16` where
the client reads two `u8`s, the bytes agree and only the split differs. Byte
totals move the exact-match rate from 30 % to only **32 %**, so the effect is
real but small: three opcodes (`0x3809`, `0xb0b4`, `0xb16a`). They settle a
protocol fact anyway — **the same byte sequence can be written as one wide field
or several narrow ones**, so field-by-field width identity was never the right
requirement. Prefix relations remain the dominant reason for non-identity.

**`0x30eb` is settled, and the client is the odd side.**
`CGObjPC::RefreshEventGuideData` (slot 155, named from `IGObj`'s own assert)
appends eight bytes; the client's entire handler is a single four-byte read that
is discarded. One sender only, so this is not an attribution artifact.

**The caveat that governs all of it, now on record.** The client and server
dumps are **two different binaries with no guarantee of matching protocol
versions** — this project already documents two *server* builds that differ. A
residual mismatch may therefore be version skew rather than a misreading, and
nothing measured here can separate the two. What the comparison does establish
is that they are close: 95 % of 128 opcodes agreeing on the first field, across
two binaries and two different mechanisms, is not what unrelated versions look
like.

No name filed; three still held. Nothing wired, no tag. Tests green.

## The sweep is incomplete, and by how much (round 465)

Settling round 464's disagreement list turned into an audit of my own round-462
artifact. Two defects, both measured, both now in the table's own header.

**Three of the seven disagreements dissolve.** `0xb069`, `0xb06a` and `0xb47b`
read `srv 4,1` against a client starting `1`. `trs_sm_partyjob::FUN_005bf7d0`
shows why: on its **error path** it calls `FUN_005bdf50`, which opens a message
of its own, and the 4-byte append belongs to *that* message. The real `0xb069`
payload is the single byte after the `0x278` open — and the client's handler
`PartyMatch_OnRecordResult` opens with `Read(&flag, 1)` and branches on `== 1`.
**They agree.**

**So the attribution unit was wrong**: appends were attached to the enclosing
function, when they must attach to the **nearest preceding open**, because one
function can write to two messages.

**And a second open idiom was missed entirely.** `FUN_005bdf50` never touches
slot `0x278` — it allocates through slot `0x48` on a global and writes the
opcode straight into the buffer at `**(buf + 0x1050)`. Measured: **258 sites,
65 distinct opcodes, 57 of them absent from the round-462 table**, which holds
203. So that sweep covered about four opcodes in five, and said it covered them
all.

**A third thing worth flagging**: `message_handlers.tsv`'s `server_senders`
column names `005bf9e0` for `0xb069`, and that function opens **no message at
all**. It is a 2026-09-17 census by a different method, and round 463's join
leaned on it — part of why the disagreement list needed this round.

Next: re-run the sweep position-aware and with both idioms. No name filed; three
still held. Nothing wired, no tag. Tests green.

## The sweep rebuilt, and the disagreement list closes (round 466)

Round 465's two defects are fixed, and the fix is measured against the client
before and after on the same opcodes rather than asserted.

**The fixes**: appends attach to the **nearest preceding open** instead of the
enclosing function, and **both** open idioms are detected — the slot `0x278`
call and the direct `**(buf + 0x1050) = opcode` store.

	                              v1 (462)      v2 (466)
	distinct opcodes found        203           233
	comparable with the client    128           133
	agree on field 1              121 (95 %)    131 (98 %)
	prefix-match                   99 (77 %)    116 (87 %)
	field-1 failures                7             2

**Five failures fixed, none introduced.**

**Two controls, in opposite directions**, which is what makes this a fix rather
than a reshuffle. The three rows that motivated it — `0xb069`, `0xb06a`,
`0xb47b` — change from `4,1` to `1`, exactly as reading
`trs_sm_partyjob::FUN_005bf7d0` predicted, because the 4-byte append belonged to
a message its error path opened through a helper. And all four round-462
controls are **unchanged**. Correcting the known-wrong rows while preserving the
known-right ones is the pair of checks worth having.

**The two survivors were already explained**, so the list is effectively closed:
`0x30eb` (the client's entire handler is one discarded 4-byte read against the
server's 8) and `0x3809` (the same two bytes as one `u16` versus two `u8`s).

**What it still is not**, recorded in the table's own header: address-order
attribution that a branch can defeat; **1,086 appends in 274 functions omitted**
because their message was opened inside a helper; and widths only, never
meanings.

No name filed; three still held. Nothing wired, no tag. Tests green.

## The first field MEANING, on three independent sources (round 467)

Rounds 461-466 recovered the protocol's field *widths*. This is the first
*meaning*, and it holds across the protocol rather than for one opcode.

**Field 1 of a reply is a result byte: 1 = success, 2 = failure followed by a
u16 error code.**

Three sources, no two sharing a method:

- **The client, reading.** Of 195 handlers whose first field is one byte, 153
  compare it to a literal immediately, and **128 of those compare against 1**.
- **The server, writing** — a different binary and mechanism. Of the 1-byte
  appends whose source slot takes a literal, the commonest are **2 (x32)** and
  **1 (x22)**.
- **Already grounded**: `Msg_SendTwoFieldReply` writes `{u8 = 2, u16 code}`
  across 160 call sites (round 443), which is the failure half on its own.

**The limits, stated with it.** The server census resolved only **109 of 1,164**
one-byte appends — the rest compute their value instead of storing a literal —
so that side is a sample. Fourteen client handlers compare against `0` and eight
against `2`, so the convention is dominant, not universal. A single handler
comparing to 1 proves nothing; the claim rests on the three agreeing.

**Deliberately not wired.** srrevamp's `RepairResult` leads with a `u32` code
rather than a `u8` result, so it diverges. But `PROTOCOL_DECISION.md` records
the current opcodes and layouts as "placeholder scaffolding, not the
destination", so changing the wire format now would be a design change rather
than a grounding fix, and would break a working client/server pair to no
present end. Recorded as a spec fact for when the real protocol is adopted.

No name filed; three still held. Nothing wired, no tag. Tests green.

## Field 2, and a hypothesis refuted (round 468)

Round 467 settled field 1 as a result byte. Field 2 follows, and its meaning is
**conditional on field 1**:

	u8  result
	    == 1  ->  the operation's own payload follows
	    == 2  ->  u16 error code, and nothing else

**Read by hand, then measured.** `UI_ALCHEMYBOX::FUN_0086dbd0` and
`FleaMarket_OnOpenStallResult` are literally that shape and nothing else. Across
the client: of **206** handlers whose first field is one byte, **147** read a
two-byte field later, and **106 of those (72 %)** have a `== 2` / `!= 1` test
**guarding** it. So the u16 is not a field every reply carries — it is read when
the result says failure, which is the reader-side counterpart of
`Msg_SendTwoFieldReply`'s `{u8 = 2, u16 code}` (round 443).

**A connecting hypothesis, tested and refuted.** It was tempting to say this
explains the prefix mismatches of rounds 463-466 — server writes both, client
reads the second only sometimes. **It does not.** Of the 10 opcodes where the
client reads a strict prefix of the server's writes, only **2** are short by
exactly one `u16`; the others are short by tails like `4,4,4,4`. The envelope
finding stands on its own; it does not account for the residual, and saying so
is cheaper than a later retraction.

**A probe defect caught before publication.** The first field-2 probe asked
which callee most often receives a freshly-read 2-byte field and answered
`FUN_00778190` in **103 handlers** — a 29-byte function that is not an error
renderer. It had matched on `param_1`, a name Ghidra reuses across unrelated
functions. Excluding generic `param_N` names drops it to **19** handlers and the
dominance vanishes. This is round 447's bare-name defect in a third form: **a
name that is common rather than unique turns an artifact into a finding.**

No name filed; three still held. Nothing wired, no tag. Tests green.

## No third lever, and one cluster worth naming (round 469)

Fields 1 and 2 fell to protocol-wide levers. This round asked whether a third
exists — does some callee dominate the consumption of later fields the way a
shared envelope dominated the first two?

**Measured on both widths, and it does not.** Censusing which function most
often receives a freshly-read field, with generic `param_N` names excluded (the
defect round 468 caught):

	field width   top consumer                     handlers   sites
	2 bytes       FUN_00778190                          19      185
	4 bytes       IGIDObject::FindObjectByID            13      345

No consumer reaches 8 % of sites. **So fields 3 onward genuinely are
per-operation** and need the client's destination variables one subsystem at a
time — the SYSTEMS row's framing is confirmed rather than assumed.

**The one cluster worth having.** `IGIDObject::FindObjectByID` (`0x9c3220`) is a
map lookup — the argument's address and a container to a find helper, compared
against the container's own sentinel globals, 0 at end and otherwise the node's
value at `+0x10`.

**What its u32 argument MEANS comes from use sites, not that structure.** Of the
13 handlers passing it a freshly-read 4-byte field, five carry independently
recovered names and **every one is a per-entity event**:
`Char_OnSkinChangeResult`, `Chat_OnChatUpdate`, `Fortress_OnItemUseInterrupted`
and two `NetProcessInNavAndSkill` handlers. A skin change, a chat line, an
interrupted item use and a movement update all happen *to a particular object*,
so the field is an **entity id**.

**A caveat carried with the name**: `IGIDObject` is the dump's *interpolated*
module attribution — its plate says "Module INTERPOLATED, not asserted" — so the
class is a neighbour inference and only the leaf name is established here.

One name filed, four now held. Nothing wired, no tag. Tests green.

## Two levers measured empty, one name landed, one heuristic confirmed (round 470)

Aimed at the 69 still-unnamed dispatch handlers. **Two candidate levers, both
measured rather than assumed, and both close to empty:**

- **Transfer the client's name.** For an unnamed server handler whose *client*
  counterpart is named, the client name should say what the operation is. Of 69
  unnamed handlers, **6** have a client counterpart that is not a bare `FUN_`
  — and five of those six are `NetProcessIn*::FUN_…`, a **module attribution,
  not a name**. Real yield: **zero**.
- **Name from the refusals raised**, as round 438 did for the COS-sell handler.
  Only **11 of 67** unnamed handlers push an error code at all, and none has a
  clean single-subsystem set — round 438's case worked because all three of its
  codes were `COSERR_*`; these mix guild with fortress, teleport with party.

**One name did come out of it.** `FUN_0051bb70` (index `0x519`, payload `u32`,
replies `0xb519`) is the **party-recall handler**, on three agreeing signals and
not on where it sits: it requires interaction id `0x27`; round 455 tied `0x27`
to `NPC_FWORLD_RECALL_PARTY`; and it refuses
`UIIT_MGS_ERR_GOD_TELEPORT_HOLE_NOT_PARTY`.

**And a better result than the name.** That id check is **inlined** — no call to
`CGObjChar::HasAvailableInteraction` appears — so round 450's census of 41
*direct callers* missed it. Sweeping for the inlined form finds exactly two, and
**one of them confirms round 455's heuristic**: the reader requiring id `0x1f`
sits in the function whose own log string is *"Siege Fortress Pulley CodeName is
not registered!!"*, and round 455 had attributed `0x1f` to
`STRUCTURE_GATE_PULLEY_*` by an entirely separate route — the codename strings
between two registrations. A heuristic attribution and an instruction-level
reader agreeing on one id is the check that heuristic was missing.

One name filed, five now held. Nothing wired, no tag. Tests green.

## The held-name backlog applied (round 471)

Six names had accumulated filed-but-unapplied across rounds 451-470, which is
past the batching threshold and, more to the point, **invisible**: a row in
`recovered_names.tsv` changes nothing in the dump until the applier runs, and
this project has lost work that way before (250 of 2,079 rows were still `FUN_`
on 2026-09-20).

Applied, guards run first per round 418, **`failed 0` on both binaries**:

	server   CGObjChar::PublishAvailableInteractions   0x4a95a0
	         OpenMarket_BeginSession                   0x51b580
	         CGameServer::RefRow_AddInteraction8       0x6a7f70
	         GObjPC_HandlePartyRecallMsg_519           0x51bb70
	client   MsgStreamBuffer::Read                     0x4f7220
	         IGIDObject::FindObjectByID                0x9c3220

**One needed a second pass.** `0x4a95a0` came back `KEEPOWNER` — the applier
kept the dump's `GObjPC` prefix over the offered `CGObjChar`. That prefix is a

`PROJSTAMP` cleared so the dumps rebuild with the names in them.

## A derived table had rotted, and round 470 measured against it (round 472)

The six names of round 471 are live in the rebuilt dumps, and coverage reads
**16.2 % server / 5.2 % client** — unchanged from round 435, which is what ~31
names against 34,207 functions should look like.

**Then a call-graph lever turned up something better than a name.** Censusing
the named callees of the "unnamed" dispatch handlers, several listed *their own
recovered name* — because the probe was matching the dump's comment plate rather
than calls. That artifact pointed at a real defect:
**`docs/protocol/server_handlers.tsv` still read `FUN_<addr>` for eleven
handlers that `recovered_names.tsv` had named rounds earlier**, including
`GObjPC_HandleEndInteractionMsg_04b` (round 449), `GObjPC_HandleCOSSellMsg_0c7`
(round 438) and `GObjPC_HandlePartyRecallMsg_519` (round 470).

**So the unnamed-handler count was 58, not 69** — and round 470 measured two
levers against the inflated list, reporting "11 of 67 raise an error code" when
two of those eleven were already named. Its conclusions survive (both levers
were close to empty either way) but its denominator was wrong.

**Fixed, and then prevented.** The name column is refreshed from the dump index,
and `internal/systems.TestHandlerTableNamesAreNotStale` now fails if a handler
row reads `FUN_<addr>` while `recovered_names.tsv` names that address. It is a
pure doc-vs-doc check, so it needs no dump and runs in CI.

**The test was verified by breaking the file**: reverting one row makes it fail
with the offending index and both names, and restoring makes it pass. A rot
detector that has never been seen to fail is not a detector.

This is the fourth derived artifact in this project found rotted — after the
work queue, GROUNDING_AUDIT, and `message_handlers.tsv`'s sender column (round
465). The common shape is that **every existing check asks whether a file is
well-formed, never whether it agrees with the file it was derived from.**

Nothing wired beyond the test, no tag. `go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...` green.

## The rot was systemic, not one table (round 473)

Round 472 found `server_handlers.tsv` carrying `FUN_<addr>` for eleven
already-named handlers and guarded it with a test. The obvious question is
whether that table was special. **It was not.**

	described_but_unnamed.tsv    26 stale rows of 690
	handler_payloads.tsv         10 stale rows of 163

**`described_but_unnamed.tsv` is the one that mattered.** Its own header says it
lists "server functions that `docs/` cites and the dump **still calls FUN_**",
so it is a *worklist* — and 26 of its entries were finished work still sitting
on it, which is precisely the failure that killed the RE_COMPLETION work queue.
Those rows were **removed**, not renamed: a named function does not belong in a
list of unnamed ones. `handler_payloads.tsv`'s name column is descriptive, so it
was refreshed in place.

**The guard now covers all three**, with a per-file remedy so the failure
message says what to do rather than only what is wrong — drop the row for the
worklist, refresh the cell for the others.

**Each new subtest was verified by breaking its own file.** Injecting one stale
row into `handler_payloads.tsv` and one into `described_but_unnamed.tsv` makes
each subtest fail with its own remedy, and restoring makes them pass. Round 472
only ever demonstrated a failure against `server_handlers.tsv`; a green subtest
on a file it has never failed on is not evidence about that file.

Three derived tables are now guarded against disagreeing with
`recovered_names.tsv`. The one still known unreliable is
`message_handlers.tsv`'s `server_senders` column (round 465), which names
functions that open no message at all — a different defect, needing a different
check, and not fixed here.

Nothing wired beyond the test, no tag. `go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...` green.

## A third send mechanism, and round 473's dismissal retracted (round 474)

Round 473 called `message_handlers.tsv`'s `server_senders` column unreliable,
generalising from round 465's reading of one function that "opens no message at
all". **Checking that generalisation found a gap in my own sweep instead.**

That column lists senders for **25 opcodes my sweep had none for**. Of the 40
functions behind them, 39 open no message directly — **and all 39 call
`Msg_SendTwoFieldReply`**, which opens the message itself with the opcode in
**ECX**. A caller of that helper sends without ever opening one, so a sweep
keyed on opens misses it by construction, and the helper has 160 call sites. The
old census was right; the dismissal was wrong.

**Third idiom added: 233 -> 262 opcodes**, and every cross-validation measure
improves against the client:

	comparable opcodes   133 -> 162
	agree on field 1      98 % -> 99 %
	prefix-match          87 % -> 89 %
	exact match           33 % -> 51 %

**The exact-match jump is a confirmation, not just a gain.** Helper-sent
messages carry `{u8, u16}` and the client reads exactly `1,2` for them — the
failure envelope rounds 467-468 recovered from a completely different direction.

**The controls caught a bug mid-flight.** The first patch wrote helper rows into
the same `defaultdict(list)` the appends use, which clobbered richer rows and
let later appends push onto the `[1,2]`: `0xb045` went `1,4,1,VAR,2 -> 1,2` and
`0xb04b` went `1 -> 1,2,1`. Both are standing round-462 controls with
known-correct values, which is exactly why they caught it — a control that is
merely green tells you nothing. Helper rows now live in a separate dict, emitted
only where no direct-open row exists for the same `(opcode, function)`.

Nothing wired, no tag. `go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...` green.

## The open helpers, and two opcodes named (round 475)

Round 474's next probe was the 1,086 appends whose message is opened inside some
other function. **48 functions are shaped like that opener** — small, more than
one caller, and they open a message. That is the route to those appends, and it
doubles as a worklist: two of the 48 were entries on round 447's unnamed-helper
list and now have an opcode against them.

**`0x34d2` is the battle arena.** 23 senders, and every one carrying a name is a
battle-arena class of the engine's own — `CBattleArenaInfoFlag`,
`CBattleArenaInfoPoint`, `CBattleArenaInfoOccupy`,
`BATTLE_ARENA_EVENT_HANDLERS::OnUpdate_Arena`.

**`0xb483` is the training camp.** `TrainingCamp_SendReply_b483` (`0x4e4580`)
fetches the singleton at `DAT_00d6a99c` — which the engine's own
`CMainProcess::GetSingleton_CTrainingCampManager` reads — and `0xb483` replies
to index `0x483`, whose handler calls `TrainingCamp_FindMemberByKey`. Two
signals; the client handler's `UI_TC` module agrees and proves nothing alone.

**A general lever, and its measured shortfall.**
`docs/protocol/opcode_subsystems.tsv` attributes an opcode to a subsystem when
every named sender's class prefix agrees, excluding generic module attributions.
It gives **55 opcodes — but only 11 on two or more agreeing senders**; the other
44 rest on a single sender, which is a lead.

**And it misses its own best case.** `0x34d2` is *absent* from that file,
because `CBattleArenaInfoFlag` and `CBattleArenaInfoPoint` are different
prefixes even though they are one subsystem. Exact-prefix equality rejects the
strongest evidence in the set, so the file under-reports and the opcode is
recorded by hand. A stem-based grouping would reach it; saying so beats shipping
a number that looks like a ceiling when it is an artifact of the test.

One name filed. Nothing wired, no tag. `go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...` green.

## The stem fix, and what it was actually worth (round 476)

Round 475 predicted its opcode→subsystem file under-reported, because exact
class-prefix grouping rejected `0x34d2` — 23 senders, all battle arena, but
`CBattleArenaInfoFlag` and `CBattleArenaInfoPoint` are different *prefixes*.
Grouping by a normalised **stem** instead (uppercase, drop the MSVC leading `C`,
drop underscores, longest common prefix) reduces both that and
`BATTLE_ARENA_EVENT_HANDLERS` to `BATTLEARENA`.

**The prediction held, and the lift was one opcode.**

	round 475, exact prefix   11 attributions (+ 44 single-sender leads)
	round 476, stem           12 attributions
	  gained  0x34d2 BATTLEARENA strength 12   <- the predicted miss
	          0xb155 MAKESTUFF   strength 2
	  lost    0x3058 CGObjChar                 <- correctly

`0x34d2` arrives as **the strongest row in the file by a wide margin** — twelve
agreeing senders against two for everything else. So the one case the old test
missed was the best evidence it had, which is the honest size of this: not a
broad gain, but the recovery of the case that mattered. A fix that had *not*
moved `0x34d2` would have meant the diagnosis was wrong.

**`0x3058` was dropped deliberately**: its senders are `CGObjChar` classes, and
that is a base class every character shares, not a subsystem. It now sits in the
generic exclusion list beside `GObjPC` and `CMainProcess`, for the same reason —
it says what a thing *is*, not which system owns the message.

**The 44 single-sender rows were removed, not re-labelled.** Round 475 shipped
them alongside real attributions with a `strength` column to distinguish them.
One named sender is a lead, and putting leads and findings in one table is
precisely the misuse this project keeps having to correct; they remain
derivable from `payload_layouts.tsv`.

Nothing wired, no tag. `go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...` green.

## The open-helper route works, and reaches 3 % (round 477)

Round 475 found 48 open-helper-shaped functions and called them the route to the
1,086 appends round 474 could not attribute. Implemented and measured, the route
is real and **narrow**.

	unattributed appends   1,086  ->  1,055     (31 recovered, ~3 %)
	sender rows              458  ->    475     (19 via a helper)
	distinct opcodes         262  ->    262     (unchanged)

**A filter the first pass missed, caught by its own output.** "Small,
multi-caller, opens a message" is not enough: a helper that **sends** its
message has closed it, so a caller's later appends cannot belong to it. **26 of
the 46 candidates send**, and including them produced a `0x3405` row attributed
through `CGObjPC::FUN_004f0a00` — which round 448 read as opening, appending
*and sending*. The contradiction with an earlier reading is what exposed it.
Requiring no send through slot `0x27c` drops those 26 and removes 12 wrong rows;
`0x3864` then appears correctly, which is round 465's hand-verified example.

**Cross-validation is unchanged** — 162 opcodes, 99 % field 1, 89 % prefix,
51 % exact — because the added rows are for opcodes the client comparison does
not reach. An increment that moves no validation metric is worth saying plainly
rather than dressing up.

**So the 1,055 that remain do not arrive this way.** Round 475's prediction that
this route would reach them was wrong by an order of magnitude; the mechanism
exists but explains 3 % of the gap, and whatever carries the rest is still
unfound.

Nothing wired, no tag. `go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...` green.

## The 1,055 are sub-builders, and two things block attributing them (round 478)

Round 477 left the question of what carries the appends that never see an open.
**They are sub-builders: functions handed an already-open message by a caller.**
Round 454 proved one — `FUN_0050faf0` opens `0xb045` and passes the message to
vtable slot `0x38c`, which appends to it — and
`CGObjChar::PublishAvailableInteractions` duly appears in the unattributed set,
which is the prediction coming true rather than a new guess.

**Attributing them one hop up reaches a quarter:**

	sub-builder candidates                   261
	  callers send exactly ONE opcode         33   attributable
	  callers send SEVERAL opcodes            31   ambiguous by construction
	  no direct caller that sends anything    197

**The 197 split into two different problems**, which is why one fix will not do:

	no direct call site at all (virtual-only)   77
	direct callers that do not themselves send ~120

The first are reached only through a vtable, so a direct-call graph cannot see
them by construction — the same class of miss as round 450's reader census and
round 470's inlined check. The second have a caller, but the *opener* is two or
more levels above, so a one-hop walk stops short.

**The 33 are deliberately NOT merged into `payload_layouts.tsv`.** Being called
by a function that sends opcode X is not the same as receiving *that* message:
the only function where the pass is actually read is the round-454 case. Adding
33 rows on "presumably the message it was handed" would put an inference beside
three mechanically-verified classes in one file, which is the mixing this
project has had to correct twice already (round 476's leads, round 465's sender
column).

Nothing wired, no tag. `go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...` green.

## Vtable edges for the virtual-only sub-builders (round 479)

Round 478 named two blockers for the sub-builders; this took the **77 that are
virtual-only**, reached through a vtable and invisible to a direct-call graph.
Method: each sub-builder's slot offset(s), then which *senders* call through
that offset, and attribute when they all send one opcode.

**The first run failed its own control, and the cause is a tooling hazard worth
more than the result.** `CGObjChar::PublishAvailableInteractions` — reached via
slot `0x38c` from `FUN_0050faf0`, which sends `0xb045` (round 454) — came back
with *no offset at all*. The offsets were being read from each function's dump
plate, and **applying a name replaces that plate with the evidence text**, so
the `slot N (offset …)` line disappears for exactly the named functions. 25 of
the 261 sub-builders had lost it, including the control. Recorded in
`RE_LOOP.md`: plates are regenerated per rebuild and describe what has been
named, not what the binary holds.

**Fixed by reading offsets from the vtables themselves** (`vt_server.json`,
round 418). The control then passes — `0x38c` → **`0xb045`** — and:

	virtual-only sub-builders              77
	  found in a class vtable              67   (10 in none: likely callback arrays)
	  offset called by one opcode's senders 10   attributable
	  ... by several opcodes' senders       46   ambiguous
	  ... by no sender                      11

**The ten attributions are internally consistent in a way a broken method would
not be**: overrides of the *same slot on different classes* land on the *same
opcode*. Slot 310 feeds `0x3057` on `CGObjNPCNPC`, `CGObjPC` and
`CGObjCOS_GoldPet`; slot 292 feeds `0x7005` on `CGObjMobile` and `CGObjPC`; slot
227 feeds `0xb045` for both the control and `CGObjPC`'s override of it.

**The 46 ambiguous are round 433's rule in action.** Pooling every sender that
calls "offset `0x38c`" regardless of the receiver's type over-collects across
class hierarchies, where one offset names unrelated methods. Separating them
needs the receiver's static type at each call site, which the disassembly does
not carry.

**Not merged into `payload_layouts.tsv`**, on round 478's reasoning: these are
edge inferences, and only the control's message-pass has actually been read.

Nothing wired, no tag. `go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...` green.

## Party gap bonus in the kill-EXP level-difference scale (Formula_ExpScaleByLevelDiff) (round 480)

`Formula_ExpScaleByLevelDiff` (`0x0040ffe0`) had been shipped without its party
half since 2026-09-15: the bonus it adds for a target well above the receiver
was recorded as "not modelled, deliberately", because the gate in front of it
(`pc[0x72e]` non-null with bit 0 of the party's `+0x10` set) was not
identified and a bonus with an unknown precondition would have applied to every
kill. The gate has been identifiable since the party size cap was read: bit 0
is the **exp-sharing** flag, per `CParty::CheckCanJoin` (`0x514560`), which caps
a party at 8 when it is set and 4 when it is clear and raises
`0x2c13 UIIT_MSG_PARTYERR_MEMBER_FULL_EXP_SHARED_PARTY` /
`0x2c14 ..._NONEEXP_SHARED_PARTY` (`docs/protocol/party.md`). This round read the
function again with objdump and wired it.

	41000d  MOV EDX,[EAX + 0x1c] ; CALL EDX ; JE none   <- IsPC (vtable slot 7)
	410018  MOV EAX,[ESI + 0x1cb8] ; TEST ; JE none     <- pc[0x72e], the party
	410022  MOV CL,0x1 ; TEST BYTE [EAX + 0x10],CL      <- exp-sharing bit
	410029  MOV EDX,[ESI + 0x34] ; MOV EDX,[EDX + 0x18]
	410033  CMP BYTE [EDX + 0x88],CL ; JNE china        <- Country == 1 (Europe)?
	41003b  europe: >=9 FLD dword [0xb45ddc]  >=7 [0xb45dd8]  >=5 [0xb45b8c]
	410062  china:  >=9 FLD dword [0xb45dd4]  >=7 [0xb45b8c]  >=5 [0xb45dd0]
	41008b  FLD [ESP + 0x8] ; FADD qword [0xb45ac0]     <- bonus + 1.0

Every threshold is `CMP EAX,N ; JL` on `victim - receiver`, so inclusive. The
five `.rdata` floats read, as `FLD dword` says they must be read: `0xb45dd0`
0.15, `0xb45b8c` 0.30, `0xb45dd4` 0.45, `0xb45dd8` 0.60, `0xb45ddc` 0.90 (the
last is the same float `ExpWindowNearBelow` already cites). `.rdata` formula
constants are shared between the dump build and the on-disk exe.

**ESI is the receiver of the experience.** The call sites load it from the
register whose `+0x1cd8`/`+0x1cdc` (the mastery-lag scale) they have just read:
`0x410233 -> 0x41023b`, `0x410660 -> 0x410668`, `0x41076f -> 0x410777`. The byte
at its ref object's `+0x88` is Country (column 14; 0 China, 1 Europe, 3 either),
the byte the equip check compares for `0x182f STRGERR_COUNTRY_MISMATCH`.

**What moved.** `leveldata.ExpDiffScale(killer, victim, expSharingParty,
europe)` adds `ExpDiffPartyBonus` when `expSharingParty`, keeping the bare-1.0
cutoff and the `[1, 4.0]` clamp; `Table.KillExp` takes `expSharingParty` and
passes `europe = false`, because every srrevamp character is China
(`character.ValidGender`, `equipment.Refusal`). The kill path calls the new
`session.killExpFor`, whose gate is `inParty`: every srrevamp party shares
experience (`party.MaxSize` is the shared cap), and the engine tests the party
pointer rather than the member count, so a party of one earns it too.
**Changed in round 485:** a party of one no longer earns it. The engine only
ever creates a party with two members (an accepted invite), so the pointer
test never meets a party of one through creation; srrevamp's create-alone path
is its own, and paid a solo bonus for clicking "create party".

The visible change: a partied level-10 killing a level-15 goes from 1.24x to
1.39x, and against a level-19 from 1.36x to 1.81x; the China peak is 1.84 and
Europe's 2.29, so the 4.0 cap stays unreachable. Solo kills are unchanged.

**Tests.** `leveldata.TestExpDiffPartyBonus` pins the ladder at gaps
-5/0/4/5/6/7/8/9/20 for both arms; `TestExpDiffScalePartyBonus` pins the whole
scale for a level-10 party killer (7 -> 1.00 through 30 -> 1.84, Europe 1.54 /
1.90 / 2.26 / 2.29) and sweeps 1..140 x party x Country inside `[1, 4.0]`;
`TestExpUnitAndKillExp` keeps its four solo values and adds the partied
114 / 36 / 432 / 28; `session.TestKillExpPartyGapBonus` checks 327 with no hub
and no party, 432 for a party of one and for both members of a party of two.
Negative case run: with the production files reverted to the old formula (only
the signatures adapted), the partied `KillExp(10, 20)` returns 327 against 432
and `ExpDiffScale(10, 15, party)` 1.24 against 1.39. `go test -count=1 -p 1
./...` green.

## Enforce the 2-12 byte guild name in both guild stores' Create (round 481)

The guild name length was recovered on 2026-09-17 (`docs/protocol/guild.md`,
"Size and level"): `CGuildManager::HandleCreateGuild` (`0x00514ce0`) tests the
name's `std::string` size with `if (local_34 - 2U < 0xb)` and otherwise sends
`Msg_SendTwoFieldReply(0x4c18)`, `UIIT_MSG_GUILDERR_INVALID_GUILDNAME_LEN`
(`error_codes.md`; `recovered_names.tsv` row `00514ce0`). `guild.MinNameLength`,
`MaxNameLength`, `ValidName` and `ErrInvalidNameLength` were written then, and
nothing called them from `Create`: a one-character guild name was still legal.

**The order, re-read from the dump this round.** The handler first calls
`FUN_00514b20`, whose last test is
`return (-(uint)(in_EAX[0x72f] != 0) & 0x4c16) + 1;` -- `0x4c17`
`GUILDERR_MEMBER_OF_ANOTHER_GUILD` for a character already in a guild, 1
otherwise -- and only on 1 does it reach the length test. `0x4c1a`
`GUILDERR_SAME_GUILDNAME_EXIST` is raised by no function in
`/var/tmp/decomp_server` (grepped as `4c1a` and `19482`), so uniqueness is
settled after both, by the job `FUN_005c5f90` sends on
(`CGuildMamager__SendOlappedGuildJobReqToSM`). `FUN_005c5f90` also returns
`0x4c18` for an empty name (`*(int *)(EBX + 0x14) == 0`), a second guard the
length test already covers.

**What moved.** `SQLStore.Create` checks `ValidName` after its membership query
and before the `INSERT` whose unique index is the uniqueness check.
`MemStore.Create` is reordered to membership, then length, then the name-taken
map (it used to test the name first). The `Store.Create` comment states the
order and its grounding; the name-length comment in `guild.go` is marked
ENFORCED and records the one divergence: the engine counts bytes of a narrow
`std::string` (capacity `0xf` at initialisation) in the client's codepage, Go's
`len()` counts UTF-8 bytes, so ASCII names agree and a non-ASCII name can be
refused here that the engine would accept. `session.guildErrorMessage` maps
`ErrInvalidNameLength` to `guild name must be 2 to 12 characters`; the client
already shows `"Error: " + error`, so no client change.

The visible change: creating a guild named `""`, `"A"` or anything over 12
bytes shows `Error: guild name must be 2 to 12 characters`. Names of 2 to 12
bytes work as before (`Silk Legion`, 11 bytes, in the existing tests).

**Tests.** `guild.TestMemStoreCreateEnforcesNameLength` and
`guild.TestCreateEnforcesNameLength` (Postgres): `""`, `"A"`, 13 and 40 bytes
give `ErrInvalidNameLength`; `"Ab"` by the same leader then succeeds, proving the
refusals wrote nothing; 12 bytes by a second leader succeeds; `"A"` by the now
guilded leader gives `ErrAlreadyInGuild`, not the length error; the SQL test
also reads back exactly one member. `session.TestGuildCreateRejectsBadNameLength`
drives `OpGuildCreate` through `LoginHandler` + `GuildHandler` over a
`MemStore`: `"A"` and 13 bytes answer with the error and `GuildID` 0, 12 bytes
founds a guild. Negative case run: with the four production files reverted, all
three fail -- `Create("")` returns nil error in both stores and `"A"` founds
guild 1 over the wire. `go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...` green.

## Refuse an untradeable item at offer time (CGStorage::TradeOfferItem 0x183a) (round 482)

The trade flag was already enforced, but at the wrong time. Since the capability
flags were recovered, `executeTrade` has refused an item whose `CanTrade`
(itemdata column 16, `fCanTrade`) is clear. It did that only after both players
had confirmed. Until then the offer was stored and sent to the partner as
`OpTradeOfferUpdated`, and the trade died at the final confirm.

**The grounding, re-read from the dump this round.**
`CGStorage::TradeOfferItem` (`0x00526910`, `error_emitters.tsv` line 115) is the
handler for putting an item into the trade window:

	if (*(byte *)(param_2 + 3) < 0xd) return 0x1806;
	piVar2 = (int *)GetItem(*(byte *)(param_2 + 3));
	if (piVar2 == (int *)0x0) return 0x1809;
	iVar3 = (**(code **)(*piVar2 + 0xc4))();
	if (iVar3 == 0) return 0x183a;
	...
	uVar1 = TradeMgr::OfferItemToPartner(DAT_00d6a95c, param_1, ...);

`0xc4` is vtable slot 49. `0x0057de80` is its base stub, which names itself
`"## Illegal ##  IGObj::CanTrade Entered!"`
(`docs/protocol/item_capability_flags.md`, "How it was found"). `0x183a` is
`UIIT_MSG_STRGERR_CANNOT_BE_TRADED` (`error_codes.md`). The refusal comes before
the item reaches `OfferItemToPartner`, so the partner is never told about it.

**What moved.** `handleTradeSetOffer` now takes `inv` and `items`.
`TradeHandler` already received both, and `cmd/server/main.go` already passes
`refItems`. Before `trades.SetOffer`, the handler calls the new
`offerTradeFlagRefusal`. It resolves the offered slot through `offerItemID`,
looks the item up, and returns `that item cannot be traded` when `CanTrade` is
false. A refusal answers `OpTradeOfferResult{OK: false}`. It does not store the
offer, clear either side's confirmation, or send the partner anything. A store
error returns `trade: checking offer: ...`.

These cases give no refusal and leave validation to the commit:
- no reference data or no inventory wired;
- no item offered;
- an empty slot, or one that holds too few;
- an item the tables do not know.

The first and last follow the same "no opinion" rule as `tradeFlagRefusal`. The
empty or short slot is left alone because `executeTrade` already re-validates
it ("offer no longer valid").

Only `0x183a` is modelled. `TradeOfferItem` has five other refusals, and none of
them is modelled. They are read off the same function body, and they are named
here only by the engine's own strings (`error_codes.md`) or not at all:
- `0x1806` when the slot byte is below `0xd`;
- `0x1809` when `GetItem` finds nothing in the slot;
- a bare `return 3`, after the `CanTrade` check, when both dwords at `+0x20`
  and `+0x24` of the item's `piVar2[0xd]` record are zero. That field is not
  identified;
- `0x18b6` `UIIT_MSG_COSPETERR_CANT_TRADE`, when vtable slot `0x54` returns 1
  and the object vtable slot `0x4bc` returns has mask `2` (bit 1) set in the byte at
  `+0x38` of its `+4` record;
- `0x18fa` `UIIT_CTL_NASRUN_NOT_TRADE`, when vtable slot `0x470` returns 1 and
  `FUN_00498610()` returns non-zero.

The `0x18fa` gate is **unnamed**. `FUN_00498610` (`getfn.sh 00498610`) reads
the item's TID word and returns true unless bit 1 is clear and
`(t & 0x1c) == 0xc`, `(t & 0x60) == 0x20`, `(t & 0x780) == 0x700`. With the
layout in `damage_pipeline.md` ("The TID layout") that is TypeID1 3, TypeID2 1,
TypeID3 14. For a matching item it calls `FUN_009754a0` and `FUN_009755c0`
and returns `FUN_00975560() == 0`. `ITEM_FORMAT.md` puts avatars at TypeID3 13
and 14 and the job suit at TypeID3 7, so this is not a job-suit test. Neither
vtable slot `0x470` nor `FUN_00975560` is named, and what the gate refuses is
not recovered beyond its error string.

`TradeOfferItem` deals only with the item. srrevamp's placeholder
`OpTradeSetOffer` carries gold and an item in one request, so a refusal also
leaves that request's gold unstored. The stored offer, gold included, stays
what it was, and a gold-only request is still accepted.

The check runs before `trades.SetOffer`, which is where srrevamp learns whether
the character is in a trade at all. So a character who is not trading and names
an item slot now gets one `inventory.Store.List` before `not trading`. A store
failure during that read returns a handler error, and the gateway closes the
session on a handler error ("handler error, closing session", `gateway.go`).
`executeTrade`'s store errors already end the same way.

The `executeTrade` check stays, and its comment now calls it the commit-time
re-check. An offer names a bag slot, not an item, so an inventory move between
offering and confirming can put an untradeable item into the offered slot.

The visible change: a starter (`_A_DEF`) or quest (`ITEM_QNO_`) item put into
the trade window is refused at once, and the client shows
`Offer failed: that item cannot be traded` (`World3D.gd`'s existing label). The
partner never sees the item. No client change.

**Tests.** The `trade_test.go` fixture is now `setupTradeTestWithItems(t, items)`
(`setupTradeTest` passes nil). It also records the trade hub and both character
ids, and `startTrade` is factored out of `TestTradeFullFlow`.
`TestTradeOfferRefusesUntradeableItem` uses a refdata `MemStore` where item 100
(Aria's) has `CanTrade` false and item 200 (Bram's) has it true. It checks five
things:
- Aria's offer of item 100 gets `OK=false` with `cannot be traded`, and
  `SessionOf(aria).OfferA` stays at slot -1 with no gold.
- The next packet Bram reads after his own offer is his `OpTradeOfferResult`
  OK, not an update about Aria's item.
- Aria then gets Bram's `OpTradeOfferUpdated` (slot 0, qty 5).
- After Bram confirms, a retried refused offer leaves `ConfirmedB` true.
- A gold-only offer is accepted and reaches Bram.

`TestOfferTradeFlagRefusal` runs over `inventory.NewMemStore(nil)`. The
no-refdata, no-inventory, slot -1, unknown-item, empty-slot and short-slot cases
give "". `CanTrade` false gives the reason, `CanTrade` true gives "", and a
lookup error that is not `ErrItemNotFound` is returned as an error.

Negative case run: `trade.go` was reverted, with a test-only stub standing in
for the helper so the package compiled. Both tests failed. Aria's offer came
back `OK:true`, the stored `OfferA` was `{Gold:50 ItemSlot:0 Quantity:1}`, and
Bram's next packet was `0x00D9` `OpTradeOfferUpdated`. The existing trade
tests stay green. `go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...` green.

## Mastery total cap is Country-selected: flat 330 for China (Mastery_LevelUp 0x59c4e0) (round 483)

`session.MasteryTotalCapPerLevel = 3` capped the sum of a character's mastery
levels at 3 x its character level. That number was never read out of a binary:
it was extrapolated from one account of a retail total of 240 at the level-80
cap. `Mastery_LevelUp` (`0x0059c4e0`) was read in full on 2026-09-16 and has no
`3 x level` branch. It switches on a byte at `(charData+0x18)+0x88` and applies
one of three rules. The 3 stayed because that byte was not identified. This
round identifies it.

	59c53c  movzx eax,BYTE PTR [eax+0x88]     <- the character's ref object
	59c543  sub eax,0x0 ; je 0x59c5d9         <- 0: flat cap
	59c54c  sub eax,0x1 ; je 0x59c567         <- 1: 240.0 and level + level
	59c551  sub eax,0x1 ; je 0x59c5ed         <- 2: straight past the cap
	59c55a  mov [esp+0xc],0x3801              <- anything else
	59c5e6  cmp eax,0x14a ; jg 0x59c5cc       <- 0: sum + requested > 330 -> 0x3805
	59c57e  fcomp QWORD PTR ds:0xb46130       <- 1: 240.0 (bytes 00000000 00006e40)

Those addresses are the on-disk exe. The Ghidra dump has the same shape
(`(sum + param_3) < 0x14b`). They agree because they are one build: the on-disk
exe also has the dump's x20 death-penalty branch, lea-encoded at `0x4e6aa2`
(`lea esi,[esi+esi*4] ; add esi,esi ; add esi,esi`). The 2026-09-18 entry "Two
server builds" says otherwise; it missed this branch, which has no `imul`. So
330 is **this server binary's own rule**. **Nothing here shows that retail used
330**, and the 2026-09-15 worry that this is a private-server binary still
stands. What this round does is ship the binary's own rule in place of an
extrapolation that no binary contains.

**The selector is Country, identified by a use-site.**
`CGItemEquip::CanBeEquipedAt` (`0x00497070`) walks the same path,
`*(*(obj+0x34)+0x18)+0x88`, on both the item and the character. It refuses with
`0x182f UIIT_MSG_STRGERR_COUNTRY_MISMATCH` unless the two bytes match or the
item's is 3. `+0x88` is where `RefObjCommon_ExtractData` stores common column 14,
and `ITEM_FORMAT.md` pins column 14 as Country (0 China, 1 Europe, 3 either).
`RefObjChar_ExtractData` (`0x006a58f0`) passes its own `this` to the same
extractor at `0x6a5908`, so a character's `+0x88` is its Country too. China
characters wear Country-0 gear through that check, so China is selector 0.
Round 480 read the same byte as Country in `Formula_ExpScaleByLevelDiff`.

So a China character's total is a **flat 330**, with no level term. Europe's is
`min(240, 2 x level)`. Selector 2 has no cap. `ITEM_FORMAT.md`'s Country
vocabulary is 0, 1 and 3, so which race 2 is stays unidentified, and the code
names it for what it does. The
decision recorded in the 2026-09-15 and 2026-09-16 entries to keep the 3 is
reversed, and those entries now say so where they stand.

**What moved.**
- `skill.go`: `MasteryTotalCapPerLevel` is replaced by `MasteryTotalCapChina = 330`
  and `MasteryTotalCapEurope = 240`.
- `masteryTotalRefusal(country, total, requested, charLevel)` returns the engine's
  code for the total-cap branch: `0x3805`, `0x3801`, or 0.
- `characterCountry` returns `equipment.CountryChina`. Every srrevamp character
  is China (`character.ValidGender`; `equipment.Refusal` refuses a Europe item on
  that ground).
- `RaiseMasteryHandler` keeps the engine's order: the total cap
  (`"mastery total at cap"`, or `"invalid mastery"` for `0x3801`), then the
  character-level cap (`0x3804`), then skill points (`0x3802`).
- Client: `hud_panels.gd` shows `total / 330` and greys LEVEL UP at 330.
  `MASTERY_TOTAL_CAP_PER_LEVEL` becomes `MASTERY_TOTAL_CAP := 330`. The
  grey-out reason is now checked in the engine's order: the total first, then
  the character level, then skill points. When both caps apply, the window
  gives the reason the server would refuse with.
- The engine's sum (`FUN_0059e7c0`) skips a mastery whose status byte
  (`*(entry+0x10)+0xc`) is 3. `FUN_0059d6f0`, the function's first check,
  treats the same state as "no such mastery" (`0x3801`). srrevamp stores no such
  state, so it sums every stored mastery. `masteryTotalRefusal`'s doc says so.
  srrevamp also still skips that first check.
- Docs: `SYSTEMS.md` anchors the row on `MasteryTotalCapChina`, and `UI_TODO.md`
  no longer says "3×level".

The visible change: a low-level character can raise more masteries at once. At
level 5, three masteries at 5 (total 15) used to be refused on a fourth as
"mastery total at cap"; now the fourth raises. At level 20 the total used to
stop at 60; now each mastery can reach 20 until the total hits 330. At level 120
the total now stops at 330 where it used to stop at 360.

**Tests.**
- `session.TestMasteryTotalRefusal` pins both constants and every selector:
  - China: 329+1 at level 1 is allowed (no level term), 330+1 at level 120 is
    `0x3805`, 0+1 is allowed.
  - Europe: 239+1 and 240+1 at level 120 (allowed, then `0x3805`), and 99+1 and
    100+1 at level 50 (allowed, then `0x3805`).
  - Country 2 at 100000 is allowed; countries 3 and 255 are `0x3801`.
- `session.TestRaiseMasteryTotalCapIsFlatForChina` drives the handler over the
  wire:
  - Level 5 with Bicheon 5: raising Bicheon is `mastery at level cap`.
  - Level 5 with 257/258/259 at 5: raising 273 gives NewLevel 1.
  - Level 120 at total 329: raising 259 gives 90. At 120/120/90, raising 273 is
    `mastery total at cap`.

Negative case run: with `skill.go` reverted and only the handler test kept, the
test failed twice. Level 5 at total 15 raising 273 got `mastery total at cap`.
Level 120 at total 330 raising 273 was allowed (NewLevel 1).
`go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...` is green. On the render box,
`client/tools/remote_godot.sh tests` ran 77 suites with 0 failing, and `check`
compiled 239 scripts. A QA render with
`SRREVAMP_QA_SKILL_STATE="sp=9,level=5,258=5,259=5,273=5" --panels skill` printed
`QA SKILL: Bicheon Lv 0, 9 SP, char Lv 5, total 15/330 -> LEVEL UP enabled`.
Under 3 x level the same state reads 15/15, disabled. A second QA render, with
`"sp=9,level=120,257=120,258=120,259=90"`, applies both caps to Bicheon. It
printed `Bicheon Lv 120, 9 SP, char Lv 120, total 330/330 -> LEVEL UP disabled:
Total mastery cap reached (330 / 330).` The old order checked the character
level first, so it would have given the character-level reason instead. That
is read from the code; the old order was not rendered.

## No 120 cap on a single mastery, and its first point is free (Mastery_LevelUp 0x59c4e0) (round 484)

`session.MasteryLevelCap = 120` refused to raise any mastery past 120. The
2026-09-15 entry read that cap off `Mastery_LevelUp` (`0x0059c4e0`) as "the cost
loop refuses to go past it". `masteryUpCost(0)` also charged the first point in
